It adds durable ExperienceRef(run_id, kind, occurrence_id) values based on existing occurrence identities and internal immutable ExperienceRecord, trial-centered ExperienceNode, ExperienceQuery(task_id, run_id, as_of), and ExperienceState views. replay_experience_graph() first uses the validated run replay path, then attaches the exact committed decision, explanation, proposal, artifact-creation, outcome, evidence, evaluation, and completed-trial records. It does not change coordinator, event-store, artifact-store, existing identity, event-byte, or package-root callable contracts.

Parent edges follow declared parent artifact occurrences to their producing trials. Relations preserve parent order and deduplicate; returned nodes sort by (logical_step, trial_id). Ancestors exclude self, siblings include self, frontier returns visible causal leaves rather than archive members, and a trace covers the target trial plus its accessible ancestors, with records sorted by event sequence plus a fixed kind order. Historical as_of boundaries are inclusive, including bootstrap step zero.

One private access predicate enforces matching task and run, inclusive logical time, local occurrence, visibility, and synthetic retraction. All inaccessible direct targets raise the same content-free ExperienceAccessDenied; collection queries omit inaccessible nodes and do not cross them. The hidden, retracted, and non-local sets exist only to test the filtering contract. They are not a public policy abstraction and establish no Milestone 11 governance contract.

M3.2 implements NoMemory, AncestorsOnly, and BestSibling with direct max_records=20 and max_chars=8_000 defaults. None and NoMemory() add no declaration, wrapper, identity input, fact, or trial policy. A non-default ContextSpec is the next run-identity input after the M1/M2 segments and is declared after bootstrap. A generic search wrapper stamps its PolicyRef into successor TrialSpec values; a separate generic coordinator operation selects or reloads the exact bundle. No coordinator branch depends on a policy or graph relation.

Without pull access, selection follows PolicyDecisionMade → PolicyDecisionExplained → ContextSelected → ProposalSubmitted; with pull access, grant issuance and audited operations sit between selection and proposal. Replay validates declaration authority, ordering, uniqueness, observed version, strictly prior visible references, and exact source values, then returns the committed bundle without invoking the selector or renderer. Context record/render usage remains separate from task Usage.

M3.3 adds run-level PullAccess, durable ExperienceSpec and per-successor ExperienceGrant, scoped pull operations, exact observations/comparisons, and cumulative ExperienceUsage. The serialized access spec follows any ContextSpec in run identity. None contributes no identity segment, event, grant, reader, or compatibility change.

The local grant fixes task, run, trial, and as_of=logical_step - 1, then enforces operation, result, record, and independently rendered-character bounds. Each structurally valid call commits an attempt before validation and then exactly one success, denial, or exhaustion. Attempt 21 under the default 20-operation limit is charged as operation 21 and audited as exhausted. Successes store the exact returned value; replay holds each success to the shared deterministic contract against committed sources and returns the committed value without re-running live retrieval, traversal, or rendering logic. The reader holds only its grant, a view of its own committed operations, a grant-scoped graph built once per grant, and a trial-bound append capability for the permitted audit facts. Identity and visibility remain single-user stubs. Principal authorization, licensing, and federation policy are deliberately deferred; future-information leakage and observation recording are not.

Evaluate push-only context, pull-only exploration, combined access, and no-memory baselines under equal budgets.

M3.4 adds no new lifecycle event. Durable and callable proposals gain an ordered derived_from tuple whose empty default is canonically omitted. A small application contract reconstructs the trial observation ledger from committed context selections and successful pull results, then serves both live completion and proposal replay. The coordinator applies resource exhaustion, derivation policy, and reported proposer failure in that order.

RunExperienceUsage is a derived application view. It sums committed bundle usage and the final cumulative pull ledger once per grant. RunSummary carries both memory declarations and this projection; RunComparison allows different memory declarations and reports exact equality flags. The canonical examples/03_experience_reuse/ experiment closes the milestone with all four memory variants under identical non-memory declarations and budgets.

docs.title: Milestone 4: durable local kernel
docs.text: Status: complete (July 24, 2026; #4, #47). The implementation uses filesystem content-addressed artifacts, an append-only SQLite event stream, explicit component manifests, atomic storage composition, and shared replay/resume validation.

docs.title: SQLite object and transition store
docs.text:
Store immutable domain objects as normalized append-only records or content-addressed envelopes. Store lifecycle changes in an append-only event ledger. Creation of an object and its corresponding transition event occurs in one transaction.

Add:

  • optimistic event-stream concurrency;
  • durable run, trial, work-item, usage, population, and experience projections;
  • stable idempotency keys and logical steps;
  • exact context bundles and experience-query results;
  • as-of search-state reconstruction;
  • explicit schema versions and migrations.

Object records are authoritative for object content. Events are authoritative for the fact that transitions occurred. Projections are disposable and rebuildable.

docs.title: Filesystem artifact store
docs.text:
.meta-evolve/
├── artifacts/sha256/...
├── runs/...
└── meta-evolve.sqlite

Identical payload bytes reuse content identity while distinct artifact occurrences retain trial, proposal, contributor, and parent lineage.

docs.title: Recovery scenario
docs.text: Terminate a deterministic run at each important transition, reconstruct a new coordinator from disk, resume from committed state, and compare it with an uninterrupted run. Closures are rejected in durable-local mode or cause an explicit capability error before execution; they never silently create a run advertised as resumable.

docs.title: Milestone 5: executable artifacts
docs.text:
Status: complete. Milestone 5 is complete through the M5.4 canonical clamp acceptance. The closure adds integrated assertions, an executed tour, and documentation only; it adds no production port, schema, registry, patch format, or authority claim.

M5.1 ships the first synchronous source-workspace vertical:

class WorkspaceProvider(Protocol):
    def materialize(self, artifact: object) -> Workspace: ...
    def capture(self, workspace: Workspace) -> object: ...
    def dispose(self, workspace: Workspace) -> None: ...


class ProposerRunner(Protocol):
    component: ComponentRef
    def validate_run(
        self,
        *,
        artifact_kind: str,
        artifact_representation: str,
        objectives: tuple[Objective, ...],
        budget: Budget,
        experience: ExperienceSpec | None,
    ) -> None: ...
    def execute(
        self,
        parents: tuple[Artifact, ...],
        context: ProposerContext,
    ) -> ProposalResult: ...

SourceTree uses the stable utf8-tree-v1 representation. PatchProposer accepts one exact-file command, while PatchResult carries the same evidence, usage, metadata, failure, and derivation information as an ordinary proposal. A decoded-value runner preserves the original callable path; the coordinator does not branch on either runner.

DirectoryWorkspaces copies immutable source into a fresh private directory, captures through the same source validation, and disposes before result commitment. A disposal failure is an infrastructure failure and prevents success commitment because M5.1 has no honest mixed success-plus-infrastructure-warning outcome.

M5.2 ships the synchronous SandboxProvider, immutable ProcessSpec and ProcessResult, and the clearly named DevelopmentSubprocessSandbox. The POSIX adapter enforces an absolute executable, workspace-contained normalized cwd, exact declared environment, timeout, independent raw-byte output bounds, whole-process-group termination, and lifecycle cleanup. Policy, timeout, resource, and infrastructure failures remain typed; ordinary nonzero exits are not interpreted. Narrow clock and process-operation seams make precedence and cleanup behavior deterministic under test. It makes no claim to secure arbitrary untrusted code. Add Git worktrees only as an optimization.

M5.3 ships CommandEvaluator, EvaluationEnvironment, and root-exported ProcessSpec. The evaluator is a declared local callable component and uses the existing callable-evaluator path. Its digest-backed component version commits the complete command, environment, scoring, adapter, and exit-protocol semantics. Task construction invokes a general optional evaluator validate_task hook after normalization; no concrete evaluator branch enters the coordinator.

The adapter materializes only a SourceTree, runs the declared process, and always disposes the workspace. Exit 0 and 1 produce passing and failing metrics; other exits become EvaluatorFailure. Existing process failures stay typed and non-rankable. Environment and bounded process-result evidence remain separate from metrics, and evaluator usage receives process wall time without claiming coordinator-owned evaluation counts. Cleanup failure overrides prior completion while retaining its classification, evidence, and usage.

The evaluator-owned grader remains outside the candidate mutation surface. The development sandbox still makes no hostile-code filesystem-isolation claim; stronger providers remain replaceable at the same structural port.

M5.4 pins deterministic content digests and semantic outcomes, while treating measured wall time as occurrence data. Reopened durable storage supports best-artifact and lineage queries; cold resume of these local live components fails explicitly and without side effects. M6 ships native SDK proposers as local-only components; portable reconstruction of patch, command, and native SDK proposer components remains later work.

The M5-owned file audit splits patch-proposer core behavior from lifecycle/resume failures and sandbox declarations/contracts from process execution. Canonical design documents remain cohesive source-of-truth exceptions to the 300-line guideline, and unrelated pre-M5 suites are not refactored as part of this closure.

docs.title: Milestone 6: native-first SDK proposer portability
docs.text:
Status: complete (July 28, 2026). Milestone 7 has since completed; Milestone 8 is next. The former M6.1–M6.3 implementation was removed. It introduced a provider framework before one adapter proved the seam, and its Claude walking skeleton coupled tests to that framework. Every M6.0 measurement and fixture remains canonical input to the replacement adapters.

M6 closed through four acceptance-gated repair slices:

  1. R1 — restore the proposer seam (complete). Put the frozen, slotted, keyword-only ProposerContext in the proposer port with required randomness, step, ordered objectives, exact context bundle, and optional experience reader. Accept non-callable propose(parent, context) objects and preserve runner precedence. Replace proposer-side Task validation with pure validate_run(...); invoke it once after binding in both run and resume, before provider/workspace activity or writes. Preserve CapabilityError, sanitize every other validator failure, and retain its cause. Widen only proposer ComponentRef adapters to structural objects. Configured proposers own a secret-safe identity payload and digest-backed version; declared local proposers remain non-resumable and fail closed in durable-local.
  2. R2 — prove one thin Claude proposer (complete). The closed meta_evolve.claude.Claude structural proposer owns its worker loop, fresh native session, prompt rendering, workspace lifecycle, fixed tool/approval/sandbox profile, output decoding, timeout interruption, cleanup, and Claude-qualified evidence. validate_run rejects unsupported artifact, budget, and experience combinations before SDK startup. Recorded replay and four separate opt-in live cases replace the removed walking skeleton. No shared provider transport or option model was added.
  3. R3 — prove Codex without reshaping R1 (complete). The independent thin Codex proposer runs at the same structural seam and shares only a test conformance helper with Claude. Native thread/turn, discovery, approvals, sandbox, structured output, and interruption differences stay inside the adapter. Four credentialed live cases, a reviewed proposer capture, and all seven Codex drift scenarios passed with gpt-5.4-mini on July 28, 2026.
  4. R4 — compare and close (complete). The provider-selectable repository example uses identical task, source, PullAccess, evaluation/trial bounds, and unbounded core token/wall declarations. Shared deterministic conformance freezes only producer-neutral outcomes. Claude and Codex bind native pull tools over the authoritative reader without a new public type, port, coordinator branch, or durable schema. Five credentialed cases and reviewed proposer and pull captures passed per provider. Claude drift matched fully; Codex R3 drift matched fully and the R4 HTTP/granular-approval mechanism was positively measured. Two closure pull_transport drift retries were honest no-tool-call model-compliance misses, without weakening deterministic conformance or the direct mechanism gates.

R2 keeps the public facade in meta_evolve/claude.py; declaration, preflight, identity, and workspace orchestration live in claude_proposer.py; deterministic prompt/context/schema conversion in claude_prompt.py; SDK options and lifecycle in claude_transport.py; immutable execution records in claude_snapshots.py; usage, evidence, and failure classification over those records in claude_normalization.py; the fixed authority profile and deadline bounds in claude_profile.py; and the synchronous worker boundary in claude_loop.py. The typed SDK inspection/conversion helper remains private and provider-specific. claude_profile.py is the single owner of the native option set, so transport configuration, recorded evidence, and configured identity cannot disagree about the ceiling actually requested.

The recorded replay record is the Claude-only proposer scenario of the existing M6.0 capture entry point, committed beside the other Claude fixtures. Its replay input and drift-comparable evidence are produced by the capture module's pure builders, so the committed record is regenerable rather than transcribed, and a shape change fails the library replay test. The committed record was recaptured from a credentialed claude-sonnet-4-5 run on July 28, 2026. meta-evolve[claude] pins claude-agent-sdk==0.2.128 and adds jsonschema>=4.26,<5 only at the adapter edge so provider-decoded output is independently validated; core dependencies remain empty.

Shipped Claude accepts SourceTree, arbitrary ordered objectives, exact pushed context, native pull access, no finite token budget, and either an unbounded wall budget or a finite wall budget satisfying timeout_seconds <= budget.wall_seconds. Its closed profile is Read/Edit/Write, acceptEdits, the claude_code preset, empty setting sources and ordinary MCP configuration, an enabled empty-network-allowlist sandbox, and four turns. Pull adds one in-process MCP server with the six experience tools and uses 12 turns. Unknown accounting after possible execution escapes the local run; workspace capture remains the candidate authority, and partial files from failed turns are never committed.

R3 mirrors the package split without sharing a production runtime: meta_evolve/codex.py is the provider-only facade; codex_proposer.py owns declaration, identity, preflight orchestration, and workspace capture; codex_prompt.py renders deterministic pushed context; codex_transport.py, codex_sdk.py, and codex_loop.py own the pinned native lifecycle; codex_home.py owns the disposable authority boundary; and codex_snapshots.py, codex_normalization.py, and codex_profile.py own SDK-free evidence, failure/accounting conversion, and the literal native profile. The root exports remain unchanged.

Shipped Codex accepts SourceTree, ordered objectives, exact pushed context, native pull access, and no finite token or wall budget. Its constructor is limited to model, instructions, optional output_schema, and an optional WorkspaceProvider. The fixed profile uses one fresh client, an ephemeral exact-cwd thread, deny-all approvals, workspace-write sandboxing, and one medium-effort turn. A disposable private home copies only regular file-backed OAuth bytes at mode 0600, excludes ambient home authority, and installs an exact-cwd untrusted gate that keeps project .codex inactive. Exact parent AGENTS.md remains workspace input through native discovery.

Typed profile readback must pass before mutation records are accepted, and it reaches only fields that response reports: project configuration changing nothing reported there is prevented by the untrusted gate rather than detected. The private home isolates configuration files, not the process environment, which the pinned SDK cannot clear, and workspace-write leaves /tmp and $TMPDIR writable. Native shell, discovery, and possible provider tools remain irreducible; no exact tool ceiling or hostile-process/network containment is claimed. Provider prose is discarded, workspace files are the sole candidate, and structured final text is independently revalidated as evidence. Codex usage is input plus output, with cached input and reasoning output retained as inclusive detail. Cancellation interrupts and drains/closes where possible, but descendant cleanup remains unconfirmed. Every finite wall budget is rejected, so an unresponsive native turn may block indefinitely. Unknown required accounting escapes rather than becoming fabricated zero usage or a resume claim.

R4 adds experience_session.py and experience_tools.py as private adapter-layer seams shared by the two bindings. The session assigns trial-local handles, projects pushed and pulled records, serializes handlers on one execution thread, latches read exhaustion and faults, and resolves the last valid ordered declaration. It reuses the pure reference-ordering function owned by application/derivation.py, so comparison interleaving cannot drift from replay validation.

Claude builds one SDK in-process MCP server and verifies connected status, tool inventory, and annotations before querying. Codex runs one authenticated stdlib loopback HTTP MCP server, writes its URL and bearer-token environment name into literal private-home TOML, and grants per-tool approval to exactly the six adapter tools while the thread remains deny_all. Full typed status is verified before the turn. Codex reader faults start a separate drain watcher; after 60 seconds it closes the client, rejects all workspace mutations, and preserves unknown-accounting semantics. The deferred exclude_tmpdir_env_var and exclude_slash_tmp settings are not silently enabled.

Both providers render prompt protocol v3. Pushed envelope references become opaque handles while values and policy-rendered content remain exact. Derivation protocol ordered-observed-handle-subsequence-v2 records that declaration remains available after read exhaustion while an unexpected reader fault still rejects it. Successful reads return structured values, handles, kinds, logical steps, truncation, and cumulative usage. Expected denial/exhaustion are content-free; malformed binding requests and unknown handles do not enter the reader. A final valid ordered derivation declaration is required for native success, and because it is unaudited it remains callable after read exhaustion. Structural provider components remain local-only.

The protocol identity rotation requires no provider recapture. Native MCP transport, bearer authentication, granular approvals, typed status and inventory, tool schemas, and provider profiles are unchanged, so the reviewed captures remain byte-identical. Prompt-dependent exhaustion behavior is covered by deterministic conformance.

The Codex-only proposer capture uses the same print-only entry point and pure replay/stable-evidence builders. Its reviewed live record contains scrubbed typed profile, terminal/item, usage, structured-output, and deterministic workspace postconditions. Exact provider step sequences remain replay/volatile observations; drift compares contract-level invariants. The optional meta-evolve[codex] extra pins openai-codex==0.144.4 and supplies adapter-only jsonschema>=4.26,<5.

The M6.0 evidence imposes these adapter requirements:

  • Count every disjoint native token category exactly once. Codex total is input plus output because cached input and reasoning output are inclusive subsets. Claude total is ordinary input plus cache creation plus cache read plus output; its ephemeral cache buckets are inclusive detail.
  • An unreported dimension stays unknown. Codex does not report cache writes or monetary cost. Claude-reported cost remains provider evidence, never a shared budget or cross-provider equivalence claim.
  • Revalidate decoded structured output in ordinary Python. Typed native tool records and machine postconditions are evidence; plausible final model text is not.
  • Verify the exact native configuration an adapter claims before mutation. Native tools and options remain provider-owned; there is no canonical tool vocabulary or generic provider configuration map.
  • A deadline is accepted only when the adapter can stop in-flight work and verify cleanup. The pinned Claude probe supplied positive sampled evidence; the pinned Codex probe left a command alive after terminal interruption, so the Codex adapter must reject such a deadline until a new mechanism is separately verified.
  • After an interrupted or lost execution, execution and accounting are unknown unless non-execution is proven. R1 adds no retry or durability claim for local structural proposers, and adapters must never turn an unknown amount into zero.

docs.title: Milestone 7: cross-domain local v1
docs.text:
Add the artifact registry and public extension contracts only after number, text, and code examples have exercised them.

The common artifact envelope contains semantic kind, representation, schema, interfaces, payload reference, content digest, parent occurrences, and provenance. Domain names such as TextArtifact, GitTreeArtifact, and SkillSetArtifact are typed constructors or views rather than a required inheritance hierarchy.

M7 P1+P2 formalized the SourceTree payload shape into an explicit codec protocol, ArtifactCodec (ports/codecs.py): every kind, including the default python-value, now resolves through a per-run CodecIndex (application/codecs.py) instead of a hard-coded dispatch. Declared interfaces resolve through the registered codec (Registry.artifact_interfaces), not through a new field on the Artifact envelope, so this added no durable schema bump — CURRENT_SCHEMA_VERSION is unchanged. Registry.register_artifact_type rejects every codec offered for an already-built-in (kind, representation) key — the built-in object included — so the four built-in keys (python-value/canonical-json, source-tree/utf8-tree-v1, text/utf8-text-v1, skill-set/utf8-tree-v1) remain non-overridable. The unit is the key, not the kind: a new representation of a built-in kind is a distinct key and registers like any other custom type.

P3 added skill-set (domain/skill_set.py), the first kind to reuse another kind's representation and the first codec with a non-empty interfaces declaration (skill-documents/v1). SkillSet wraps SourceTree construction and adds one rule, layout: every path matches skills/<name>.md. It carries no manifest — M8's HarnessArtifact defines those against a real consumer — and no content validation, since content meaning belongs to whoever reads the skills. Its codec is a fourth built-in rather than a registered custom type: the durable-local gate exists because a registered codec is a live object with no verifiable manifest, and a codec shipped with the library is verifiable exactly like the other three, so skill-set runs stay durable and resumable. That registration works for third parties is proven separately by tests/test_artifact_type_registry.py.

Proposed candidates route through the same CodecIndex as the seed, in application/proposal_completion.py — the original plan scoped only seed encoding — so a candidate the codec rejects becomes a typed InvalidOutput that fails its trial without raising into the run, and a custom artifact type now works through proposer output as well as input. application/runtime.py's durable-local validation block fails closed with CapabilityError when a task's (kind, representation) is not one of the built-in keys: a registered codec is a live object rather than a source function, so require_source_function cannot reach it, and a resumed run would otherwise rebuild payloads with unverified code.

The codec index is a per-run dependency. application/runtime.py and application/resume.py construct it once and return active results through the private Run._reopen(run_id, storage, codecs) path, preserving the exact codec objects used for that run. The public Run(run_id, storage, *, registry: Registry | None = None) constructor builds a read-only index with CodecIndex.with_extras(registry.artifact_types()) when a registry is supplied, merging its custom codecs with all built-ins while the built-ins retain precedence. This intentionally exposes every codec in that registry to decoding; the replayed run projection still selects the artifact kind read by each query, and the constructor grants no execution or mutation authority. Without a registry it remains the built-in reopening path. Codec declaration validation lives once in registry_support.validate_artifact_codec: kind, representation, and every interface name are non-empty and whitespace-exact, while an empty interface tuple remains valid. Both registry registration and the published codec suite call that same validator.

P4 demonstrated the milestone's exit gate. tests/test_four_domain_kernel.py drives number, text, repository, and skill-set runs through one meta.run call site; everything M7 permits a use case to vary lives in one Domain record, and no assertion is written for a single domain. The four leave an identical kernel record — same event sequence, usage, scores, logical steps, and audited experience — while declaring four distinct kinds over three representations, two of which share utf8-tree-v1. No domain needed a coordinator branch, special case, or workaround, and the phase changed no file under src/: the generality was already there to be measured, which is what makes the result a proof rather than a repair.

The purity allowlists are decisions, not accidents. Two properties are pinned by tests/test_application_purity.py, each with an explicit allowlist whose every member carries its justification in the test file itself, and each with a companion test that fails once a member stops being needed — so an exemption cannot quietly outlive its reason.

  • Imports. Application modules import no concrete adapter except storage.py (composes the default memory/filesystem/sqlite stores), unit_of_work.py (owns the atomic durable commit across both stores), run_support.py (constructs the callable-adapter runners for run and resume), and runtime.py (wires the public run() entry point). All four are wiring: something has to name the concrete implementations a default meta.run composes, and the allowlist exists to keep that set visible and small rather than to excuse it.
  • Type dispatch. Nothing calls isinstance against a concrete artifact type outside application/codecs.py and adapters/. The codec is the artifact-type dispatch — encode must refuse a value of the wrong type before it can become a payload — and adapters translate at the edge, where an external system's output first has to become a declared artifact value or a typed failure. The watched set is derived rather than listed: any class in meta_evolve.domain declaring string KIND and REPRESENTATION — the pair Task(artifact=...) reads — falls under the gate the moment it exists, and a guard test pins the derived set so a fifth artifact type is a visible decision rather than a silent widening.

P5a added the milestone's one new storage surface, the read-only listing Storage.runs() -> tuple[RunId, ...], so the CLI's list verb (and any caller whose ids have left the terminal scrollback) can reach Run, resume, and compare again. Two decisions are worth recording.

Enumeration is an optional capability, not a widened port. EventStore keeps exactly append and read; the listing is a separate one-method protocol, ports.RunIndex, that both bundled stores implement. Both required methods are run-scoped, so an implementation can be addressable without being enumerable — one stream handed in at construction, a backend exposing only GET /runs/{id}/events, a store sharded so that "all runs" spans shards. Requiring enumeration of every implementation would earn complexity from a hypothetical rather than the current gate, and would break the hand-built Storage(artifact_store, event_store) pair that LocalOnlyUnitOfWork exists to serve. Storage.runs() checks isinstance(self.events, RunIndex) and raises CapabilityError otherwise; it never reports a non-enumerable store as an empty one. This follows the is_durable principle — a capability is declared by the component, never inferred from a concrete type — but not its mechanism: durability needs a separate boolean because it is invisible in a commit strategy's method set, whereas here the capability is the method, so implementing it is the declaration and a parallel flag could only disagree with it.

Ids, sorted. The listing returns RunIds rather than a richer record: Run.summary() already owns per-run detail, and a richer listing would force the SQLite backend to decode every envelope just to enumerate. Ordering is lexicographic by id, not insertion — in-memory insertion order is a dict accident and SQLite has no insertion column short of rowid, an implementation detail unstable across VACUUM and interleaved appends. Sorting makes the two backends provably agree, which is the property callers depend on. Run ids are run-<sha256>, so the order carries no chronological meaning and is documented not to.

P5b added meta_evolve.cli and the meta-evolve entry point: five verbs — run, list, inspect, resume, compare — over the same public API, using stdlib argparse, no configuration DSL, and no capability logic of its own. A run takes an experiment module exposing one experiment() factory with no import-time side effects; the command line supplies only --storage and --mode. list is one verb beyond the milestone's four because run ids are content-derived digests rather than names anyone retypes from memory: without enumeration, every other verb is unreachable once an id leaves the terminal. Exit codes are 0 for success, 1 for a domain failure (RunError), and 2 for a usage or experiment-module error; anything else keeps its traceback rather than being flattened into a message.

Closed by the M7 defect-repair pass. compare_runs previously refused two incompatible runs with a bare ValueError from _require_equal (application/comparisons.py), which is not a RunError and so escaped the command line's typed-failure translation, reaching the user as a traceback. _require_equal now raises RunsNotComparable, a RunError carrying the declaration that differed as structured data rather than only in its message. The message text is unchanged, so prose matching still works; the command line now reports it as one error line and exit code 1 like every other typed failure.

The other four decisions of that pass. The surfaces themselves are docs/programming-model.md's; what is recorded here is why each landed the way it did.

  • One accessor, not a second view type. Run.trials() returns the existing TrialView, which gained a state field set from the projection records rather than re-derived from other view fields. failure was deliberately left alone: splitting it is breaking, and it still could not express "unevaluated", which is an authorization outcome rather than a fault. The seed trial is included, because three of the six workarounds it replaced depended on unpacking it.
  • CapabilityError is reserved abort control flow, escaping both the proposer and the evaluator boundary unwrapped. RunError is deliberately not in either escape tuple: examples 08, 16 and 17 call summary() on an inner run inside their evaluator, which raises NoSuccessfulEvaluation, so a broad escape would crash three shipped examples. Because CapabilityError is publicly exported, the contract binds user code and is documented, not merely implemented.
  • The name-only report keys on the run-local version sentinel, never on origin == "local". CommandEvaluator is local-origin and versions itself with a configuration digest; keying on origin would condemn exactly the local comparisons that are controlled. ComponentRef.configured_local refuses that sentinel for the same reason, and derives origin and the retained adapter rather than accepting them, since Task's declaration hook admits a component only when it is local and holds that exact callable by identity.
  • Declarable turn limits keep their existing defaults exactly. The defaults emit byte-identical native profiles, so no component.version and no Claude run id moves. native_profile takes the limit keyword-required instead of choosing between two constants, so a normalizer and a transport cannot silently disagree about what was sent. Rejected: max(requested, PULL_MIN) — silently rewriting a chosen number is the defect class being removed.

P6 published the conformance kit and the tutorial.

Published conformance covers two of the seven component types. meta_evolve.conformance ships subclassable pytest suites, on the pandas ExtensionArray model, for artifact codecs (ArtifactCodecTests) and for repository-editing proposers (RepositoryProposerTests, PullRepositoryProposerTests). Evaluators, search policies, context policies, workspaces, and sandboxes are not published, and they are not uniform among themselves: search policies, workspaces, and sandboxes keep reusable function-based suites under tests/ (policy_contract.py, workspace_contract.py, sandbox_contract.py, alongside the store suite in store_contract.py) that an author outside this repository cannot reach, while evaluators and context policies have concrete tests and no reusable suite at all. This paragraph previously projected all seven, and that was a plan rather than a description. The class form buys a subclass hook worth nothing to a suite whose only callers live beside it, so a suite converts when it is published and is published when an extension author needs one; the remaining five are additive work of exactly this shape. tests/ subclasses the published classes for the four built-in codecs and both providers, so the kit and the kernel's own conformance are the same code and cannot drift. pytest is imported by that subpackage and nowhere else in the package, pinned by an AST scan plus a subprocess check that importing meta_evolve never loads it, and surfaced as a conformance extra beside claude and codex.

The codec suite checks round trips, rejection signaling, identity independence, repeated calls within one process, and common open/socket entry points. The last two are deliberately scoped evidence: they do not prove arbitrary purity or cross-process reproducibility. A separate built-in test creates artifacts in fresh interpreters under two fixed PYTHONHASHSEED values and compares their content digests.

The tutorial is executed, not illustrated. docs/adding-an-artifact-domain.md is written as one script split across fenced python blocks, followed by a single fenced text block holding the output it claims. tests/test_add_a_domain_tutorial.py joins the code back together, runs it in a fresh interpreter from an empty directory with no PYTHONPATH, and compares stdout byte for byte; it also checks that the script imports nothing but the meta_evolve root and the standard library, that every repository path the page links to exists, and that the page's "four built-in keys" claim still matches BUILTIN_CODECS. The tutorial's own codec then runs the published ArtifactCodecTests, which is the step the page tells its reader to take. Extraction beat mirroring the code into a test: a mirror drifts silently in exactly the direction that matters, because nothing forces the copy a reader sees to be the copy that ran.

docs.title: Milestones 8–9: harness and policy evolution
docs.text:
Add a typed MutationSurface describing mutable paths, fixed interfaces, required validation, and authority ceiling. Harness and policy candidates may modify only candidate-controlled fields. Task suites, hidden evaluation, enclosing budgets, permissions, and promotion remain experiment- or governance-controlled.

Local episode suites may use closures and are explicitly marked non-portable. Durable suites use versioned factories or typed manifests. Do not introduce a stringly typed template DSL; any textual rendering maps to a validated object model.

Evaluate harness and policy artifacts through fresh bounded inner runs on held-out tasks. Nested random seeds, budgets, environments, cache keys, and evidence remain explicit.

docs.title: Milestone 10: trusted distribution
docs.text:
Only after local semantics are stable:

  • add WorkAttempt and durable lease acquisition, renewal, expiration, cancellation, and completion;
  • retain one logical Trial across delivery retries;
  • introduce trusted worker identities and capability matching;
  • add atomic budget reservation and settlement;
  • make idempotent result submission explicit;
  • define consistency requirements per state type;
  • load-test simulated populations before paid agent fleets.

Worker liveness and queue estimates are ephemeral. Accepted outcomes, evaluations, budgets, and promotion decisions are durable. Out-of-order wall-clock completion must not alter logical random choices or reveal future experience.

docs.title: Milestone 11: contributed and federated network
docs.text:
Add signed manifests, scoped contributor identities, task-specific trust policies, visibility, licensing, embargoes, attribution, retraction, disputes, and reputation. Exchange policy-filtered subgraphs rather than assuming universal access.

References may be redacted, tombstoned, or inaccessible while preserving enough metadata to maintain causal structure. Untrusted execution, evaluator collusion, poisoning, sybil attacks, reward hacking, and correlated replication remain separate threats with separate controls.

docs.title: Interface staging
docs.text: Capability First implementation Later implementation Proposer local callable SDK agent, human workflow, composite harness Evaluator pure callable isolated grader, simulator, proof checker Artifact store in-memory payloads content-addressed filesystem or object store Event store in-memory list SQLite, then durable service Search greedy and best-of-N populations, Pareto, islands, learned allocation Experience no memory exact graph traversal, then measured semantic retrieval Workspace absent directory copy, Git tree/worktree, remote volume Sandbox absent development subprocess, container, hardened remote sandbox Identity absent or local stub trusted worker, then signed contributor identity

docs.title: What not to build first
docs.text:
• every module in the destination package tree;
  • a custom graph or vector database;
  • a peer-to-peer protocol or token economy;
  • a thousand-agent deployment;
  • a web dashboard before event and query semantics stabilize;
  • universal agent communication;
  • learned scheduling without strong baselines;
  • unrestricted self-modification;
  • a template DSL when local closures and typed durable manifests suffice;
  • scientific-discovery claims without domain evidence and replication.

docs.title: Near-term definition of done
docs.text:
Meta-Evolve has a credible first release when a user can define a task, seed artifact, proposer, and evaluator through the canonical small API; choose a search and context policy; run callable and SDK-backed proposers in appropriate execution profiles; evaluate immutable successors; inspect exact causal experience; resume durable runs after failure; and compare runs under equal budgets.

Everything beyond that should extend the same contracts rather than replace the kernel.

docs.title: Bounded live-agent track
docs.text:
This track is optional, paid, and capped at 12 provider calls:

Exercise Provider Model Maximum calls Repository proposal Claude claude-sonnet-5 1 Repository proposal Codex gpt-5.4-mini 1 Experience A/B Claude claude-sonnet-5 4 Held-out skill evolution Claude claude-sonnet-5 6 Total 12

The environment variables below are explicit paid-work markers. The repository's credentialed drift tests require them and CI never sets them. The example scripts themselves do not inspect the variables; running each shown command is the final consent boundary. Stop after any exercise without invalidating the earlier observations.

docs.title: 1. One repository proposal per provider
docs.text: Both commands use the same SourceTree task, evaluator, one-trial budget, Greedy policy, and pull declaration through the common proposer seam.

docs.title: Claude proposal
docs.text:
• Prerequisites: uv sync --extra claude; authenticate Claude Code through an existing login or ANTHROPIC_API_KEY.
  • Opt-in marker: META_EVOLVE_LIVE_CLAUDE=1.
  • Provider and model: Claude, claude-sonnet-5.
  • Call ceiling: one session.
  • Variability: candidate bytes, token use, tool sequence, latency, and success can change between runs.
  • Confounders: Claude's native tools, approval profile, process environment, adapter timeout, and provider service state.
META_EVOLVE_LIVE_CLAUDE=1 uv run --extra claude \
  python examples/06_sdk_coding_agent/main.py --provider claude

docs.title: Codex proposal
docs.text:
• Prerequisites: uv sync --extra codex; run codex login and confirm it created a regular file-backed auth.json.
  • Opt-in marker: META_EVOLVE_LIVE_CODEX=1.
  • Provider and model: Codex, gpt-5.4-mini.
  • Call ceiling: one session.
  • Variability: candidate bytes, token use, tool sequence, latency, and success can change between runs.
  • Confounders: Codex's native tools, approval profile, private-home copy, inherited environment, writable temporary paths, and provider service state.
META_EVOLVE_LIVE_CODEX=1 uv run --extra codex \
  python examples/06_sdk_coding_agent/main.py --provider codex

Compare only the shared facts: both proposers receive the same declared task and their captured candidate is evaluated independently. Do not infer parity in quality, tools, tokens, cost, compute, containment, interruption, or wall time. The canonical examples/06_sdk_coding_agent/main.py owns these declarations.

docs.title: 2. Claude experience A/B
docs.text:
• Prerequisites: the Claude setup above, including SDK support for the in-process experience server.
  • Opt-in marker: META_EVOLVE_LIVE_CLAUDE=1.
  • Provider and model: Claude, claude-sonnet-5.
  • Call ceiling: four sessions: at most two trials in each of two arms.
  • Variability: either arm may pass early; outputs, tokens, latency, and tool use vary. The deterministic grader does not.
  • Confounders: one task and one hidden house convention; both arms use fresh sessions and an equal 12-turn ceiling, but provider state remains uncontrolled.
META_EVOLVE_LIVE_CLAUDE=1 uv run --extra claude \
  python examples/12_experience_ab/main.py

Read attempts, trials-to-first-pass, tokens, and pull counters together. A tie after real reads is a null result: experience made no measured difference. A tie with zero reads means the capability was unused, so the run did not test whether read experience helped. The examples/12_experience_ab/README.md contains the live transcript, controlled eight-repetition measurement, and its limits. The same report is driven without credentials by tests/test_experience_ab_example.py.

docs.title: 3. Claude held-out skill evolution
docs.text:
• Prerequisites: the Claude setup above.
  • Opt-in marker: META_EVOLVE_LIVE_CLAUDE=1.
  • Provider and model: Claude, claude-sonnet-5.
  • Call ceiling: six sessions: three outer candidates, each scored on two held-out episodes.
  • Variability: episode responses decide candidate scores, so the winning skills and stopping point can change even with the same random seed.
  • Confounders: two small house-convention episodes, one model, a local episode-suite closure, and a 120-second session bound. This is curriculum evidence, not a broad skill benchmark.
META_EVOLVE_LIVE_CLAUDE=1 uv run --extra claude \
  python examples/08_skill_evolution/main.py

The model runs inside the evaluator, so the evaluator component identity names the model, episode names, and session bound. That prevents Run.compare from ranking two silently different model configurations. The examples/08_skill_evolution/README.md owns the live measurement and caveats; the call arithmetic is pinned by tests/test_skill_evolution_example.py.

docs.title: Failures are outcomes, not bad scores
docs.text:
A score of 0.0 means the evaluator ran successfully and measured zero. These facts carry no score and must never be converted to zero:

  • provider or infrastructure failure;
  • timeout or turn-limit failure;
  • invalid candidate or missing derivation;
  • evaluator or grader failure;
  • an episode that produced no candidate.

They are typed trial or evaluation outcomes. If every candidate has one, there is no best score. Report the failure kinds and details. In skill evolution, an unfinished episode becomes EvaluatorFailure; it does not lower the candidate's episode average. In the A/B report, typed failures stay named in the attempt sequence rather than disappearing or becoming 0.0.

docs.title: Capability honesty: Codex has no finite wall deadline
docs.text:
The M6 measurement record concludes RuntimeCapabilities.interruptible=False for the pinned Codex SDK surface. The shipped Codex adapter preserves that fact: any finite Budget.wall_seconds is rejected during validate_run, before provider traffic or run events, because native interruption does not verify descendant cleanup. The repository exercise therefore declares evaluation and trial limits but no finite wall limit.

Claude has measured interruption support and an adapter timeout. A finite core wall budget is accepted only when the Claude timeout fits inside it. This is a narrow capability difference, not evidence that the providers are otherwise equivalent.

docs.title: Optional advanced work: prompt optimization
docs.text:
The prompt-optimization example is deliberately outside the 12-call pass. Its maximum is 14 Claude sessions, and the cases shown to the rewriter are not a second unseen validation split. Use it only as a separate, more expensive study of eval-driven rewriting and overfitting risk.

No live example or credentialed provider test runs in CI. The deterministic tests exercise the same seams with fake transports; live runs remain explicit operator actions.

Continue with the contributor code tour to follow the records these examples create through the kernel.

docs.title: M8 design capstone
docs.text:
Design this one bounded experiment:

Start from a worker harness with a planner prompt and context policy. Let an outer proposer change only those two surfaces. Score each candidate on fresh held-out repository tasks under equal budgets. Compare it with the unchanged harness, then leave promotion to an external decision.

Write a decision-complete proposal for issue #8. Do not add runtime types, package directories, or placeholder examples. M8 is the next milestone; this capstone is design only.

docs.title: Map the design onto current seams
docs.text:
M8 concept Existing seam to extend Required design decision HarnessArtifact Artifact kind/representation plus ArtifactCodec and Registry Define a typed manifest of component references and declared interfaces; preserve composite content identity and occurrence lineage MutationSurface Proposer result validation, codec validation, workspace capture, and policy violations Name mutable prompt and context-policy fields; reject changes to evaluator, tasks, secrets, permissions, budgets, history, and promotion Held-out evaluation Evaluators that launch bounded inner meta.run calls, as demonstrated by skill evolution Define a portable versioned episode suite, fresh inner runs, explicit nested seeds and budgets, and aggregate evidence Harness comparison Run.compare, summaries, usage, typed failures, and evaluator component identity Compare baseline and candidate under compatible tasks, suites, budgets, models, and environments; expose quality, cost, and failure behavior External promotion Search records a best result but grants no production authority Specify a separate governance-owned promotion rule and record; never let a candidate or evaluator deploy itself

The M8 milestone owns the goal, deliverables, acceptance gate, and out-of-scope list. The architecture owns authority. The inner and outer loop sketch owns the target relationship, not a shipped API promise.

docs.title: Artifact and identity
docs.text:
• What exact fields make up the harness manifest?
  • Which fields affect the HarnessArtifact content digest?
  • How do two occurrences with equal content retain distinct causal identity?
  • How are every component reference and its behavior-affecting configuration made visible to comparison and replay?

docs.title: Mutation authority
docs.text:
• What two paths or typed parameters may the first proposer change?
  • Which validator rejects a change outside the MutationSurface?
  • How does rejection remain an inspectable typed outcome without creating a successor artifact?
  • Why can the candidate never alter the held-out suite, evaluator, permissions, enclosing budgets, audit history, or promotion rule?

docs.title: Held-out evaluation and budgets
docs.text:
• What is the portable episode-suite representation and version boundary?
  • How is each inner run guaranteed fresh rather than reused from candidate state?
  • Which nested seeds, evaluation/trial/token/wall budgets, environments, and cache keys are declared?
  • How are episode failures retained without averaging them into low scores?

docs.title: Comparison and promotion
docs.text:
• Which declarations must match between the baseline and candidate experiment?
  • Which quality, cost, robustness, and typed-failure views are reported?
  • What evidence is sufficient for an external promotion decision?
  • Where is the explicit handoff from search selection to governance, and how is a rejected promotion retained?

docs.title: Replay and extension seams
docs.text:
• Which new durable facts are required, and can existing batch grammar express them without a coordinator branch on harness type?
  • Can replay rebuild every decision without rerunning an inner episode?
  • Which independently testable port needs a reference adapter?
  • What conformance suite proves a second mutation surface can plug in without changing the coordinator?

docs.title: Current blockers
docs.text:
1. Custom codecs are local-only. A live registered codec has no verified manifest, so a custom HarnessArtifact cannot yet enter honest durable-local resume.
  2. No portable episode-suite representation exists. Current nested examples close over local Python episode lists; M8 needs a versioned representation or factory before durable replay.
  3. Conformance coverage remains incomplete. Published suites cover codecs and repository proposers, while evaluator and context-policy suites are still missing and tracked by #98.
  4. Hidden configuration requires explicit component identity. Models, episode names, timeouts, environments, and other behavior-affecting closure state must enter a component version or manifest before comparison is valid.

Do not solve one by hiding it. A local-only prototype must say local-only. A name-only closure must appear as name-only. A missing suite must remain a tracked acceptance risk.

docs.title: Acceptance evidence to propose
docs.text:
• Valid planner-prompt and context-policy mutations pass through one ordinary meta.run coordinator path.
  • Attempts to change hidden evaluation, permissions, budgets, or promotion are typed rejections with no successor artifact.
  • Composite digest, distinct occurrence identity, parent lineage, and component provenance are deterministic and replayed from committed records.
  • Every candidate is evaluated on fresh held-out inner runs with exact nested usage and typed failures.
  • Baseline comparison refuses mismatched suite, model, environment, or budget identity before ranking.
  • Resume reaches the same logical result without rerunning committed episodes.
  • A second mutation-surface implementation passes the same conformance suite without a coordinator special case.
  • Promotion remains an explicit external outcome, never an automatic side effect of best().

docs.title: Final review
docs.text:
Your proposal is ready only if a reviewer can answer all of these from it:

  • Who owns each mutable field and each fixed control?
  • What gives artifacts, components, episodes, and runs their identities?
  • Where are parent lineage and derived observations recorded?
  • Which layer charges every unit of nested work?
  • Which failures have no score, and where are they retained?
  • What can replay reconstruct without external execution?
  • What makes the baseline comparison scientifically valid?
  • Who may promote the winner, using what recorded evidence?

If any answer depends on “the implementation will know,” expose the declaration or boundary that makes it checkable.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
This roadmap grows Meta-Evolve through small, testable vertical slices. Every milestone must produce a runnable demonstration, preserve the contracts established by earlier milestones, and add only the infrastructure required by its acceptance tests.

The first product target is a local, extensible improvement system in which a user can define an artifact, task, evaluator, proposer, search policy, and context policy; run a bounded experiment; let agents inspect prior work; replay or resume the run; and compare results under equal budgets. Harness evolution, meta-evolution, trusted concurrency, and federation build on that local product.

The harness-evolution demonstration (milestone 8) is the flagship product demo — "point this at your agent and eval set, get a measurably better agent, and inspect exactly why each change was kept." Earlier milestones should keep that demonstration in view rather than treating it as a distant capstone.

Before the numbered milestones, a disposable API spike validated the user-facing interface against both deterministic code and a real model. The spike is a design probe, not a shortcut into the durable implementation. It is complete; see its status below.

docs.title: Development rules
docs.text:
1. Every milestone has one canonical example that runs with a documented command.
  2. Every new port has an in-memory or deterministic reference adapter and a conformance suite.
  3. The coordinator contains no branches for particular artifact types, proposers, evaluators, or search policies.
  4. Durable behavior is specified through domain events and observable results, not adapter internals.
  5. New infrastructure is introduced only when a milestone's proof requires it.
  6. Failures remain typed: poor task performance, invalid output, timeout, resource exhaustion, policy violation, and infrastructure failure are not interchangeable.
  7. Tests are deterministic by default. Tests requiring credentials, network access, or hardened infrastructure are explicitly separated.
  8. Each milestone updates examples, tests, and user-facing documentation together.
  9. The programming model is the canonical public API contract; other documents link to it rather than redefining signatures.
  10. Canonical examples are first-class user-facing documentation, not test fixtures: each must be short, copy-pasteable, and runnable from a clean checkout, and the simple callable path never requires or surfaces kernel vocabulary such as Trial, OperatorSpec, or WorkItem.

docs.title: Pre-milestone API spike
docs.text: Status: complete (July 16, 2026). Both demonstrations ran through the same small public surface under experiments/00_api_spike/, including a real gpt-5.4-mini Codex SDK prompt-optimization run. The exit gate passed: findings are recorded in real_model_findings.md and folded into the programming model's evidence section. Closed by #23.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Exercise the smallest declarative API before durable domain models and package boundaries are fixed.

docs.title: Demonstrations
docs.text:
Build a disposable one-to-three-file implementation that runs:

  1. deterministic integer improvement with Greedy and BestOfN;
  2. one real-model prompt-optimization task whose proposer and evaluator each require only a small user function.

The spike should test the canonical Task, meta.run, proposer, evaluator, search, and Run.best()/lineage() surface from the programming model.

docs.title: Questions it must answer
docs.text:
• Can a plain callable be used as a proposer and evaluator in local mode?
  • Is the distinction between task, seed, proposer, evaluator, and search obvious in working code?
  • Does changing search policy require no change to task or proposer code?
  • Can failures and multi-metric evaluations be represented without exposing orchestration machinery?
  • Which values must become durable records, and which abstractions are premature?

docs.title: Exit gate
docs.text:
• Both examples run through the same small public surface.
  • The programming model is revised from observed use rather than aspiration alone.
  • Any deliberately unsupported capability is named explicitly.
  • None of the spike's internal structure becomes a kernel contract without Milestone 1 justification.

docs.title: Out of scope
docs.text: Replay, crash recovery, ports and adapters, stable schemas, experience grants, workspace isolation, provider portability, and production-quality model integration.

docs.title: Common definition of done
docs.text:
A milestone is complete only when:

  • its canonical example runs from a clean checkout;
  • its acceptance tests pass locally and in CI where the required capabilities are available;
  • events, artifacts, evaluations, and policy decisions retain causal lineage;
  • public contracts and durable schemas are documented and versioned;
  • newly added adapters pass their conformance suites;
  • resource use and failure outcomes are observable;
  • no later-milestone infrastructure was added speculatively;
  • the next milestone can build on the result without replacing the kernel.

docs.title: Release checkpoints
docs.text: Checkpoint Included milestones Meaning Kernel proof 1–3 The abstractions compose, policies are replaceable, and agents can reuse prior experience. Durable local engine 4–6 Runs persist, real code can execute, and one SDK agent works end to end. Local v1 7 Several artifact domains use one public kernel without special cases. Evolution system 8–9 Harnesses and search policies can be evaluated as artifacts under external controls. Distributed v2 10 Trusted workers execute concurrently with correct leases, retries, and budgets. Federated direction 11 Independent installations exchange authorized, verifiable experience.

docs.title: GitHub tracking
docs.text:
The implementation roadmap issue tracks the release checkpoints. Each milestone issue is an acceptance epic and can be decomposed into smaller implementation issues when work begins.

Milestone Issue spike #23 — Pre-milestone API spike (complete) 1 #1 — Deterministic in-memory kernel (complete) 2 #2 — Replaceable search policies (complete) 3 #3 — Shared experience and agent-directed exploration (complete) 4 #4 — Durable local runs and crash recovery (complete) 5 #5 — Executable artifacts and external evaluation (complete) 6 #6 — Native-first SDK proposer portability (complete) 7 #7 — Cross-domain generality and local v1 (complete) 8 #8 — Typed harness evolution 9 #9 — Policy artifacts and meta-evolution 10 #10 — Trusted concurrency and distributed workers 11 #11 — Contributed and federated experience exchange

docs.title: Milestone 1: deterministic kernel
docs.text: Status: complete (July 21, 2026; #1, #32). The canonical number search, exact budget accounting, retained-event projection rebuild, built-in Greedy decision reproduction, failure replay, and the remaining acceptance tests now pass. Restart and resume were deliberately deferred to, and are now shipped by, Milestone 4.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Prove the smallest complete improvement loop without language models, subprocesses, databases, or distributed workers.

docs.title: Canonical demonstration
docs.text:
An integer artifact begins away from a hidden target. Deterministic proposers add or subtract fixed values, a pure evaluator rewards proximity to the target, and a sequential coordinator runs until its evaluation budget is exhausted or the target is reached.

select parent
  → allocate bounded work
  → produce proposal
  → create successor artifact
  → evaluate with evidence
  → append events
  → update projected state
  → choose the next action

docs.title: Deliverables
docs.text:
• Frozen, serializable domain models for tasks, artifacts, proposals, trials, trial outcomes, evaluations, evidence, budgets, usage, policies, and typed events; a work-item delivery record stays internal to the kernel and out of user-facing types.
  • Opaque typed identifiers and schema versions on durable envelopes.
  • In-memory artifact and event stores.
  • A deterministic callable proposer adapter and pure-function evaluator adapter.
  • A sequential coordinator that validates transitions, authority, and budgets.
  • A minimal SearchProgram.next(state) decision contract; remaining budget is part of projected state.
  • Typed OperatorSpec values produced by operator policies rather than durable raw strings.
  • Logical ordering, deterministic tie-breaking, and recorded named random substreams.
  • examples/01_number_search/ with a documented run command.

docs.title: Expected behavior
docs.text:
• The same task, initial artifact, policy, seed, and budget produce the same logical decisions and final projected state.
  • Every artifact and evaluation can be traced to the trial, proposal, and search decision that caused it.
  • Trial identity remains distinct from duplicate delivery or completion attempts.
  • Duplicate completion is idempotent.
  • Exhausted budgets prevent additional work.
  • Invalid proposals and evaluator failures are recorded without being treated as low scores.
  • The run can be rebuilt from its event stream without agent-local state.

docs.title: Acceptance tests
docs.text:
• Reachable and unreachable target scenarios.
  • Exact evaluation and usage accounting.
  • Deterministic replay from an empty projection.
  • Decision reproduction with the same named random substreams and trial seeds.
  • Optimistic append conflict in the in-memory event store.
  • Duplicate work completion.
  • Invalid transition and budget-exhaustion rejection.
  • Failure taxonomy serialization and replay.

docs.title: Out of scope
docs.text: SQLite, filesystem persistence, subprocesses, real agents, semantic search, snapshots, concurrency, and user interfaces beyond the example command.

docs.title: Milestone 2: replaceable search policies
docs.text: Status: complete. M1 supplies the Greedy baseline and the generic preparation boundary. M2.1 adds durable archive decisions, linked decision explanations, and the first reusable policy-contract gate. M2.2 adds the public BestOfN(max_trials=20) preset, independent seed expansion, and historical decision reproduction through the same contract. M2.3 adds the public Population(size=3, tournament_size=2, max_trials=20) preset with explicit rank-ordered archive membership, deterministic tournament selection, and a corridor test showing retention of a temporarily worse branch. M2.4 adds strict compatible-run comparison and the canonical equal-budget three-policy benchmark.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Prove that search behavior is a replaceable policy and that different policies can be compared fairly without changing the coordinator.

docs.title: Canonical demonstration
docs.text: Run independent best-of-N, greedy hill climbing, and a small population policy against the same integer task, initial artifact, seed rules, and evaluation budget. Produce a comparison report containing best score, evaluations, usage, and lineage references.

docs.title: Deliverables
docs.text:
• Independent best-of-N policy.
  • The M1 Greedy baseline covered by the shared M2 policy conformance suite.
  • Small population retention policy.
  • Deterministic selection and tie-breaking rules.
  • Explicit admission, stopping, and budget-allocation decisions.
  • A run-comparison projection or report.
  • One publishable benchmark example: an honest, reproducible equal-budget comparison (for example, greedy with context reuse versus independent best-of-N) presented as a notebook or report a reader can rerun, serving as the project's first credibility artifact.
  • examples/02_policy_comparison/.

docs.title: Expected behavior
docs.text:
• Policies consume the same projected state and return typed decisions.
  • Replacing a policy requires no coordinator, runtime, evaluator, or storage changes.
  • Every policy decision records its inputs, policy version, rationale metadata, and observed logical step.
  • Comparisons normalize results by the same declared budget.
  • A policy cannot directly mutate projections or grant itself additional budget.

docs.title: Acceptance tests
docs.text:
• All three policies pass one shared policy conformance suite.
  • Equal inputs produce deterministic decisions.
  • Tie cases have stable outcomes.
  • Population admission and eviction replay correctly.
  • A historical policy decision can be reproduced without future evaluations.
  • Adding a minimal test policy requires only implementing the policy contract.

docs.title: Out of scope
docs.text: Pareto archives, novelty search, islands, bandits, MCTS, learned allocation, and policy evolution.

docs.title: M2.4 completion
docs.text:
Run.summary() and Run.compare() are immutable derived views over committed records. Fair comparison requires identical evaluator/proposer declarations, primary objective, task and effective run budgets, artifact kind, and initial artifact declaration and digest. Policy choice, policy configuration, and root seed may differ; exact primary scores tie without a usage or policy tiebreaker.

The canonical examples/02_policy_comparison/ sweep uses target 12, moves (-2, 1, 5), initial value 0, nine evaluations, eight successor trials, and root seeds 0 through 39. Its executed notebook reports complete score and usage distributions and representative star, chain, and tree-branch lineages, with an explicit small-illustration evidence disclaimer. The companion executed milestone_2_tour.ipynb introduces M2.1 through M2.4 from the public callable path before showing optional kernel-level inspection.

docs.title: Milestone 3: shared experience and agent-directed exploration
docs.text: Status: complete (July 24, 2026; #3). M3.1 adds the read-only temporal experience projection, M3.2 adds bounded replayable policy-pushed context, M3.3 adds audited, strictly-prior agent-pulled access, and M3.4 adds declared derivation, run-aggregate experience usage, memory-strategy comparison, and the canonical four-variant demonstration.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Make prior trials useful to later agents through both policy-pushed context and agent-pulled investigation.

docs.title: Canonical demonstration
docs.text: Agent A produces several failed trials. Agent B searches those trials, opens a relevant proposal and evaluation, compares siblings, and uses the observed failure to choose a successful transformation. The new proposal records the exact experience B observed and used.

docs.title: Deliverables
docs.text:
• An in-memory ExperienceGraph projection with occurrence-based node, ancestor, child, inclusive-sibling, causal-leaf frontier, trace, and inclusive historical state_at queries.
  • A scoped, read-only ExperienceReader with exact filtering and traversal.
  • ExperienceGrant bounds for task, run, logical time, result count, context size, and resource use; identity and visibility remain single-user stubs.
  • ContextPolicy implementations for NoMemory, AncestorsOnly, and BestSibling.
  • Events for automatic context selection, experience queries, opened records, and comparisons.
  • Immutable ContextBundle records and exact query-result records, including ordering and truncation.
  • Stable references from observed experience into Proposal.derived_from.
  • examples/03_experience_reuse/ covering push-only, pull-only, and combined access.

docs.title: Expected behavior
docs.text:
• Agents distinguish experience that existed from experience they actually observed.
  • An as_of argument may narrow but never widen a work item's logical-time grant.
  • Cross-task, out-of-run, retracted, or future experience is not returned.
  • M3.2 context selection obeys record and rendering bounds without consuming task usage; M3.3 pull operations count against their ExperienceGrant.
  • The derivation graph remains acyclic while semantic relationships may be typed cross-links.
  • Content deduplication does not collapse distinct causal occurrences.

docs.title: Acceptance tests
docs.text:
• Agent B improves by consulting Agent A's recorded failure.
  • Push-only, pull-only, combined, and no-memory variants run under equal budgets.
  • Ancestor, sibling, and historical-state queries return expected results.
  • Attempts to cross task, run, or logical-time boundaries fail.
  • Query result limits and usage limits are enforced.
  • Replay reconstructs the same observed-context references and derived-from edges.

docs.title: Out of scope
docs.text: Embeddings, vector databases, learned retrieval, graph databases, filesystem projections, principal-based authorization, licensing enforcement, and cross-installation experience.

docs.title: M3.1 completion
docs.text:
replay_experience_graph() derives one trial-centered node per committed trial occurrence through the validated run replay path. ExperienceRef uses the run, record kind, and existing occurrence identity; identical artifact payloads therefore remain distinct causal occurrences. Exact decision, explanation, proposal, artifact-creation, outcome, evidence, evaluation, and completed-trial records are retained without defining another lifecycle.

Queries are scoped by task, run, and an optional inclusive logical step. Ancestors exclude self, siblings include self, frontier means visible causal leaves rather than archive membership, and a trace spans the target trial and its accessible ancestors while preserving committed event order with a fixed intra-event kind order. Missing, wrong-kind, cross-scope, future, hidden, retracted, and synthetic non-local direct targets all receive one opaque denial. Collection reads omit inaccessible occurrences and do not traverse through them.

Only ExperienceRef is durable and exported through meta_evolve.domain. Graph and query views remain outside the package-root callable API. M3.1 adds no reader grant, pushed context, retrieval, durable graph store, authentication, licensing, or proposal-derivation contract.

docs.title: M3.2 completion
docs.text:
meta.run(context=...) accepts NoMemory, AncestorsOnly, BestSibling, or a compatible declared policy. None and NoMemory() preserve pre-M3.2 identity, stream, trial specs, and proposer behavior except that the internal ProposerContext now exposes a synthesized empty bundle. Non-default configuration contributes one final serialized ContextSpec identity segment.

ContextPolicyDeclared follows bootstrap evaluation. A transparent search-program wrapper stamps its policy reference only into successor specs, and a generic coordinator operation commits one ContextSelected after the decision explanation and before proposer invocation. Bundles snapshot exact typed records, stable reference order, canonical rendering, reason, truncation, and ContextUsage; record and character bounds are independent from task Usage.

AncestorsOnly flattens accessible ancestors in graph-node and committed-record order. BestSibling excludes the current node, ranks only successful sibling evaluations through rank_evaluations, and preserves completion-order ties. Replay validates the committed records against their strictly prior visible sources and returns the committed bundle without rerunning selection or rendering. Context declaration and selection facts remain inspectable in the experience graph but cannot themselves become policy candidates.

docs.title: M3.3 completion
docs.text:
meta.run(experience=...) accepts the run-level ExperienceAccess protocol; PullAccess(max_operations=20, max_results=20, max_records=100, max_chars=32_000) is the shipped declaration. None normalizes completely away. A non-default access declaration contributes the final serialized ExperienceSpec identity segment after any ContextSpec.

Every successor receives a fresh immutable ExperienceGrant bounded to the same task/run and as_of=trial.logical_step - 1. Its ExperienceReader supports exact conjunctive search filters, open, ancestors, inclusive siblings, and right-minus-left numeric comparison. Results preserve committed ordering, exact structured snapshots, canonical prefix-bounded rendering, truncation, and cumulative operation/result/record/character usage. Failed evaluations remain inspectable and never become synthetic losses.

The audited lifecycle is grant → (attempt → success|denial|exhaustion)* → proposal. Attempts charge before validation, opaque denials disclose no protected content, and over-ceiling calls receive a separate content-free exception. Replay validates authority, placement, reproducible operation identities, cumulative charging, and terminal matching, and holds every success to the shared deterministic contract: records must equal committed sources inside the effective boundary, references must stay visible, deltas must derive from the paired records, and rendering must prefix the canonical rendering of the committed records. Selection, traversal, filtering, and comparison logic is never re-run, and committed outcomes are returned directly. Context and pull-audit facts remain graph-inspectable but are excluded from both push and pull candidate sets, and naming them in a search filter is a malformed request. Pull usage does not change task budgets, logical steps, or named randomness.

docs.title: M3.4 completion
docs.text:
Proposal and callable ProposalResult now carry an explicit ordered derived_from declaration. One shared pure validator reconstructs pushed and pulled observations from committed records and requires a unique, strictly-prior same-run subsequence. Resource exhaustion precedes derivation policy failure; both coordinator-imposed failures clear edges and commit no candidate. Valid typed proposer failures and failed independent evaluations retain their declared lineage.

Canonical serialization omits empty derivation and rejects an explicitly encoded empty default, so old proposal, event, context, and replay bytes remain unchanged at schema version 1. RunExperienceUsage, Run.experience_usage(), and expanded summaries report context and pull totals. Comparisons continue to require equal task/run budgets and core declarations while allowing different memory strategies, with exact declaration-match flags.

The runnable examples/03_experience_reuse/ experiment gives no-memory, push-only, pull-only, and combined variants the same task, proposer, evaluator, chain search, seed, and task/run budget. It records early evaluator failures, then succeeds only when prior failure evidence is reused and cited. Replay reconstructs the same derivation edges. The companion executed milestone_3_tour.ipynb introduces M3.1 through M3.4 from the public callable path, with push_pull_lab.ipynb and derivation_comparison_lab.ipynb as focused kernel-level labs.

docs.title: Milestone 4: durable local runs and crash recovery
docs.text: Status: complete (July 24, 2026; #4, #47). Durable artifacts and events, atomic commit, verified manifests, corruption detection, migration, recovery-frontier replay, and context/experience-aware resume satisfy the acceptance gate without changing the M1–M3 logical identities or trajectories.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Persist the kernel without changing its logical behavior and prove that interrupted runs resume safely.

docs.title: Canonical demonstration
docs.text: Start a deterministic run, complete several trials, terminate the process, rebuild the coordinator and projections from disk, resume from the committed frontier, and compare the outcome with an uninterrupted run.

docs.title: Deliverables
docs.text:
• SQLite append-only event store with optimistic concurrency.
  • Content-addressed filesystem artifact store.
  • Durable run, trial, population, work-item, usage, and experience projections.
  • Stable idempotency keys and committed logical steps.
  • A resume command or documented API.
  • Migration/versioning strategy for durable schemas.
  • examples/04_crash_recovery/.

docs.title: Expected behavior
docs.text:
• SQLite and in-memory adapters satisfy the same event-store contract.
  • Identical payload bytes reuse content identity while occurrence provenance remains distinct.
  • Only atomically committed object records and transition events affect reconstructed state.
  • Restarting does not repeat completed logical work or lose remaining budget.
  • Historical state is initially reconstructed from immutable object records and transition events; snapshots are optional future caches.
  • Corrupt or incompatible durable data fails explicitly rather than being silently ignored.

docs.title: Acceptance tests
docs.text:
• Interrupted and uninterrupted deterministic runs reach equivalent logical results.
  • Restart before and after each important transition.
  • Duplicate completion across a restart.
  • Optimistic concurrency conflicts across two store clients.
  • Artifact deduplication with distinct causal occurrences.
  • Projection rebuild from empty projection tables using durable object records and transition events.
  • Durable schema-version rejection and supported migration tests.

docs.title: Out of scope
docs.text: Graph databases, remote databases, object stores, parallel workers, filesystem snapshots, and backup services.
