Milestone 1 record construction keeps the common path narrative while retaining raw frozen constructors for canonical deserialization:

seed = Artifact(id=artifact_id, payload=initial_value)
proposer = ComponentRef.proposer("package:mutate", "1")
evaluator = ComponentRef.evaluator("package:score", "1")

outcome = TrialOutcome.succeeded(
    trial_id=trial_id,
    proposal_id=proposal_id,
    artifact_ids=(candidate_id,),
)
evaluation = Evaluation.succeeded(
    id=evaluation_id,
    trial_id=trial_id,
    artifact_id=candidate_id,
    evaluator=evaluator,
    metrics={"score": 1.0},
)

Artifact computes its digest when omitted and validates an explicit digest supplied by a decoder. TrialOutcome.failed(...) and Evaluation.failed(...) construct the corresponding typed failure paths. Plain callable adapters use ComponentRef.local_proposer(...) and ComponentRef.local_evaluator(...).

The atomic unit offered to a search algorithm is a TrialSpec:

TrialSpec(
    task_id=task_id,
    parent_ids=(artifact_id,),
    proposer=proposer_ref,
    operator=OperatorSpec(kind="patch"),
    context_policy=context_policy_ref,
    budget=Budget(tokens=50_000, wall_seconds=900),
    random_seed=trial_seed,
)

The coordinator accepts the specification as a first-class immutable Trial with its own identity. WorkItem is the scheduling envelope used to deliver that logical trial, while a lease or future WorkAttempt represents one retry. Retries do not create new trials.

SearchDecision
  → TrialSpec
  → Trial
      → WorkItem
          → WorkAttempt or lease retry
      → TrialOutcome
          → Proposal
          → Artifact occurrence(s)
          → trace and usage
      → Evaluation(s)

ExperienceNode = a read projection over these records

The coordinator interprets an ordinary trial through one fixed protocol:

async def execute_trial(spec, run):
    context = context_policy.select(run.state, spec)
    context = coordinator.commit_context_bundle(context)
    trial = coordinator.start_trial(spec, context)

    work = coordinator.allocate(trial)
    execution = await proposer_runner.execute(work, context)
    coordinator.commit_proposal(trial, execution.proposal)
    artifact = await artifact_store.capture(execution.candidate)

    outcome = coordinator.complete_trial(trial, execution, artifact)
    evaluation = await evaluator.evaluate(run.task, artifact)
    coordinator.record_evaluation(outcome, evaluation)
    return TrialResult(outcome=outcome, evaluation=evaluation)

proposer_runner adapts a local callable, deterministic mutator, workspace-backed SDK runtime, or another proposer without changing the protocol. TrialResult is a coordinator-facing evaluated view over the separately durable outcome and evaluation, not another experimental identity.

Provider usage belongs to the execution that caused it. Tokens, wall time, and other resource measurements from both proposer execution and evaluation roll up against the applicable task, run, and trial budgets. An evaluation limit alone must never be reported as the total model-spend limit.

Each operation validates budgets and authority and appends typed records and events. The snippet shows the logical sequence, not a database transaction or permission bypass. Any hypothesis or prediction used for calibration must be committed before the evaluator reveals the predicted evidence. Workflows requiring stronger preregistration may split proposing and applying into separate phases.

For a merge or synthesis operation, parents may contain several artifacts. For replication, training, or scientific experimentation, the decision and result types can be extended without changing the meaning of an ordinary trial.

OperatorPolicy and OperatorSpec occupy different levels. A policy chooses what operation to perform; the durable trial records the resulting typed specification. User-facing strings such as "patch" may be accepted as shorthand but are normalized before a trial is committed.

docs.title: The durable search contract
docs.text:
The public algorithm contract should remain small:

class SearchProgram(Protocol):
    archive: ArchivePolicy

    def next(self, state: SearchState) -> SearchDecision:
        """Return the next bounded action from committed state."""

The current durable decision types are:

SearchDecision = TrialSpec | ArchiveUpdate | Stop

ArchiveUpdate is a policy declaration over an already completed evaluation. It records admission or rejection, an optional eviction, and the complete rank-ordered member IDs. It allocates no work and consumes no budget. Current membership is projected from these decisions rather than held in policy-local state.

Later milestones may add typed decisions without expanding the method surface:

SearchDecision = (
    TrialSpec
    | TrialBatch
    | ReplicationSpec
    | MigrationSpec
    | Stop
)

The coordinator loop is therefore:

while True:
    state = projections.search_state(run_id)
    decision = search.next(state)
    committed = coordinator.record(decision)

    if isinstance(decision, Stop):
        break

    if committed.trial is not None:
        await coordinator.execute(committed.trial)

SearchProgram.next is re-entered from committed projected state at every logical step. Its Python stack and local variables are not durable state. Anything that affects a later decision must be derivable from events, artifacts, policy configuration, or versioned policy state recorded through the coordinator.

This gives ordinary Python policies a simple interface while preserving replay and crash recovery.

Each newly committed decision is immediately followed by a linked PolicyDecisionExplained fact. A policy may optionally return its rationale and the names of random streams it used; the runtime derives the actual seeds from SearchState.randomness. A description of a trial decision must name the "trial" stream, because that stream seeds the trial itself. Deterministic fallbacks explain trials, archive updates, and stops for policies implementing only next(state). These additive facts do not consume budget or advance logical decision numbering, and retained M1 streams without explanations remain readable.

The M1 in-memory guarantee covers replay from retained events and decision reproduction. Durable storage, restarting a process, and resuming committed work are separate Milestone 4 guarantees, shipped through Milestone 4.5 for the durable-local profile (see resume, above).

For the shipped Greedy, BestOfN, and Population presets, RunStarted retains a search declaration with the policy reference, the frozen declared configuration, and the authorized proposer reference. That is enough to reconstruct the bound policy against the recorded run budget and reproduce its historical TrialSpec, ArchiveUpdate, or Stop decisions. Custom programs remain identified by their policy reference and are responsible for declaring any configuration that affects next().

docs.title: Randomness and replay
docs.text:
Randomness is explicit input, not hidden policy-instance state. A run has a root random_seed; each policy decision and trial receives a recorded deterministic substream derived from the root seed, policy version, logical decision identity, and a stable stream name.

This guarantee ends at the boundary of a nondeterministic external component. For example, random_seed does not force a hosted model provider to reproduce a response. The run records the exact provider request, response, model identity, trace reference, and usage it observed; replay consumes those records rather than silently resampling and claiming equivalence.

The following rules apply:

  • retries of one logical trial reuse its recorded trial seed;
  • worker identity and wall-clock completion order never affect random choices;
  • policy implementations do not keep unrecorded mutable RNG state;
  • named substreams isolate selection, allocation, mutation, and evaluation randomness;
  • replay consumes recorded decisions, while decision reproduction reconstructs the exact RNG substream observed by the original policy.

SearchState.randomness exposes those named deterministic streams. It is not a process-global random generator.

docs.title: Composable policy pieces
docs.text:
Most search algorithms should be configurations of small policies rather than new coordinators:

search = meta.Search(
    selector=meta.Best(),
    allocator=meta.RoundRobin(proposers),
    operator=meta.Patch(),
    archive=meta.TopK(k=1),
    stop=meta.TrialLimit(50),
)

The common pieces are:

Policy Responsibility Selector Choose parent artifacts from committed state. Allocator Choose a proposer and assign bounded compute. OperatorPolicy Choose patch, rewrite, merge, replicate, train, or another typed operation. ContextPolicy Push a bounded context bundle before execution. ArchivePolicy Admit, reject, retain, or evict evaluated artifacts. StopPolicy Stop from budget, success, convergence, or explicit cancellation. MigrationPolicy Exchange candidates between populations when configured.

These policies are explicit and versioned. meta.Search can implement next by composing them. Algorithms that need custom behavior can implement SearchProgram directly without replacing execution or persistence.

docs.title: Independent best-of-N
docs.text:
Best-of-N always expands the seed and retains the best evaluated result:

best_of_n = meta.BestOfN(max_trials=20)

The shipped preset uses policy reference best-of-n@1. The seed evaluation participates in the same stable top-1 result view but does not count toward max_trials; ties retain the earliest successful evaluation, and failed proposals or evaluations are not rankable. Every successor has the seed as its only parent, so successful candidates form a star rather than an improvement chain.

The future composed spelling of the same policy is:

best_of_n = meta.Search(
    selector=meta.SeedOnly(),
    allocator=meta.RoundRobin(proposers),
    operator=meta.IndependentProposal(),
    archive=meta.TopK(k=1, objective="score"),
    stop=meta.TrialLimit(n=20),
)

Conceptually:

for _ in range(n):
    candidate = await trial(parent=seed)
    archive.consider(candidate)

return archive.best()

The conceptual loop is useful for understanding the algorithm. The actual implementation uses next(state) so a run can resume after any committed trial.

docs.title: Greedy improvement
docs.text:
Greedy search expands the current incumbent and retains a candidate only when it is better under the declared objective and constraint policy:

greedy = meta.Search(
    selector=meta.ArchiveBest(),
    allocator=meta.RoundRobin(proposers),
    operator=meta.Mutate(),
    archive=meta.TopK(k=1, require_improvement=True),
    stop=meta.AnyOf(
        meta.SuccessReached(),
        meta.TrialLimit(50),
        meta.NoImprovement(10),
    ),
)

Its custom next implementation, if needed, remains small:

class Greedy(SearchProgram):
    archive = TopK(k=1, require_improvement=True)

    def next(self, state):
        if self.stop(state):
            return Stop("budget, success, or plateau")

        return TrialSpec(
            task_id=state.task_id,
            parent_ids=(state.archive.best().artifact_id,),
            proposer=self.allocator.choose(state),
            operator=self.operator.choose(state),
            context_policy=self.context,
            budget=self.allocator.budget(state),
        )

docs.title: Population and evolutionary search
docs.text:
Population search changes the selector and archive, not the execution loop. The shipped steady-state preset is:

population = meta.Population(size=3, tournament_size=2, max_trials=20)

The preset uses policy reference population@1. It retains explicit, rank-ordered top-size membership through one record-only ArchiveUpdate per evaluation, always processing the final evaluation before it stops. Parents come from a tournament: tournament_size distinct members are drawn from the named selection stream — a self-contained integer draw, so recorded decisions reproduce on any Python version — and the highest-ranked sampled member is expanded. Score ties retain the earlier evaluation, and failed proposals or evaluations are rejected rather than scored. Because parents must be admitted members, a run whose seed evaluation fails stops with population_empty instead of expanding a non-member seed; Greedy and BestOfN instead fall back to the seed. Membership grants no promotion authority: run.best() remains the derived result view.

The future composed spelling of richer population policies is:

population = meta.Search(
    selector=meta.Tournament(size=3),
    allocator=meta.AdaptiveRoundRobin(proposers),
    operator=meta.WeightedChoice(
        mutate=0.75,
        crossover=0.20,
        restart=0.05,
    ),
    archive=meta.TopK(k=32, diversity_key="strategy"),
    stop=meta.TrialLimit(500),
)

A crossover decision simply names several parents:

return TrialSpec(
    task_id=state.task_id,
    parent_ids=(parent_a.id, parent_b.id),
    proposer=proposer,
    operator=OperatorSpec(kind="merge"),
    context_policy=context_policy,
    budget=trial_budget,
)

No shared mutable checkout is required. The proposer receives private materializations of immutable parent artifacts and produces one successor.

docs.title: Pareto and quality-diversity archives
docs.text:
Multi-objective search is primarily an archive decision:

pareto = meta.Search(
    selector=meta.ParetoTournament(),
    allocator=meta.Bandit(arms=proposers),
    operator=meta.Mutate(),
    archive=meta.ParetoArchive(
        maximize=["correctness", "novelty"],
        minimize=["latency_ms", "cost_usd"],
        constraints=["tests_passed"],
    ),
    stop=meta.EvaluationLimit(1_000),
)

MAP-Elites or another quality-diversity method can use the same loop with a keyed archive:

archive = meta.GridArchive(
    dimensions=["strategy_family", "memory_style"],
    cell_policy=meta.BestBy("correctness"),
)

Evaluation retains the full objective vector, uncertainty, evidence, and resource use. The archive does not need to collapse them into one permanent scalar.

docs.title: Islands and migration
docs.text:
An island model is a view over several populations plus an occasional typed migration decision:

class Islands(SearchProgram):
    archive = IslandArchive(count=4, capacity=16)

    def next(self, state):
        if state.step > 0 and state.step % 100 == 0:
            return MigrationSpec(
                sources=state.islands,
                topology="ring",
                count=2,
            )

        island = state.islands[state.step % len(state.islands)]
        parent = tournament(island.members, state.randomness)
        return TrialSpec(
            task_id=state.task_id,
            parent_ids=(parent.id,),
            proposer=choose_proposer(island, state),
            operator=OperatorSpec(kind="mutate"),
            context_policy=DiversityPreserving(),
            budget=state.budget.next_trial(),
        )

The migration event changes projected membership; it does not move mutable files between directories.

docs.title: Bandit allocation and tree search
docs.text:
Bandit allocation changes which proposer, operator, or branch receives compute:

allocator = meta.UCB(
    arms=meta.ProposerOperatorPairs(proposers, operators),
    reward="score_gain_per_cost",
)

MCTS-style search uses projected node statistics when choosing a trial:

class TreeSearch(SearchProgram):
    archive = TreeArchive()

    def next(self, state):
        node = select_ucb_path(state.tree)

        return TrialSpec(
            task_id=state.task_id,
            parent_ids=(node.artifact_id,),
            proposer=self.allocator.choose(state, node),
            operator=self.operator.choose(state, node),
            context_policy=AncestorsAndSiblings(),
            budget=state.budget.next_trial(),
        )

Visit counts, value estimates, and virtual losses are projected policy state. Decisions record the statistics they observed so completion order cannot silently rewrite historical reasoning.

docs.title: Experience-aware agents
docs.text:
Search chooses where to expand. Context policies and the ExperienceReader determine how prior experience reaches an agent:

run = meta.run(
    task=task,
    seed=seed,
    proposer=agent,
    search=meta.Greedy(max_trials=50),
    context=meta.AncestorsOnly(max_records=20, max_chars=8_000),
    experience=meta.PullAccess(
        max_operations=20,
        max_results=20,
        max_records=100,
        max_chars=32_000,
    ),
)

M3.2 ships NoMemory, AncestorsOnly, and BestSibling. None and NoMemory() normalize completely away. A non-default policy adds a serialized ContextSpec segment to run identity, is declared after bootstrap, and stamps only successor TrialSpec values. M3.3 appends ExperienceSpec after that segment when PullAccess is declared.

Under durable-local (Milestone 4.5) the declared ContextSpec/ExperienceSpec are folded into the run's atomic genesis batch and each selected context bundle and audited experience operation commits durably, so an interrupted run resumes to the same logical result: resume rebuilds the context policy from the registry and the experience bounds from the recorded ExperienceSpec (see the resume description above). This requires the context policy be a registered, deterministic, source-digestible component; the shipped presets satisfy that bar.

Inside a capable proposer:

def improve(parent, context):
    failures = context.experience.search(
        record_kinds=("outcome", "evaluation"),
        failure_kinds=("proposer_failure", "evaluator_failure"),
        limit=5,
    )
    trials = context.experience.search(record_kinds=("trial",), limit=2)
    comparison = context.experience.compare(
        trials.references[0],
        trials.references[1],
    )
    return revise(parent, failures.records, comparison.deltas)

Every attempt and exact returned value is audited. The proposer may inspect only the scope and logical time granted to its trial. M3.3 enforces logical-time bounds, read budgets, and exact observation recording because these prevent future-information leakage. Principal identity, licensing, and multi-tenant visibility enforcement belong to later trust milestones.

The combined lifecycle is PolicyDecisionMade → PolicyDecisionExplained → ContextSelected? → ExperienceGrantIssued? → (ExperienceOperationAttempted → resolution)* → ProposalSubmitted. Each grant is strictly prior at trial.logical_step - 1. A caller may narrow as_of but cannot widen it. Record/result limits and canonical rendering are independently prefix-bounded; all pull usage is cumulative within the grant and separate from task Usage. Every valid attempt is charged before validation and resolves to an exact committed success, opaque denial, or content-free budget exhaustion. Reproduction returns committed bundles and operation outcomes without rerunning selectors, traversal, filtering, comparison, or rendering.

M3.4 adds an ordered ProposalResult.derived_from tuple. Live completion and replay validate it through one pure contract against the exact committed observation ledger: pushed bundle references first, then each successful pull result and its structured record references in operation order — comparison records in their committed interleaved rendering order — with first-occurrence deduplication. Invalid authority becomes an opaque PolicyViolation; resource exhaustion has precedence and neither coordinator-imposed failure commits an artifact or edge. Legitimate typed proposer failures and independently failed evaluations may retain valid edges.

Run.experience_usage() and RunSummary.experience_usage aggregate push and pull channels without charging task resources. Summaries retain exact context and pull specs, while comparisons permit different memory strategies and report whether each declaration matches. Empty derivation uses omitted-default canonical encoding, preserving all pre-M3.4 proposal and event bytes without a schema-version change. The runnable examples/03_experience_reuse/ experiment compares all four memory variants under identical non-memory declarations and budgets.

docs.title: Inner and outer loops
docs.text:
“Inner” and “outer” describe a relationship between runs; they are not separate engines.

outer run optimizes a HarnessArtifact or PolicyArtifact
    ↓ evaluates one outer candidate through an episode suite
inner runs optimize or solve ordinary task artifacts
    ↓ return evidence and aggregate measurements
outer evaluator returns measurements and evidence
    ↓ outer archive or promotion policy admits or rejects

Conceptually, a harness outer loop is only:

for candidate_harness in outer_search:
    episodes = []

    for task in heldout_tasks:
        episodes.append(
            meta.run(
                task=task,
                seed=task.seed,
                proposer=candidate_harness,
                search=inner_search,
                budget=inner_budget,
            )
        )

    outer_evaluation = aggregate(episodes)
    outer_archive.consider(candidate_harness, outer_evaluation)

The actual outer search is still implemented through next(state), and EpisodeSuite records each inner run, aggregation input, and budget. The loop above exposes the relationship without implying that a Python iterator is durable state.

An inner run improves an artifact under a particular harness or search policy:

inner_spec = meta.RunSpec(
    task=repository_task,
    seed=repository_seed,
    proposer=candidate_harness,
    search=meta.Greedy(max_trials=20),
    budget=Budget(evaluations=20, tokens=500_000),
)

The outer task treats the harness itself as the candidate artifact:

harness_task = meta.Task(
    artifact_kind="harness",
    evaluator=meta.EpisodeSuite(
        tasks=heldout_repository_tasks,
        build_inner_run=lambda harness, task: inner_spec.replace(
            task=task,
            proposer=harness,
        ),
        aggregate=meta.MeanAndFailureRate(),
        episode_budget=Budget(evaluations=20, tokens=500_000),
    ),
    objectives=[
        meta.Maximize("heldout_correctness"),
        meta.Minimize("mean_tokens"),
    ],
)

outer_run = meta.run(
    task=harness_task,
    seed=baseline_harness,
    proposer=harness_mutator,
    search=meta.Population(size=8, max_trials=40),
    budget=Budget(evaluations=40),
)

The closure is valid in local mode, where the run is marked non-portable and may not survive process restart. durable-local and distributed modes require a versioned inner-run factory or manifest rather than an anonymous Python closure. InnerRunTemplate is a validated typed object model, not a separate stringly typed template language.

The outer candidate may change only declared harness surfaces. It cannot change held-out tasks, evaluator code, episode budgets, secrets, permissions, audit history, or promotion rules.

docs.title: Policy meta-evolution
docs.text:
Policy evolution uses exactly the same nesting. The candidate artifact is now a serialized search policy:

policy_task = meta.Task(
    artifact_kind="search-policy",
    evaluator=meta.EpisodeSuite(
        tasks=heldout_task_distribution,
        build_inner_run=meta.InnerRunTemplate(
            seed=meta.TaskSeed(),
            proposer=worker_agent,
            search=meta.CandidatePolicy(),
            budget=Budget(evaluations=50),
        ),
        aggregate=meta.RobustAggregate(
            metrics=["best_score", "cost", "failure_rate"],
        ),
    ),
)

meta.run(
    task=policy_task,
    seed=baseline_policy,
    proposer=policy_mutator,
    search=meta.BestOfN(max_trials=20),
)

The outer BestOfN is not the policy being evaluated. It chooses among policy candidates. Each candidate controls fresh inner episodes, and its score comes from held-out outcomes under an independent outer evaluator.

docs.title: Budget nesting
docs.text:
Every loop has a separate budget boundary:

outer run budget
└── number of harness or policy candidates evaluated
    └── episode-suite budget per candidate
        └── inner run budget per task and seed
            └── trial budget per proposer execution

Unused inner budget does not become outer authority. A candidate cannot raise any enclosing budget. Cache reuse is valid only when task, candidate, evaluator, environment, seed, data split, and relevant budget semantics match.

docs.title: Other workflows through the same loop
docs.text: The artifact and evaluator change while the control plane remains stable.

docs.title: Prompt optimization
docs.text:
meta.run(
    task=classification_task,
    seed=TextArtifact(initial_prompt),
    proposer=reflective_text_mutator,
    search=meta.Pareto(
        maximize=["accuracy"],
        minimize=["prompt_tokens"],
    ),
)

docs.title: Skill-set evolution
docs.text:
meta.run(
    task=skill_transfer_task,
    seed=SkillSetArtifact([]),
    proposer=failure_driven_skill_agent,
    search=meta.Population(size=16),
    context=meta.RelatedFailure(limit=10),
)

docs.title: Scientific experimentation
docs.text:
class ScientificSearch(SearchProgram):
    archive = EvidenceArchive()

    def next(self, state):
        if state.claims.need_replication():
            return ReplicationSpec(
                experiment=state.claims.highest_value_unreplicated(),
                independent_environment=True,
            )

        return TrialSpec(
            task_id=state.task_id,
            parent_ids=state.claims.relevant_artifacts(),
            proposer=state.proposers.choose_role("experiment-design"),
            operator=OperatorSpec(kind="experiment"),
            context_policy=ContradictionsAndEvidence(),
            budget=state.budget.next_trial(),
        )

Simulation or execution evidence updates a scoped claim; it does not automatically become a validated scientific discovery.

docs.title: The simplicity test
docs.text:
A new use case should normally require only:

artifact_codec = ...
task = Task(evaluator=...)
proposer = ...
search = ...

meta.run(task=task, seed=seed, proposer=proposer, search=search)

It should not require:

if artifact.type == "my-new-domain":
    coordinator.do_something_special()

When an algorithm does not fit next(state) -> SearchDecision, first ask whether it needs a generally useful typed decision such as replication, migration, merge, training, or human review. Add such a decision only when its transition, authority, budget, and event semantics are clear.

docs.title: Research and Systems References
docs.text:
This is a working map of neighboring ideas. Meta-Evolve should implement, compose, and compare these approaches rather than rename one of them as a universal solution.

Claims about capabilities in these papers belong to the cited systems. Their inclusion here does not mean Meta-Evolve has reproduced their results.

docs.title: Experience Graphs / Trellis
docs.text:
Experience Graphs: The Data Foundation for Self-Improving Agents treats the causal state produced by long-horizon search—attempts, executable artifacts, prompts, tool outputs, rewards, siblings, search statistics, and lineage—as governed database state.

Important implications for Meta-Evolve:

  • stateless agents can recover and collaborate through durable shared experience;
  • online search, causal traversal, semantic reuse, temporal reconstruction, observability, and training views operate over one logical model;
  • the system must preserve the state observed when a decision was made, not only final mutated search statistics;
  • experience retrieval is a policy with an exploration-versus-anchoring tradeoff;
  • derived skills and training views inherit provenance and access constraints.

The paper reports preliminary domain-specific results for cross-session reuse in kernel optimization, including faster early convergence and fewer buggy nodes, while aggressive reuse reduced strategy diversity and missed the best final candidate. This motivates controlled context-policy experiments rather than a general claim that more memory always improves search.

Trellis overlaps with Meta-Evolve's data plane, not its entire product scope. Meta-Evolve focuses additionally on programmable harness and search abstractions, execution adapters, contributed agents/evaluators/compute, verification, and federation.

docs.title: DSPy
docs.text:
DSPy provides a declarative programming model for modular LM programs and optimizers that compile prompts and demonstrations against metrics.

Meta-Evolve should integrate DSPy in both directions:

  • wrap a DSPy program as a versioned harness component;
  • use a DSPy optimizer for an inner prompt/program compilation loop;
  • expose Meta-Evolve examples and evaluators as DSPy-compatible data and metrics;
  • capture compiled programs as immutable artifacts;
  • let an outer Meta-Evolve policy compare DSPy with other optimizers.

The boundary is: DSPy programs LM pipelines; Meta-Evolve programs and evolves populations of executable systems, including DSPy pipelines.

docs.title: GEPA
docs.text: GEPA uses reflective textual mutation and Pareto selection to optimize LM components from task feedback. It is a reference for TextArtifact mutation, evidence-aware reflection, and Pareto retention.

docs.title: Feedback Descent
docs.text: Feedback Descent motivates structured comparison feedback followed by feedback-derived prompt edits. The research lab isolates that mechanism without claiming to reproduce its results.

docs.title: AutoData
docs.text: AutoData motivates evolving data-generation recipes with solver-based quality signals. The local lab's same-model/different-context restricted/informed setup is explicitly a teaching simplification and confounder.

docs.title: EvoSkill
docs.text: EvoSkill motivates failure-driven discovery, consolidation, and held-out selection of reusable skills. Meta-Evolve should express this as evolution of SkillArtifact and SkillSetArtifact objects rather than a special memory subsystem.

docs.title: Meta-Harness
docs.text:
Meta-Harness moves optimization beyond prompts to the source code and control logic surrounding a fixed model. It motivates HarnessArtifact, typed mutation surfaces, full execution history, and external authority boundaries.

Its agentic proposer can selectively inspect the source, scores, and execution traces of prior candidates through a filesystem instead of receiving only compressed feedback. Meta-Evolve should preserve this agent-directed exploration as a scoped ExperienceReader capability alongside policy-pushed context. A read-only filesystem projection can provide compatibility for coding agents, while structured graph tools add causal traversal, logical-time queries, provenance, and governance.

docs.title: Asari inference-stack optimization
docs.text:
Asari's inference-optimization report describes many agents improving a pinned vLLM serving stack through a discover/build, evaluate, verify, and self-improve loop. It reports changes across kernels, schedulers, load balancing, and configuration, using hierarchical performance benchmarks, measurement-noise controls, and token-distribution correctness checks.

A bounded Meta-Evolve version maps cleanly onto current seams:

  • a small SourceTree overlay holds candidate kernel and configuration edits;
  • a Claude or Codex proposer investigates and changes that overlay;
  • a custom evaluator builds it against an evaluator-owned base, verifies model behavior, and returns performance metrics, uncertainty, evidence, and usage;
  • context or audited experience exposes earlier profiler and failure evidence;
  • search retains alternatives while lineage records which evidence informed each change; and
  • an external decision, never the candidate, owns production promotion.

The shipped CommandEvaluator is only a binary, single-metric exit-code adapter, so a trustworthy experiment needs a domain evaluator that parses repeated benchmark samples. A local sequential precursor is feasible, but a whole-stack implementation also needs typed mutation surfaces and portable episodes from M8 and M9, plus trusted parallel GPU workers from M10. Cross-run knowledge transfer must be introduced explicitly rather than silently widening M3's same-run experience boundary.

Meta-Evolve does not reproduce Asari's results. The scoped future work is tracked in issue #118: start with one kernel on one trusted GPU, preserve null and negative results, and defer many-agent whole-stack optimization until its dependencies ship.

docs.title: AIDE²
docs.text: Weco's AIDE² report describes a bi-level experiment in which an outer autoresearch loop rewrites an inner research agent, evaluates each rewrite across heterogeneous tasks under a fixed cost, and selects using private scores. Its reported empirical claims belong to that system. Meta-Evolve's autoresearch teaching example demonstrates only the small nested-run, budget, evidence, and split boundaries; it is not a reproduction or evidence of recursive self-improvement.

docs.title: AlphaEvolve
docs.text: AlphaEvolve demonstrates coding-agent-driven evolutionary search for algorithmic and scientific problems. It is a reference for program artifacts, evaluator-guided evolution, and populations of executable candidates.

docs.title: FunSearch
docs.text: FunSearch combines LLM-generated programs with automated evaluation and evolutionary selection for mathematical discovery. It illustrates why executable artifacts and objective evaluators are powerful while also showing that the evaluator and representation bound the discovery process.

docs.title: OpenEvolve
docs.text: OpenEvolve is an open evolutionary coding-agent framework and useful implementation reference for program databases, evaluation, and search loops. Meta-Evolve should seek adapter compatibility where practical rather than duplicate APIs without benefit.

docs.title: EvoX
docs.text: EvoX motivates treating both solutions and the search strategy as evolving artifacts. This corresponds to nested task evaluation of PolicyArtifact and SearchProgram candidates.

docs.title: Group-Evolving Agents
docs.text: Group-Evolving Agents studies evolution at the level of composite agent groups and shared experience. It is relevant to TopologyArtifact, performance-novelty selection, and group-level mutation.

docs.title: Agent0 and Dr. Zero
docs.text: Agent0 and Dr. Zero explore proposer-solver co-evolution and self-generated curricula under verifiable rewards. They motivate explicit curriculum, checkpoint, training-job, and evaluator artifacts with separate validation boundaries.

docs.title: AERO
docs.text: AERO couples self-questioning, answering, criticism, and iterative model updates. It is relevant to synthetic-experience artifacts and external training loops consuming experience-graph views.

docs.title: CORAL
docs.text: CORAL is relevant to parallel coding agents, evaluated repository successors, shared knowledge, islands, and migration. In Meta-Evolve this becomes one GitTreeArtifact task configuration rather than the universal runtime model.

docs.title: Quality diversity and island models
docs.text: Quality-diversity methods, novelty search, MAP-Elites, Pareto archives, and island models are important baselines for maintaining heterogeneous strategies and avoiding premature convergence. They should be implemented as replaceable population and migration policies.

docs.title: MemGPT
docs.text: MemGPT frames agent memory as a hierarchy that moves information between limited context and external storage. Meta-Evolve's ContextPolicy operates at this transport boundary, while the experience graph defines durable causal search state beneath it.

docs.title: Graphiti and structured memory
docs.text: Graphiti is relevant to temporal knowledge graphs and dynamic synthesis of agent memory. Meta-Evolve additionally needs executable artifacts, objective rewards, search-policy state, training views, and causal sibling/path queries.

docs.title: Event sourcing and content addressing
docs.text:
Event sourcing, temporal databases, MVCC/change-data capture, content-addressed storage, reproducible build systems, and scientific provenance systems provide established foundations for immutable facts, current projections, time travel, lineage, deduplication, and audit.

Meta-Evolve should reuse conventional database and storage systems until its measured workload demonstrates a need for specialized physical design.

docs.title: Research questions for Meta-Evolve
docs.text:
• When does heterogeneous agent diversity improve compute-normalized progress?
  • Which context policies accelerate reuse without suppressing novelty?
  • Which topologies and migration policies avoid premature convergence?
  • How should compute be allocated among exploration, exploitation, repair, synthesis, and replication?
  • Which graph features predict the value of expanding or abandoning a branch?
  • How do skills and discoveries transfer across models, harnesses, tasks, and domains?
  • Which consistency guarantees are sufficient for concurrent search?
  • How should access changes and retractions propagate into derived skills, datasets, and checkpoints?
  • Can learned or evolved search policies generalize to held-out task distributions?
  • When do nested improvement loops plateau, destabilize, or exploit evaluators?
  • What evidence and replication policies predict real scientific validity?

docs.title: SealQA research labs
docs.text:
This is a standalone guide to four small evaluated-improvement mechanisms. You do not need to open a notebook to understand the experiments. The notebooks are optional executable companions linked from each chapter.

The labs ask one recurring question:

How can an agent improve a prompt, data recipe, local harness, or reusable skill while evaluation, budgets, hidden answers, and promotion remain outside the candidate's control?

They use eight frozen LongSeal examples because LongSeal combines a concrete question with one useful document hidden among conflicting or irrelevant documents. That makes failures easy to inspect: the agent may retrieve the wrong fact, trust stale evidence, combine incompatible documents, or format the right fact incorrectly.

These are teaching implementations. They do not reproduce the cited papers, publish an official SealQA score, or establish that one method improves Claude.

docs.title: Where the notebooks are
docs.text:
You can read everything in these documentation chapters. If you want the live cells as well, use the optional notebook links:

Chapter Optional notebook Maximum Claude sessions Feedback Descent Open notebook 5 AutoData Open notebook 7 Meta-Harness precursor Open notebook 4 EvoSkill Open notebook 8 Complete curriculum 24

The complete curriculum uses at most 24 sessions.

The canonical files live under examples/18_sealqa_research_labs/. The documentation site publishes byte-identical copies; the build never executes them.

docs.title: The common experimental substrate
docs.text:
All four labs share the same declarations:

Declaration Value Why it matters Provider Claude The shipped adapter has measured interruption support. Model claude-haiku-4-5-20251001 Every arm uses one pinned model identity. max_turns 50 Bounds an ordinary agent session. pull_max_turns 50 Gives pull-enabled sessions the same turn ceiling. Adapter timeout 1,800 seconds Requests interruption after 30 minutes. Inner wall budget 1,860 seconds Leaves one minute for adapter and coordinator cleanup. Live opt-in META_EVOLVE_LIVE_CLAUDE=1 Prevents CI or casual imports from spending money.

You can verify the deterministic boundary without credentials or a provider call:

uv run python examples/18_sealqa_research_labs/inspect_substrate.py
Output
sessions: {'feedback_descent': 5, 'autodata': 7, 'meta_harness': 4, 'evoskill': 8}
total sessions: 24
inner bounds: turns=50 timeout=1800 wall=1860
solver fields: ('id', 'question', 'documents', 'metadata')
hidden answer visible: False

Each Claude call is one ordinary inner meta.run over a SourceTree workspace:

public workspace + instructions + JSON schema
                    │
                    ▼
             one Claude session
                    │
          ┌─────────┴─────────┐
          ▼                   ▼
 structured value       typed failure
 evidence + usage       no rankable metric

The outer lab is plain Python orchestration. It has no aggregate wall budget because all provider work is already bounded by the inner sessions; its local grading and validation are deterministic and tested.

docs.title: How the shared components actually work
docs.text:
The labs are small because they reuse one session adapter and change only the outer dataflow. A SessionRequest contains five explicit inputs:

label         durable human-readable role, such as feedback.editor
instructions  what this one agent session may do
schema        the exact JSON object it must return
workspace     candidate-visible SourceTree files
experience    optional bounded read grant over prior evidence

ClaudeSessionRunner.run(request) converts that request into an ordinary Meta-Evolve run:

meta.run(
    task=meta.Task(
        evaluator=session_evaluator,
        artifact=meta.SourceTree,
        objectives=(meta.Maximize("completed"),),
        budget=INNER_BUDGET,
    ),
    seed=request.workspace,
    proposer=bounded_claude_agent,
    search=meta.Greedy(max_trials=1),
    experience=request.experience,
)

Here the inner evaluator answers only “did this session complete and retain its declared structured output?” Algorithm-specific scoring happens afterward in evaluator-owned Python. This separation prevents the model from deciding whether its answer, generated item, prompt edit, harness edit, or skill is good.

The returned SessionRecord contains exactly one of a structured value or a typed failure, plus provider evidence, usage, and pull counters. Independent schema validation runs even for injected test transports, so tests and live execution cannot disagree about what counts as valid output.

The outer lab then supplies the research algorithm by connecting these generic pieces:

Principle Concrete component What may change? meta.Text, SourceTree, or SkillSet artifact How is a change proposed? One schema-constrained session request What observations guide it? Explicit workspace files or bounded experience What counts as success? Evaluator-owned exact grade or deterministic gate Which work is retained? LabResult sessions, artifacts, measurements, usage What stops runaway work? Session arithmetic plus turn, timeout, and wall bounds

That is how a research idea becomes a small algorithm here: choose the mutable artifact, decide which recorded observation reaches the next proposer, keep measurement external, and spell out the comparison. The four chapters differ mainly in those connections—not in a new framework for each paper.

docs.title: Why Claude, and why Haiku
docs.text:
Two separate decisions sit behind the provider row above.

Claude rather than Codex. Every lab requires a finite adapter timeout so a stuck session becomes a typed failure instead of an unbounded bill. The shipped Claude adapter accepts timeout_seconds alongside a finite inner wall budget. The Codex adapter refuses this contract by design: it rejects finite wall budgets because native interruption does not verify descendant cleanup (src/meta_evolve/adapters/codex_proposer.py, measured in experiments/06_sdk_capabilities/). Separately, OpenAI has announced that GPT-5.4 and GPT-5.4 mini retire from ChatGPT-authenticated Codex on August 31, 2026, which would strand a committed capture pinned to those models.

Haiku rather than a larger Claude model. Every Claude model receives the same adapter guarantees, so this is purely a cost decision: the worst case is 24 sessions of 30 minutes each. The pinned ID follows Anthropic's documented model-version scheme. Overriding the model is allowed but enters evaluator identity, so results from an overridden run cannot be silently compared against a committed capture.

docs.title: What is frozen and what may change
docs.text:
The fixture assigns exactly one role to each row:

Rows Evaluator-owned role 1 Feedback Descent development case 2 AutoData grounding case 3 Meta-Harness diagnostic case 4 Meta-Harness unseen validation case 5–6 EvoSkill induction cases 7–8 EvoSkill held-out cases

The artifact being improved changes from lab to lab:

Lab Mutable artifact Fixed outside candidate authority Feedback Descent meta.Text solver prompt Question, documents, answer, comparator, budget AutoData meta.Text generation recipe Frozen evidence, quality checks, budget Meta-Harness precursor planner.md, context_policy.json in a SourceTree Validation row, permissions, budgets, history, promotion EvoSkill one Markdown document in meta.SkillSet Held-out rows, base agent, grader, budget

This is the core Meta-Evolve authority boundary: a candidate may propose a new artifact, but it cannot score itself, reveal hidden evaluation, enlarge its budget, rewrite history, or promote itself.

docs.title: Leakage boundary
docs.text:
The committed fixture contains evaluator-only fields so local exact grading is possible. Solver and proposer views deliberately remove:

  • the reference answer;
  • source and gold URLs;
  • upstream document IDs and gold-document labels;
  • the row's teaching role or split assignment.

Solvers receive stable local IDs such as doc-01, plus document title, date, and text. A gold document can therefore be present in the evidence without a flag that tells the solver which one it is.

Feedback Descent's comparison session is an evaluator, so it may see the hidden reference answer. The prompt editor never sees it. AutoData's generated reference_answer is created by the generator for a synthetic item; it is not the hidden answer of the frozen SealQA row.

docs.title: Failure and scoring semantics
docs.text:
The labs use normalized exact-answer grading: Unicode is normalized, casing is folded, and repeated whitespace is collapsed. The remaining text must match exactly. This is intentionally simple and deterministic; it is not SealQA's official evaluation method.

A valid answer produces a metric such as:

{"exact": 1.0}  # normalized exact match
{"exact": 0.0}  # valid answer, but wrong

The following outcomes have no metric and cannot be ranked:

  • malformed structured output;
  • missing or unchanged proposal where an edit is required;
  • timeout or turn exhaustion;
  • provider or infrastructure failure;
  • policy violation, such as editing a protected harness control.

That distinction matters. “The model answered incorrectly” is evidence about the artifact; “the provider timed out” is not a low-quality answer.

docs.title: Evidence, lineage, and identity
docs.text:
Every session retains its label, structured value or typed failure, provider evidence, token/wall usage, and experience-use counters. Each lab also records the relationship between artifacts:

seed artifact ── evidence-guided proposal ──► successor artifact
      │                                          │
      └──────── evaluator-owned score ───────────┘

Behavior-affecting declarations enter identity: model, instructions, structured schema, turn limits, adapter timeout, inner budget, workspace digest, evidence digest, pull bounds, fixture-row checksum, and grading mode. A comparison can therefore detect configuration drift instead of silently ranking different experiments.

docs.title: How to run the curriculum
docs.text:
From the repository root:

uv sync --extra claude --group dev
# Authenticate Claude Code using its supported login flow.
META_EVOLVE_LIVE_CLAUDE=1 uv run --extra claude \
  python examples/18_sealqa_research_labs/run_all.py all

Replace all with feedback_descent, autodata, meta_harness, or evoskill to run one chapter. The command makes paid provider requests. It does not retry until an improvement appears.

docs.title: Current capture status
docs.text:
No live output is claimed yet. The implementation and deterministic tests are complete, but no credentialed 24-session output has been committed. The build environment did not have the explicit live opt-in. Consequently, these chapters explain what every result means without inventing an observed improvement.

The first authorized capture should be run once and preserved honestly. A tie, regression, typed failure, unused experience record, or null result is part of the finding—not a reason to rerun until the story looks better.

docs.title: Recommended reading order
docs.text:
1. Feedback Descent: improve a prompt from structured textual feedback.
  2. AutoData: improve a synthetic-data recipe using solver behavior and deterministic gates.
  3. Meta-Harness precursor: widen the mutable artifact while enforcing an explicit authority boundary.
  4. EvoSkill: convert recorded failures into a reusable skill and evaluate only on held-out rows.

The Meta-Harness chapter is a pre-M8 teaching precursor. M8 remains the sole owner of HarnessArtifact, MutationSurface, portable episode suites, replay, and promotion. Update or retire the lab when M8 ships; see the M8 design capstone.

docs.title: Start here: one improvement loop
docs.text:
Meta-Evolve repeatedly creates a candidate, evaluates it, and decides whether that candidate should influence the next attempt. Begin with a three-item checklist so every value has an obvious meaning and no randomness gets in the way.

From the repository root, run:

uv run python examples/00_checklist/main.py
Output
3
[0, 1, 2, 3]

Run uv sync --locked once before the command if this checkout has not been installed yet.

The first line says the best artifact represents three completed items. The second line is its lineage: the exact chain of artifacts that led there.

docs.title: The problem in everyday language
docs.text:
Imagine a checklist with three items:

start:       0 of 3 complete
attempt 1:   1 of 3 complete
attempt 2:   2 of 3 complete
attempt 3:   3 of 3 complete — success

We deliberately represent the checklist by only its completed-item count. This is a teaching artifact, not a realistic productivity application.

docs.title: The complete program
docs.text:
from meta_evolve import Budget, Greedy, Maximize, Task, run


ITEMS = 3


def complete_one(parent, _context):
    return parent + 1


def count_completed(candidate):
    return candidate


task = Task(
    evaluator=count_completed,
    objectives=(Maximize("completed", satisfy=ITEMS),),
    budget=Budget(evaluations=4, trials=3),
)
result = run(
    task=task,
    seed=0,
    proposer=complete_one,
    search=Greedy(max_trials=3),
)

def main():
    print(result.best())
    print([trial.artifact.value for trial in result.lineage()])


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Read it as five declarations:

Declaration Value here Responsibility Task Complete all three items Defines evaluation, success, and limits Seed 0 The initial artifact Proposer Add one Creates a candidate from the chosen parent Evaluator Return the completed count Measures the candidate independently Search Greedy Chooses what to build on and when to stop

Those components are separate because changing how candidates are generated should not silently change what counts as success.

docs.title: Follow one attempt
docs.text:
The seed is evaluated first and scores 0. Then one successor attempt is:

Greedy chooses parent 0
  → complete_one(0) proposes 1
  → count_completed(1) returns score 1
  → Greedy sees an improvement and retains 1

The same cycle turns 1 into 2, then 2 into 3. The objective declares 3 satisfactory, so the run stops.

The proposer creates a value; it does not give that value a score. The evaluator scores it; it does not choose the next parent. The coordinator keeps these roles and their records separate.

docs.title: Read the result object
docs.text:
The run returns more than the final value. These are the public inspection methods used throughout the learning path:

"""Read the completed checklist through the public result API."""

from main import result


summary = result.summary()
print("best:", result.best())
print("primary score:", summary.primary_score)
print("task usage:", summary.usage)
print("winning lineage:", list(summary.winning_lineage))
Output
best: 3
primary score: 3
task usage: Usage(evaluations=4, trials=3, tokens=0, wall_seconds=0.0)
winning lineage: [0, 1, 2, 3]

best() decodes the winning artifact. summary() exposes the selected score, resource use, and winning lineage without requiring internal event or storage objects. Later chapters use trials() for every attempted outcome and compare() for compatible runs.

docs.title: Understand the budget
docs.text:
Budget(evaluations=4, trials=3)
  • The seed consumes one evaluation.
  • Each of three successor attempts consumes one trial and, when valid, one evaluation.
  • Therefore this complete path needs four evaluations and three trials.

Greedy(max_trials=3) is the policy's stopping limit. Budget(...) is the coordinator-enforced resource ceiling. Neither the proposer nor its candidate can increase either one.

docs.title: Understand Greedy
docs.text:
Greedy keeps a single current best artifact, called the incumbent:

candidate is better? ── yes ──► use it as a future parent
          │
          no
          ▼
record the result, but keep the previous parent

Every checklist proposal improves the score, so the winning lineage contains every step. Later examples include rejected attempts; those remain recorded evidence but do not become ancestors of the winner.

docs.title: Why the separation matters
docs.text:
Suppose an unreliable proposer claims that 100 items are complete. It still cannot award itself success. In a real task, an evaluator would inspect the actual artifact and return independent evidence. Evaluation, budgets, stored history, and external promotion remain outside candidate authority.

Task ── owns evaluator, objective, and budget
 │
seed ── evaluated first ──► Search chooses a parent
                              │
                              ▼
                         Proposer creates candidate
                              │
                              ▼
                    independent Evaluator measures it
                              │
                              ▼
                 result is recorded; Search decides again

The coordinator owns this loop. This boundary stays the same when the artifact is a prompt, source tree, skill set, dataset recipe, or agent harness.

docs.title: Where randomness belongs
docs.text:
This first run has no random behavior. Its proposer always returns parent + 1, so it does not use the supplied proposer context.

The next chapter first compares search shapes with this deterministic example. Only then does it introduce the number-search benchmark, where a proposer samples several possible moves. There, recorded randomness is useful because the experiment intentionally studies uncertain proposals. It is not required to understand Meta-Evolve's basic loop.

docs.title: Check your understanding
docs.text:
1. Why are there four evaluations but only three trials?
  2. Which component decides that a score of 3 is sufficient?
  3. Can the proposer change the budget?
  4. What does [0, 1, 2, 3] describe?
Answers 1. The seed is evaluated before any successor trial begins. 2. The objective inside `Task` declares `satisfy=3`. 3. No. The coordinator enforces the task and run declarations. 4. The causal lineage of the winning artifact, not merely a list of scores.

docs.title: Change and predict
docs.text:
Change ITEMS from 3 to 5 without changing either budget.

Predict before running: the path still reaches only 3, because three trials can create only three successors. The run ends honestly with the best artifact it found; failing to satisfy the objective is not a provider or evaluator failure.

Restore the file afterward because the committed example is shared evidence.

docs.title: Learning path
docs.text:
Continue in this order. Every page is a standalone chapter with the complete mental model, annotated declarations, saved output, component boundaries, answered interpretation questions, and one small experiment. The linked notebooks are optional executable companions, not required reading.

  1. Understand search policies.
  2. Compare uncertain search fairly.
  3. Reuse experience.
  4. Inspect pushed and pulled experience.
  5. Trace derivation and valid comparison.
  6. Recover a durable run.
  7. Evolve an immutable source tree.

After the shipped learning path, the optional SealQA research labs connect four recent research mechanisms to the M7 artifact and experience seams. They are live-only, credentialed, and deliberately make no claim of reproducing published results.

The deterministic autoresearch setup then shows how an outer Meta-Evolve run can evaluate improvements to an inner researcher on public, private, and held-out tasks under fixed nested budgets.

Then use the operations and extensions lab to run the command line, add a local domain, and choose the right conformance gate.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
Artifact : A versioned value being improved, such as a number, text, source tree, or skill set.

Candidate : A proposed artifact occurrence with causal parents.

Evaluation : Independent evidence about one candidate. A typed failure has no score.

Lineage : The causal path from a result back to its seed.

Budget : A coordinator-enforced limit on work or resources.

Experience : Prior recorded observations exposed through bounded push or pull access.

For the exact API contract, continue to the programming model. For authority and identity invariants, see the architecture.

docs.title: Build an autoresearch loop with Meta-Evolve
docs.text:
Suppose you already have an agent that can improve a solution. How would you test changes to the research procedure itself without letting that procedure change its own benchmark, budget, or promotion rule?

This chapter builds the smallest complete answer. It runs offline in a fraction of a second, and you do not need to open the optional notebook to understand it.

The design is inspired by Weco's AIDE² report. It borrows the report's inner-task/outer-researcher experimental shape with fixed cost and private selection. It does not reproduce AIDE² or provide evidence of recursive self-improvement.

docs.title: The result first
docs.text:
Run this from the repository root:

uv run python examples/19_autoresearch/main.py
Output
autoresearch teaching run: outer=(evaluations=3,trials=2) inner=(evaluations=5,trials=4)
recipe=(1,) public={'public-large': 0.14285714285714285, 'public-small': 0.3333333333333333} private_quality=0.180556
recipe=(1, 2) public={'public-large': 0.2, 'public-small': 1.0} private_quality=0.321429
recipe=(1, 2, 4) public={'public-large': 0.3333333333333333, 'public-small': 0.5} private_quality=0.600000
selected=(1, 2, 4)
held_out_baseline={'held-out-small': 0.16666666666666666, 'held-out-large': 0.09090909090909091}
held_out_selected={'held-out-small': 0.5, 'held-out-large': 0.14285714285714285}
promotion=none

The selected recipe does better in this constructed example. That shows the wiring works; it is not a scientific result.

Each trial retains only its public report as candidate-visible evidence:

[
    (str(trial.artifact.value), tuple(item.kind for item in trial.evidence))
    for trial in result.trials()
    if trial.artifact is not None
]
Output
[('{"moves":[1]}', ('autoresearch-public-report',)),
 ('{"moves":[1,2]}', ('autoresearch-public-report',)),
 ('{"moves":[1,2,4]}', ('autoresearch-public-report',))]

docs.title: The two levels
docs.text:
“Inner” and “outer” describe which thing is being improved:

outer Meta-Evolve run
│
├─ artifact: a recipe for conducting inner research
├─ proposer: change that recipe once
├─ evaluator: measure the changed researcher under a fixed protocol
└─ search: retain a recipe only when private quality improves
       │
       ├─ inner run on public task A
       ├─ inner run on public task B
       ├─ inner run on private task A
       └─ inner run on private task B

after outer selection
├─ seed researcher on held-out tasks
├─ selected researcher on the same held-out tasks
└─ report the comparison; promote nothing

An inner run improves an integer on a small black-box landscape. The candidate research recipe says which move sizes it may try. (1,) makes slow local progress. (1, 2, 4) can cover more distance under the same four-trial limit.

The integer task is intentionally unimportant. In a real project, replace it with model training, a solver, a coding agent, or another measured research task. The outer contract stays the same.

docs.title: The five Meta-Evolve declarations
docs.text:
The outer loop uses the ordinary public API:

return meta.run(
    task=meta.Task(
        evaluator=evaluate_researcher,
        artifact=meta.Text,
        objectives=(meta.Maximize("private_quality"),),
        budget=OUTER_BUDGET,
    ),
    seed=SEED,
    proposer=propose_researcher,
    search=meta.Greedy(max_trials=OUTER_TRIALS),
    context=meta.AncestorsOnly(max_records=CONTEXT_RECORDS),
    budget=OUTER_BUDGET,
    random_seed=0,
)

Read it as a sentence: Task fixes evaluation and limits; SEED is the starting recipe; propose_researcher proposes a successor; Greedy retains improvements; and AncestorsOnly supplies public reports from parent lineage.

The coordinator records every candidate, score, proposal hypothesis, evidence reference, decision, usage total, and causal parent.

docs.title: The candidate-controlled surface
docs.text:
The complete mutable artifact is tiny JSON:

{"moves":[1,2,4]}

decode permits only the moves key, one to four integer moves, and values between 1 and 8. An invalid recipe produces a typed InvalidOutput with no metric, so malformed output can never outrank a valid researcher.

import meta_evolve as meta

outcome = lab["evaluate_researcher"](meta.Text('{"moves":[0]}'))
print("failure:", type(outcome.failure).__name__)
print("metrics:", dict(outcome.metrics))
Output
failure: InvalidOutput
metrics: {}

Everything else is experiment-controlled:

Control Owner Move recipe Candidate Public, private, and held-out tasks Evaluator Inner and outer budgets Experiment private_quality calculation Evaluator Greedy admission Search policy Whether a winner is deployed Governance / user

This separation is the safety and validity mechanism. “Self-improvement” does not mean self-authorized evaluation or deployment.

docs.title: One candidate evaluation
docs.text:
evaluate_researcher first validates the recipe. It then performs four inner runs under byte-identical declarations:

public = score(researcher, PUBLIC_TASKS)
private = score(researcher, PRIVATE_TASKS)
return EvaluationResult(
    metrics={"private_quality": fmean(private.values())},
    evidence=(
        EvidenceDraft(
            kind=PUBLIC_REPORT,
            data={"scores": public, "inner_trials_per_task": INNER_TRIALS},
        ),
    ),
)

Public per-task outcomes become inspectable evidence. Private task names, targets, and per-task outcomes are not placed in evidence. The outer search policy receives only their aggregate metric for selection.

The deterministic proposer extracts only autoresearch-public-report records. Its ProposalResult.derived_from points to the report it used. This preserves the causal claim “this change was based on that observation.”

docs.title: Exact budget arithmetic
docs.text:
The seed and two successors give the outer run:

3 outer evaluations = 1 seed + 2 proposals
2 outer trials      = 2 proposals

Each outer evaluation runs four benchmark tasks. Each task permits the seed plus four inner proposals:

5 inner evaluations per task
× 4 tasks per outer evaluation
× 3 outer evaluations
= 60 inner evaluations used for selection at most

After selection, the seed and winner each run on two held-out tasks:

5 × 2 policies × 2 held-out tasks = 20 post-selection evaluations at most

The nested runs own their own hard budgets. The outer budget counts outer candidate evaluations; it does not pretend that a nested benchmark call is one unit of physical work. A production setup should additionally aggregate token, GPU-hour, dollar, and wall-clock usage at the evaluator boundary.

docs.title: Why three task splits?
docs.text:
The public tasks provide feedback for proposing the next researcher. The private tasks decide whether the proposal survives. Held-out tasks are touched only after the search has selected a winner.

Split Candidate model may see details? Affects selection? Public Yes Indirectly, through proposals Private No Yes, through aggregate quality Held-out No during search No

If the outer model sees private targets or per-task results, “private” is only a label. If held-out results influence another proposal, those tasks have become part of development and a new untouched suite is required.

docs.title: Replacing the deterministic proposer with an agent
docs.text:
The deterministic proposer keeps CI credential-free. A model-backed wrapper should preserve this boundary:

ProposerContext → allowlisted public evidence → private workspace
  → one bounded agent session → validated ProposalResult
  → derived_from references and usage

Do not give the model raw outer context because it contains the aggregate private metric needed by trusted search. Build an allowlisted workspace. The prompt-optimization example shows how a callable outer proposer can run a bounded source-tree agent one level down and lift the result back into meta.Text.

For a source-code researcher, change the artifact to meta.SourceTree, use an exact mutation allowlist, and evaluate each candidate in a fresh workspace. Keep benchmark source, credentials, permissions, and promotion controls outside that tree.

docs.title: What the comparison may claim
docs.text:
This tiny example supports one narrow statement: under the declared toy tasks and equal inner budgets, the selected recipe has higher private and held-out quality than the seed.

It does not establish real-domain autonomy, superiority to experts, statistical robustness, out-of-distribution generalization, accelerating improvement, reward-hacking safety, or readiness for automatic deployment.

Those claims require larger protocols, repeated runs, fixed physical costs, external baselines, untouched tasks, and adversarial checks. Negative results, ties, typed failures, and rejected proposals must remain in the record.

docs.title: Relationship to M8
docs.text:
This is a pre-M8 composition of shipped M7 pieces: meta.Text, nested meta.run, typed evidence and failures, lineage, budgets, and an ordinary search policy. It introduces no production harness type or runtime behavior.

M8 remains the owner of HarnessArtifact, MutationSurface, portable episode suites, replay, and promotion. When M8 ships, update this example to use those contracts or retain it only as the explicitly small composition. See the M8 design capstone.

docs.title: Leakage and validity checklist
docs.text:
Before adapting the pattern, answer these questions:

  1. Can candidate code read private task files, environment variables, grader output, or prior held-out results?
  2. Are baseline and candidate evaluated on exactly the same tasks, seeds, model identity, tool permissions, and physical budget?
  3. Can a candidate increase concurrency, retries, context, or model calls and thereby buy a better score?
  4. Are malformed output, timeout, policy violation, and infrastructure failure unrankable typed outcomes rather than zeros?
  5. Does every proposal identify the public evidence it actually used?
  6. Is held-out evaluation run once after selection and excluded from promotion unless promotion policy explicitly owns it?

docs.title: Change and predict
docs.text:
Change INNER_TRIALS from 4 to 2, update INNER_BUDGET consistently, and predict which recipe wins before rerunning the example. Then ask whether the winner changed because its research strategy is generally better or because the experiment changed the resource regime.

The optional notebook runs the same canonical module; this page contains the complete explanation.

docs.title: Understand search policies
docs.text:
The first run showed the core loop without randomness. This chapter keeps that simple checklist long enough to explain what search actually controls. It adds uncertain number proposals only after the deterministic case is clear.

Open the canonical executed notebook if you want to rerun its cells. The notebook begins at the number-search part; this standalone chapter adds the gentler checklist introduction first.

docs.title: What it teaches
docs.text:
One improvement attempt contains two decisions that are easy to confuse:

  1. The search policy chooses a parent artifact.
  2. The proposer turns that parent into a new candidate.

The evaluator measures the candidate. Search uses the retained evidence to decide what receives the next attempt.

Search chooses parent → Proposer creates candidate → Evaluator scores it
         ▲                                                   │
         └──────── coordinator records the outcome ──────────┘

Search does not rewrite artifacts or select the proposer's future parent.

docs.title: Stage 1: the deterministic checklist
docs.text:
The artifact is the number of completed checklist items. The seed is 0, one proposal completes one item, and score is the resulting count.

ITEMS = 3

def propose(parent, _context):
    return parent + 1

def evaluate(candidate):
    return candidate

There is only one possible candidate from any parent:

Parent Candidate Score 0 1 1 1 2 2 2 3 3

The common task declares what success and permitted work mean:

task = meta.Task(
    evaluator=evaluate,
    objectives=(meta.Maximize("completed", satisfy=ITEMS),),
    budget=meta.Budget(evaluations=4, trials=3),
)

The seed costs one evaluation. Three more fund the successor trials. No policy can exceed this ceiling.

docs.title: Greedy builds a chain
docs.text:
result = meta.run(
    task=task,
    seed=0,
    proposer=propose,
    search=meta.Greedy(max_trials=3),
)

Greedy maintains one best-so-far artifact, called the incumbent. Because every candidate improves the checklist, each one becomes the next parent:

0 → 1 → 2 → 3

This is a chain. Greedy is useful when small improvements compose: fixing one issue makes a useful base for fixing the next.

docs.title: BestOfN makes independent attempts
docs.text:
Now change only the search declaration:

search=meta.BestOfN(max_trials=3)

BestOfN always gives the proposer the original seed. The proposer therefore receives 0 three times and returns 1 three times:

       ┌─ 1
0 ─────┼─ 1
       └─ 1

This is a star. The best artifact is 1, with lineage [0, 1]. Separate candidate occurrences remain separate recorded attempts even when their content is equal.

BestOfN is useful when attempts should not build on one another—for example, sampling several independent answers or prompt drafts. It buys breadth, not multi-step refinement.

The checklist exposes the key difference without any luck:

Policy Parent for attempt 2 Can compose steps? Best here Greedy 1 Yes 3 BestOfN 0 No 1

Neither result means one policy is universally better. This particular problem requires composition, so its structure favors Greedy.

docs.title: Population keeps several possibilities
docs.text:
Population retains a bounded ranked archive instead of one incumbent:

seed
├─ candidate A ── successor
├─ candidate B
└─ candidate C ── successor

That tree matters when branches may lead somewhere different. The checklist cannot produce useful diversity, so Population only adds machinery there. Its size limits retained candidates; tournament_size controls how strongly parent selection favors higher-ranked members.

Practical rule: if attempts should be independent, start with BestOfN. If improvements compose, start with Greedy; use Population when losing alternatives may matter later. Confirm that choice with equal-condition evaluation evidence.

docs.title: Stage 2: add uncertain proposals
docs.text:
Only now introduce the notebook's benchmark. The seed is 0, the target is 12, and a proposal adds one of -2, 1, or 5:

TARGET = 12
MOVES = (-2, 1, 5)

def propose(parent, context):
    move = context.rng.choice(MOVES)
    return parent + move

def evaluate(candidate):
    return -abs(candidate - TARGET)

The score is negative distance because the objective maximizes:

Candidate Distance from 12 Score 0 12 -12 5 7 -7 11 1 -1 12 0 0

Higher is better: -1 is better than -7, and 0 means the target was reached. This scoring trick belongs to this benchmark, not to Meta-Evolve itself; evaluators can return ordinary positive metrics too.

docs.title: What the RNG is doing
docs.text:
context.rng is a recorded random stream supplied for that logical decision. The proposer uses it because this benchmark intentionally allows multiple moves from one parent.

result = meta.run(
    task=task,
    seed=0,
    proposer=propose,
    search=meta.Greedy(max_trials=8),
    random_seed=1,
)

The root random_seed makes local choices repeatable. It does not:

  • determine what score means;
  • choose a parent on the proposer's behalf;
  • make a hosted language model deterministic;
  • turn replay into a fresh rerun.

The checklist needed no RNG because its proposer had exactly one action. Here, randomness represents uncertainty in which candidate gets proposed.

docs.title: Read the three search shapes
docs.text:
With eight successor trials:

  • Greedy can accumulate moves along one improving chain.
  • BestOfN can reach only -2, 1, or 5, because every attempt starts at seed 0.
  • Population can accumulate moves along several retained branches.
for name, result in runs.items():
    summary = result.summary()
    print(
        name,
        f"score={summary.primary_score}",
        f"usage={summary.usage}",
        f"lineage={list(summary.winning_lineage)}",
    )
Output
Greedy score=0 usage=Usage(evaluations=6, trials=5, tokens=0, wall_seconds=0.0) lineage=[0, 5, 10, 11, 12]
BestOfN score=-7 usage=Usage(evaluations=9, trials=8, tokens=0, wall_seconds=0.0) lineage=[0, 5]
Population score=-2 usage=Usage(evaluations=9, trials=8, tokens=0, wall_seconds=0.0) lineage=[0, 1, 2, 7, 8, 9, 14]

Greedy stopped early after satisfying score 0. The other policies used all nine evaluations. This single run demonstrates mechanism; it does not establish that Greedy is generally superior.

The public result object lets us inspect the winner, score, causal path, and the seed evaluation without reading coordinator internals:

result = runs["Greedy"]
summary = result.summary()
print("best:", result.best())
print("primary score:", summary.primary_score)
print("winning lineage:", list(summary.winning_lineage))
print("seed metrics:", dict(result.trials()[0].metrics))
Output
best: 12
primary score: 0
winning lineage: [0, 5, 10, 11, 12]
seed metrics: {'score': -12}

trials() includes the seed and every attempted successor. lineage() keeps only the causal ancestors of the selected artifact. Rejected candidates and typed failures remain recorded even when they are absent from that winning path.

docs.title: What to notice
docs.text:
• Parent selection and candidate generation are different responsibilities.
  • Greedy produces a chain; BestOfN produces a star; Population produces a tree.
  • The best policy depends on whether improvements compose and diversity matters.
  • Randomness belongs to a component that needs it; it is not mandatory setup.
  • The seed is evaluated before successor trials and therefore costs evaluation budget.
  • Search selects a best artifact inside a run; it does not externally deploy or promote that artifact.

docs.title: Interpretation questions
docs.text:
1. Why does deterministic BestOfN stop at one completed checklist item?
  2. Why is Population unnecessary for that checklist proposer?
  3. Why can number-search BestOfN never reach 12?
  4. What is the difference between replay and rerunning with the same root seed?
Answers 1. Every attempt expands seed `0`, and the proposer adds exactly one. 2. It cannot create different alternatives from the same parent, so there is no useful diversity to retain. 3. Every proposal is one move from `0`; the only reachable values are `-2`, `1`, and `5`. 4. Replay reads committed decisions and outcomes. Rerunning invokes components again and can diverge when external systems are nondeterministic.

docs.title: Change and predict
docs.text:
First stay with the checklist. Change its proposer from parent + 1 to parent + 2 and set the target to 4.

Predict before running:

  • Greedy reaches 4 through [0, 2, 4] and stops early.
  • BestOfN repeatedly proposes 2 from seed 0 and never reaches 4.
  • The distinction still comes from parent selection, not randomness.

Then return to the unchanged number benchmark. The next chapter repeats it over many root seeds and explains what a fair policy comparison may claim.

Next: compare uncertain search fairly.

docs.title: Compare search policies fairly
docs.text:
The previous chapter explained how policies behave on one run. This chapter shows how to compare them without accidentally changing the task, budget, or measurement at the same time.

Open the canonical executed notebook if you want the cells. The benchmark, output, and interpretation are complete below.

docs.title: What it teaches
docs.text:
A policy comparison is valid only when the things that define performance are held fixed. In this benchmark, all three policies share:

  • target 12 and score -abs(candidate - 12);
  • seed artifact 0;
  • proposer moves (-2, 1, 5);
  • nine evaluations and eight successor trials;
  • root seeds 0 through 39;
  • objective direction and satisfaction threshold.

Only the search policy and its own configuration differ.

docs.title: Why one run is not enough
docs.text:
The proposer samples a move from a recorded random stream. One root seed can favor one policy by chance. A sweep repeats the same declared comparison over 40 root seeds and aggregates outcomes:

for root_seed in range(40):
    runs = [
        meta.run(
            task=TASK,
            seed=0,
            proposer=propose,
            search=make_policy(),
            random_seed=root_seed,
        )
        for make_policy in POLICY_FACTORIES
    ]

This is still a small deterministic illustration, not a claim about all search problems. Multiple seeds reveal variability inside this benchmark; they do not create task diversity.

docs.title: What must stay equal
docs.text:
Use this table when designing a comparison:

Declaration Why changing it confounds the result Task/evaluator Changes what “good” means Objective order Changes ranking and stopping Artifact kind Changes valid candidate representation Seed artifact Changes the starting difficulty Proposer identity Changes which candidates can be produced Effective budget Lets one arm buy more attempts or time Evaluation environment Changes the conditions being measured

Policy choice, policy configuration, and root random seed may differ because they are the independent variables this benchmark is studying.

Run.compare() checks these declarations before returning a comparison. It does not infer equality from similar output or function names.

docs.title: The observed distributions
docs.text:
The committed benchmark reports:
