Policy Solved Best-score behavior Why BestOfN 0/40 Always -7 Only one-step values -2, 1, 5 are reachable Greedy 15/40 Scores range -9 to 0 Improvements accumulate along one chain Population 14/40 Scores range -10 to 0 Several branches compete for a three-member archive

“Solved” means the best score equals 0, not merely that the run completed. BestOfN's invariant -7 is not bad luck: it is a proof from its topology and the move set. Its best reachable candidate is always 5.

Greedy and Population sometimes stop early after reaching the satisfaction threshold. Their evaluation-count distributions therefore include values below nine. BestOfN never solves and always consumes nine evaluations.

docs.title: Read a distribution, not just a mean
docs.text:
Ask the report object for the exact solve count and score distribution:

greedy = next(report for report in reports if report.policy == "Greedy")
print(f"Greedy solved: {greedy.solve_count}/{greedy.run_count}")
print("Greedy scores:", dict(greedy.score_distribution))
Output
Greedy solved: 15/40
Greedy scores: {-9: 1, -8: 1, -5: 3, -4: 2, -3: 3, -2: 3, -1: 12, 0: 15}

That tells more than an average:

  • 15 runs solved exactly;
  • 12 finished one unit away;
  • a small tail performed much worse;
  • success is not guaranteed by the policy.

Population solves almost as often but has a different tail. If one application cares about worst-case quality, solve rate alone is insufficient. A serious study would predeclare the summary statistics and uncertainty treatment rather than selecting whichever view looks best afterward.

docs.title: Lineage explains the mechanism
docs.text:
The report prints one representative winning lineage per policy:

topologies = {
    "BestOfN": "star spoke",
    "Greedy": "chain",
    "Population": "winning tree branch",
}
for report in reports:
    print(
        f"{report.policy}: {topologies[report.policy]} "
        f"{list(report.representative_lineage)} "
        f"(seed {report.representative_seed})"
    )
Output
BestOfN: star spoke [0, 5] (seed 0)
Greedy: chain [0, 5, 10, 11, 12] (seed 1)
Population: winning tree branch [0, 5, 10, 11, 12] (seed 0)

Identical winning values do not imply identical search. Population may have spent trials maintaining sibling branches that are absent from this one path. Use result.trials() for all attempts and result.lineage() for causal ancestry of one artifact.

docs.title: How Run.compare() protects the claim
docs.text:
for other_name in ("BestOfN", "Population"):
    comparison = runs["Greedy"].compare(runs[other_name])
    winner = comparison.winner.policy.name if comparison.winner else "tie"
    print(
        f"Greedy vs {other_name}: winner={winner}, "
        f"same_random_seed={comparison.same_random_seed}",
    )
Output
Greedy vs BestOfN: winner=greedy, same_random_seed=True
Greedy vs Population: winner=greedy, same_random_seed=True

The comparison first verifies compatibility. If evaluator, proposer, objective, budget, artifact kind, or initial artifact differs, it raises rather than presenting a misleading winner.

Exact primary-score equality is a tie. Lower token use or fewer evaluations does not silently break a score tie because that would introduce an undeclared secondary objective. Declare cost as an objective or constraint if it should affect ranking.

docs.title: Identity is a declaration, not omniscience
docs.text:
Local callable identity uses a declaration based on module and qualified name. Two callables with matching names are not mathematically proven equivalent. Configured adapters should hash behavior-affecting fields into their component version, and durable registered components should declare configuration.

For example, changing a model ID, timeout, hidden case suite, or grader threshold while preserving the same component identity makes a comparison look controlled when it is not. Identity must cover everything that can change behavior but is not already represented by task and run declarations.

docs.title: Claims this benchmark supports
docs.text:
It supports:

  • the three shipped policies produce different topology and distributions on this exact number-search task;
  • BestOfN cannot compose moves and therefore cannot solve this task;
  • Greedy and Population sometimes solve under the equal declared budget;
  • committed summaries and lineages reproduce the recorded outcomes.

It does not support:

  • Greedy is generally superior to population search;
  • 40 deterministic root seeds provide broad statistical evidence;
  • the result transfers to language models, source code, or noisy evaluators;
  • local callable names prove behavioral equivalence across code changes.

docs.title: What to notice
docs.text:
• Fairness is a property of declarations and evaluation conditions, not equal row counts in a report.
  • A root-seed sweep studies stochastic variation, not task generalization.
  • Early satisfaction changes actual usage while the maximum budget stays equal.
  • Lineage gives a mechanistic explanation for observed score distributions.
  • A comparison reports ties honestly and never uses usage as a hidden tiebreaker.

docs.title: Interpretation questions
docs.text:
1. Why is BestOfN's 0/40 result deterministic despite random moves?
  2. Why may Greedy use fewer evaluations than BestOfN under an equal budget?
  3. Can we conclude Population is worse because it solved one fewer seed?
  4. Why is changing a timeout a comparison change even if no timeout occurs?
Answers 1. Every independent proposal is one move from zero, and the best reachable value is always `5`. 2. Greedy sometimes reaches the declared satisfaction threshold and stops; equal budgets are ceilings, not mandatory spending. 3. No. This benchmark is small, task-specific, and does not quantify whether the one-run difference is stable or meaningful elsewhere. 4. Timeout changes the authorized execution regime and could affect which results are observable; identity and compatibility must describe potential behavior, not only what happened once.

docs.title: Change and predict
docs.text:
Add 12 to MOVES.

Before running:

  • BestOfN can now solve whenever at least one of eight independent samples chooses 12; its formerly fixed -7 distribution must change.
  • Greedy and Population can also solve in one step, but they already had multi-step paths to the target, so the mechanism changes less radically.
  • The proposer identity or version must change because its behavior changed.

Run the sweep in a temporary copy. Do not compare the changed run to the original as though only policy differed—the proposer declaration is now a new experimental condition.

Next: reuse prior experience while preserving temporal and authority boundaries.

docs.title: Reuse experience without losing causality
docs.text:
An improvement loop becomes more useful when a later proposal can learn from earlier failures. It becomes much harder to trust if “memory” is an invisible global variable. This chapter shows how Meta-Evolve exposes prior work as bounded, time-scoped, audited experience.

Open the canonical executed notebook only to run the cells. The entire mechanism and result are explained here.

docs.title: What it teaches
docs.text:
Meta-Evolve splits experience reuse into four ideas:

Graph       what committed records existed at a logical time
Push        what a policy selected before a proposal began
Pull        what the proposer chose to inspect during its work
Derivation  which observed records the proposal says it actually used

Evaluation remains independent. Reading a previous failure may influence a proposal, but it cannot change the grader, grant more budget, or turn a failed evaluation into a success.

docs.title: The running problem
docs.text:
The seed is 0. Ordinary proposals add one. Candidates 1, 2, and 3 are known traps: the evaluator returns a typed EvaluatorFailure, not a score. After observing two distinct failures, the proposer can jump to 10.

def evaluate(candidate):
    if candidate in {1, 2, 3}:
        return EvaluatorFailure(message=f"known trap at {candidate}")
    return candidate

def propose(parent, context):
    failures = observed_failures(context)
    candidate = 10 if len(failures) >= 2 else parent + 1
    return ProposalResult(candidate=candidate, derived_from=used_refs)

The budget is always four evaluations and three successor trials. A custom chain search makes each successful candidate the next parent so the experiment isolates experience access rather than parent-selection behavior.

docs.title: Four controlled variants
docs.text:
The task, seed, proposer, evaluator, search, root seed, and budget are fixed. Only experience declarations change:

Variant Pushed context Pull capability no-memory No No push-only Failed ancestors No pull-only No Bounded reader combined Failed ancestors Bounded reader

This is a valid A/B-style design because memory strategy is the declared independent variable. Run.compare() reports whether context and pull declarations match instead of pretending the arms are identical.

docs.title: The observed result
docs.text:
for name, (result, _) in results.items():
    summary = result.summary()
    print(
        name,
        f"score={summary.primary_score}",
        f"task_usage={summary.usage}",
        f"memory_usage={summary.experience_usage}",
    )
Output
no-memory score=0 task_usage=Usage(evaluations=4, trials=3, tokens=0, wall_seconds=0.0) memory_usage=RunExperienceUsage(context=ContextUsage(records=0, chars=0), pull=ExperienceUsage(operations=0, results=0, records=0, chars=0))
push-only score=10 task_usage=Usage(evaluations=4, trials=3, tokens=0, wall_seconds=0.0) memory_usage=RunExperienceUsage(context=ContextUsage(records=3, chars=3295), pull=ExperienceUsage(operations=0, results=0, records=0, chars=0))
pull-only score=10 task_usage=Usage(evaluations=4, trials=3, tokens=0, wall_seconds=0.0) memory_usage=RunExperienceUsage(context=ContextUsage(records=0, chars=0), pull=ExperienceUsage(operations=7, results=8, records=20, chars=20559))
combined score=10 task_usage=Usage(evaluations=4, trials=3, tokens=0, wall_seconds=0.0) memory_usage=RunExperienceUsage(context=ContextUsage(records=3, chars=3295), pull=ExperienceUsage(operations=7, results=8, records=20, chars=20855))

All arms spend evaluations=4, trials=3. Only memory-aware variants can observe both earlier traps and produce 10. The final no-memory proposal tries 3 and fails.

This demonstrates the mechanism on a constructed task. It does not prove memory generally helps; experience can also distract a proposer, suppress novelty, or consume model context.

docs.title: The temporal experience graph
docs.text:
The graph is a read model over committed occurrences:

step 0: seed proposal → artifact 0 → evaluation score 0
step 1: decision → proposal 1 → artifact 1 → evaluator failure
step 2: decision → proposal 2 → artifact 2 → evaluator failure
step 3: decision → proposal 10 → artifact 10 → evaluation score 10

Occurrences matter. Two trials that produce byte-identical artifacts remain different causal events because they may have different parents, observations, usage, and failures.

An ExperienceQuery(as_of=2) may see committed records through logical step 2; it cannot see step 3. This prevents future leakage during replay and live proposal.

historical = graph.state_at(ExperienceQuery(
    task_id=graph.task_id,
    run_id=combined.id,
    as_of=2,
))
print("visible steps as_of=2:", [node.logical_step for node in historical.nodes])
print("frontier steps:", [node.logical_step for node in state.nodes])
Output
visible steps as_of=2: [0, 1, 2]
frontier steps: [0, 1, 2, 3]

docs.title: Push: policy-selected context
docs.text:
A context policy runs before the proposer. The example's FailedAncestors policy walks the current parent lineage and selects only failed evaluations:

projection = combined._projection()
for selected in projection.context_selections:
    refs = tuple(record.ref.kind for record in selected.bundle.records)
    print(
        f"step={selected.bundle.records[-1].logical_step if refs else '-'}",
        f"reason={selected.bundle.reason!r}",
        f"refs={refs}",
        f"usage={selected.bundle.usage}",
    )
print("M3.2 declaration:", projection.context_declaration.spec)
Output
step=- reason='failed ancestor evaluations' refs=() usage=ContextUsage(records=0, chars=0)
step=1 reason='failed ancestor evaluations' refs=('evaluation',) usage=ContextUsage(records=1, chars=1098)
step=2 reason='failed ancestor evaluations' refs=('evaluation', 'evaluation') usage=ContextUsage(records=2, chars=2197)
M3.2 declaration: ContextSpec(policy=PolicyRef(name='failed-ancestors', version='1', origin='local'), max_records=20, max_chars=8000)

The committed ContextBundle contains:

  • exact structured records and references;
  • a canonical rendered form for a text consumer;
  • the selection reason;
  • truncation status;
  • record and character usage.

It is a snapshot, not a live database handle. Replay checks the recorded bundle instead of calling the selector again.

docs.title: Pull: proposer-directed inspection
docs.text:
PullAccess grants a trial-limited reader. The proposer can search, open, traverse, or compare prior records within declared caps:

meta.PullAccess(
    max_operations=20,
    max_results=20,
    max_records=100,
    max_chars=32_000,
)

Every operation is recorded as an attempt followed by success, opaque denial, or exhaustion. On the final trial, the example searches two failed evaluations, opens both, and compares their trial occurrences.

The grant's as_of boundary is fixed before proposal execution. A tool call cannot move it forward and inspect the trial currently being produced.

docs.title: Observation is not use
docs.text:
A proposer may receive ten records and rely on only two. derived_from names the ordered references it claims caused the proposal:

return ProposalResult(
    candidate=10,
    derived_from=(failure_one_ref, failure_two_ref),
)

The coordinator validates that each reference was actually visible through the committed push-then-pull observation ledger. Invented, future, duplicate, or out-of-order references become a typed policy failure; no candidate is committed.

docs.title: Memory usage is separate from task usage
docs.text: The result output above reports task and memory usage independently. Experience reads do not consume evaluation/trial budget, but they are still measured. A production experiment must also count how retrieved characters affect provider tokens and cost.

docs.title: Authority map
docs.text: Component May do May not do Context policy Select prior records under caps See future records or mutate history Pull grant Authorize bounded read operations Expand its own limits Proposer Observe granted records and propose Change evaluator or award a score Coordinator Validate visibility, usage, derivation Invent proposal intent Evaluator Return metric or typed failure Rewrite the candidate

docs.title: What to notice
docs.text:
• The first successor has no prior failure to reuse.
  • Typed failures can be valuable evidence without becoming low scores.
  • Push is chosen by policy; pull is chosen by the proposer under a grant.
  • Both channels are bounded and recorded at a logical time.
  • derived_from records claimed use, not everything that was visible.
  • Experience improves this toy result without changing task budget.

docs.title: Interpretation questions
docs.text:
1. Why can the first proposal not cite an evaluator failure?
  2. Why is a failed evaluation useful but unrankable?
  3. What prevents a pull-enabled proposer from reading its future result?
  4. Why record derivation separately from the context bundle?
Answers 1. Only the seed evaluation exists before the first proposal, and it succeeds. 2. It contains diagnostic information, but no valid metric exists for search ranking. 3. The grant has a committed strictly-prior `as_of` boundary. 4. Visibility does not prove causal use; derivation records the proposer's narrower explicit claim.

docs.title: Change and predict
docs.text:
Change the task so only one observed failure is required before jumping to 10.

Predict: each memory-aware variant should succeed one trial earlier; the no-memory arm still cannot. The task budget ceiling stays four evaluations, but actual usage may shrink if the objective has a satisfaction threshold.

Next: inspect push and pull records in detail.

docs.title: Inspect pushed context and pulled experience
docs.text:
The previous chapter introduced two routes to prior work. This chapter follows the exact records so you can decide which route belongs in a real agent setup.

Open the canonical executed notebook only if you want to manipulate the saved experiment.

docs.title: What it teaches
docs.text:
Push and pull answer different questions:

Push: “What should every proposer receive before it starts?”
Pull: “What should this proposer be allowed to investigate while working?”

They can expose the same underlying evaluation, but the decision maker, timing, audit record, and cost are different.

docs.title: Start from one trial
docs.text:
Before a successor proposal runs, the coordinator prepares two independent inputs:

projected history
   │
   ├─ context policy.select(...) ──► immutable ContextBundle
   │
   └─ experience declaration ──────► trial-scoped ExperienceGrant
                                          │
proposal starts                           └─ search/open/compare tools

Both are limited to prior committed logical time. Neither provides evaluator, budget, storage-write, or promotion authority.

docs.title: Pushed context step by step
docs.text:
The FailedAncestors policy selects failed evaluations from the current parent's ancestry. Its output over three proposals is:

push_run = results["push-only"][0]
push_projection = push_run._projection()

for index, selected in enumerate(push_projection.context_selections, start=1):
    records = selected.bundle.records
    labels = tuple(
        f"{record.ref.kind}@{record.logical_step}" for record in records
    )
    print(
        f"trial={index}",
        f"selected={labels}",
        f"chars={selected.bundle.usage.chars}",
    )
Output
trial=1 selected=() chars=0
trial=2 selected=('evaluation@1',) chars=1098
trial=3 selected=('evaluation@1', 'evaluation@2') chars=2197

Why the sequence grows:

  1. Before trial 1, no successor has failed.
  2. Trial 1 evaluates candidate 1 and fails.
  3. Before trial 2, that one failure is an ancestor observation.
  4. Trial 2 evaluates candidate 2 and fails.
  5. Before trial 3, both failures are available.

The final selection exposes the exact bundle metadata:

bundle = push_projection.context_selections[-1].bundle
print("reason:", bundle.reason)
print("truncated:", bundle.truncated)
print("usage:", bundle.usage)
print("refs:", tuple(
    f"{record.ref.kind}@{record.logical_step}" for record in bundle.records
))
Output
reason: failed ancestor evaluations
truncated: False
usage: ContextUsage(records=2, chars=2197)
refs: ('evaluation@1', 'evaluation@2')

Structured proposers can inspect records; a model adapter can use the bounded rendered form. Recording both prevents the rendered prompt from becoming the only evidence of what was supplied.

docs.title: Why a bundle is a snapshot
docs.text: Once selected, a bundle cannot observe newly committed work. The proposal gets stable input, replay can validate exact references and bytes, and concurrent workers cannot silently see different “latest” histories. Replay reads the snapshot rather than rerunning FailedAncestors under changed code or data.

docs.title: Pull grants step by step
docs.text:
Each successor receives a fresh grant whose as_of equals the last committed logical step:

pull_run = results["pull-only"][0]
pull_projection = pull_run._projection()

for issued in pull_projection.experience_grants:
    operations = pull_projection.operations_for(issued.grant.trial_id)
    print(f"grant as_of={issued.grant.as_of}")
    for attempt, resolution in operations:
        result = getattr(resolution, "result", None)
        count = len(result.references) if result is not None else 0
        print(
            f"  {attempt.request.operation:<7}",
            f"{type(resolution).__name__:<28}",
            f"refs={count}",
        )
Output
grant as_of=0
  search  ExperienceOperationSucceeded refs=0
grant as_of=1
  search  ExperienceOperationSucceeded refs=1
  open    ExperienceOperationSucceeded refs=1
grant as_of=2
  search  ExperienceOperationSucceeded refs=2
  open    ExperienceOperationSucceeded refs=1
  open    ExperienceOperationSucceeded refs=1
  compare ExperienceOperationSucceeded refs=2

An operation has two durable phases:

ExperienceOperationAttempted
          │
          ├─► ExperienceOperationSucceeded(result references + bounded data)
          ├─► ExperienceOperationDenied(opaque reason)
          └─► ExperienceOperationExhausted(which cap was reached)

Recording the attempt separately matters for crash recovery: if a process dies after the attempt commits but before resolution, resume can recognize and roll forward that incomplete operation.

docs.title: The four useful pull operations
docs.text: Search returns bounded matching references; open resolves an authorized reference; traverse follows causal relationships; and compare returns structured views of named occurrences. All remain inside the temporal grant and consume operation, result, record, and character caps.

docs.title: The canonical observation ledger
docs.text:
Derivation validation needs one deterministic order across both channels. The ledger is built as:

1. pushed bundle references, in bundle order
2. successful pull result references, in operation order
3. structured references contained in those results
4. duplicates removed at their first occurrence

For the combined arm's final proposal, inspect the ledger and declaration together:

combined_run = results["combined"][0]
combined = combined_run._projection()
final = combined.completed_trials[-1].trial.id
proposal = combined.proposal_for(final)
ledger = observation_ledger(combined, final)

print("ledger kinds:", tuple(reference.kind for reference in ledger))
print("declared kinds:", tuple(ref.kind for ref in proposal.derived_from))
positions = tuple(ledger.index(ref) for ref in proposal.derived_from)
print("declared positions:", positions)
print("ordered subsequence:", positions == tuple(sorted(positions)))
Output
ledger kinds: ('evaluation', 'evaluation', 'trial', 'trial', 'decision', 'decision', 'decision_explanation', 'decision_explanation', 'proposal', 'proposal', 'artifact', 'artifact', 'outcome', 'outcome')
declared kinds: ('evaluation', 'evaluation', 'trial', 'trial')
declared positions: (0, 1, 2, 3)
ordered subsequence: True

Those positions are (0, 1, 2, 3), a valid ordered subsequence. The proposer may omit observed records it did not use, but it may not reorder or invent them.

docs.title: Choosing push, pull, or both
docs.text:
Choose When it fits Push Every proposal needs a stable compact briefing and predictable size Pull Relevant history depends on what the proposer discovers Both A required briefing should coexist with selective investigation

Combined access may expose the same fact twice, so measure duplicated content.

docs.title: Usage accounting
docs.text:
The public result API reports the committed totals:

for name, (result, _) in results.items():
    usage = result.experience_usage()
    print(
        f"{name:<10}",
        f"context=({usage.context.records}, {usage.context.chars})",
        f"pull=({usage.pull.operations}, {usage.pull.results},",
        f"{usage.pull.records}, {usage.pull.chars})",
    )
Output
no-memory  context=(0, 0) pull=(0, 0, 0, 0)
push-only  context=(3, 3295) pull=(0, 0, 0, 0)
pull-only  context=(0, 0) pull=(7, 8, 20, 20559)
combined   context=(3, 3295) pull=(7, 8, 20, 20855)

Counts are cumulative over the run. results counts returned result objects; records counts structured records contained in them. They need not match.

Memory usage is not evaluation/trial usage. For a live model, however, rendered characters often become provider tokens, so the evaluator or proposer should also report actual token and wall usage.

docs.title: Failure and denial semantics
docs.text:
Exhaustion and denial are not empty search results:

  • empty success means the query was authorized and matched nothing;
  • denial means policy refused the operation without leaking protected detail;
  • exhaustion means an explicit grant cap was reached;
  • infrastructure failure means the reader could not reliably answer.

Adapters must preserve these differences. A silent fallback from pull to “no memory” changes the experiment and hides a failure.

docs.title: What to notice
docs.text:
• Push records the experimenter's selection; pull records the agent's choices.
  • Grants are trial-scoped and strictly prior.
  • A search reference and an opened record are separately auditable.
  • The ledger is push-then-pull and deduplicated deterministically.
  • Memory access has its own cumulative accounting.
  • Neither channel can modify the durable graph.

docs.title: Interpretation questions
docs.text:
1. Why not give the proposer a mutable graph object directly?
  2. What does an empty successful search prove?
  3. Why are push records ordered before pull results in the ledger?
  4. When is pull worth its larger usage footprint?
Answers 1. It would create ambient, time-varying authority and make replay impossible to validate exactly. 2. The operation was authorized and no visible prior record matched; it does not mean the reader failed. 3. Push is observed before proposal execution; pull observations occur later in committed operation order. 4. When selective investigation can find relevant evidence that a stable small pushed bundle cannot anticipate, and the added cost is measured.

docs.title: Change and predict
docs.text:
Set PullAccess.max_operations=3.

The final proposer needs four operations—search, open, open, compare. Predict that the fourth attempt exhausts the grant, pull usage stops at the cap, and a proposal that requires the comparison reference cannot validly cite it. The coordinator must record exhaustion rather than silently omit the operation.

Next: trace declared derivation and comparison.

docs.title: Trace derivation and compare memory strategies
docs.text:
Seeing a record and using it are different facts. This chapter shows how a proposal makes a causal-use claim, how the coordinator validates it, and how runs with different memory declarations can still be compared honestly.

Open the canonical executed notebook only for executable inspection.

docs.title: What it teaches
docs.text:
ProposalResult.derived_from is not a free-form citation. It is an ordered set of typed references to prior records the proposer was authorized to observe.

available history ── push/pull policy ──► observation ledger
                                              │
proposal declares derived_from ───────────────┘
                                              │ validate
                                              ▼
                                     committed causal edges

The edge survives regardless of whether the proposed artifact later scores, fails evaluation, or loses search selection.

docs.title: Follow the constructed run
docs.text:
All four variants spend the same task usage:

for name, (result, _) in results.items():
    outcomes = tuple(
        trial.failure.kind
        if trial.failure is not None
        else trial.metrics["score"]
        for trial in result.trials()
    )
    print(
        f"{name:<10}",
        f"outcomes={outcomes}",
        f"task_usage={result.summary().usage}",
    )
Output
no-memory  outcomes=(0, 'evaluator_failure', 'evaluator_failure', 'evaluator_failure') task_usage=Usage(evaluations=4, trials=3, tokens=0, wall_seconds=0.0)
push-only  outcomes=(0, 'evaluator_failure', 'evaluator_failure', 10) task_usage=Usage(evaluations=4, trials=3, tokens=0, wall_seconds=0.0)
pull-only  outcomes=(0, 'evaluator_failure', 'evaluator_failure', 10) task_usage=Usage(evaluations=4, trials=3, tokens=0, wall_seconds=0.0)
combined   outcomes=(0, 'evaluator_failure', 'evaluator_failure', 10) task_usage=Usage(evaluations=4, trials=3, tokens=0, wall_seconds=0.0)

The no-memory arm produces three evaluator failures after its seed. Push, pull, and combined arms observe the first two failures and produce 10 on the third proposal.

This separates three stages:

  1. observation may influence proposal;
  2. the proposal commits an artifact and causal claim;
  3. independent evaluation decides whether that artifact is rankable.

docs.title: Exact committed edges
docs.text:
Read each committed proposal's derivation in logical-step order:

for name in ("push-only", "pull-only", "combined"):
    result, _ = results[name]
    projection = result._projection()
    print(name)
    for submitted in projection.proposals:
        trial = projection.completed_trial(submitted.proposal.trial_id).trial
        kinds = tuple(ref.kind for ref in submitted.proposal.derived_from)
        print(f"  step={trial.logical_step} derived_from={kinds}")
Output
push-only
  step=1 derived_from=()
  step=2 derived_from=('evaluation',)
  step=3 derived_from=('evaluation', 'evaluation')
pull-only
  step=1 derived_from=()
  step=2 derived_from=('evaluation',)
  step=3 derived_from=('evaluation', 'evaluation', 'trial', 'trial')
combined
  step=1 derived_from=()
  step=2 derived_from=('evaluation',)
  step=3 derived_from=('evaluation', 'evaluation', 'trial', 'trial')

Why trial references matter: an evaluation says how an artifact was measured; a trial occurrence carries the causal attempt in which it appeared. The artifacts could even have equal content while their trial identities differ.

docs.title: A failed evaluation does not erase derivation
docs.text:
Suppose step 2 legitimately uses the step-1 failure, proposes candidate 2, and then candidate 2 also fails evaluation. The causal statement remains true: the earlier failure influenced the proposal. Removing the edge would confuse “the idea did not work” with “the idea was never used.”

Typed outcome and causal lineage are orthogonal:

Proposal valid? Evaluation valid? Artifact committed? Derivation kept? Rankable? Yes Yes Yes Yes Yes Yes Typed evaluator failure Yes Yes No Typed proposer failure Not run No Valid refs may be recorded on failure evidence No Invalid derivation Not run No No No

docs.title: Validation rules
docs.text:
A derivation declaration must be:

  • made of typed ExperienceRef values;
  • unique;
  • strictly prior to the proposal;
  • authorized by its push/pull observation ledger;
  • in the same order as first observation.

The coordinator, not the proposer, enforces those rules. An unauthorized edge becomes PolicyViolation and no candidate is committed.

Failure precedence is deliberate:

resource exhaustion
  outranks invalid derivation
    outranks proposer-reported failure

This reports the strongest coordinator-owned fact. A proposer cannot hide an invalid causal claim by also returning a convenient failure.

docs.title: Replay preserves the graph
docs.text:
Committed proposals contain the derivation references. Replaying the retained event stream rebuilds identical graph edges:

result, storage = results["combined"]
events = storage.events.read(result.id)
left = replay_experience_graph(result.id, events)
right = replay_experience_graph(result.id, tuple(events))
query = ExperienceQuery(task_id=left.task_id, run_id=result.id)

left_edges = tuple(node.derived_from for node in left.state_at(query).nodes)
right_edges = tuple(node.derived_from for node in right.state_at(query).nodes)
print("replayed derivation equal:", left_edges == right_edges)
print("edge sizes:", tuple(len(edge) for edge in left_edges))
Output
replayed derivation equal: True
edge sizes: (0, 0, 1, 4)

Replay does not call the context selector, reader, filtering logic, or renderer. It validates the facts that were actually committed at that logical time.

Empty derivation is omitted from canonical serialization for compatibility with older proposal bytes. Non-empty derivation is encoded and round-trips exactly. An explicitly encoded empty default is rejected as non-canonical so one logical value has one byte representation.

projection = result._projection()
bootstrap = projection.bootstrap.proposal
derived = projection.proposals[-1].proposal
bootstrap_bytes = serialization.dumps(bootstrap)
derived_bytes = serialization.dumps(derived)

print("empty derivation omitted:", "derived_from" not in bootstrap_bytes)
print("non-empty derivation encoded:", "derived_from" in derived_bytes)
print("round trip exact:", serialization.loads(derived_bytes) == derived)
Output
empty derivation omitted: True
non-empty derivation encoded: True
round trip exact: True

docs.title: Fair comparison when memory differs
docs.text:
The experiment is specifically asking whether memory access changes outcomes, so context and pull declarations are allowed to differ. Compatibility still requires equal:

  • evaluator and proposer declarations;
  • objectives and artifact contract;
  • task and run budgets;
  • initial artifact digest;
  • other behavior-affecting task conditions.

The comparison reports the intended differences, including a true self-tie:

baseline = results["no-memory"][0]
for name, (other, _) in results.items():
    comparison = baseline.compare(other)
    winner = comparison.winner.primary_score if comparison.winner else "tie"
    print(
        f"no-memory vs {name:<10}",
        f"winner={winner}",
        f"same_seed={comparison.same_random_seed}",
        f"same_context={comparison.same_context_declaration}",
        f"same_pull={comparison.same_experience_declaration}",
    )
Output
no-memory vs no-memory  winner=tie same_seed=True same_context=True same_pull=True
no-memory vs push-only  winner=10 same_seed=True same_context=False same_pull=True
no-memory vs pull-only  winner=10 same_seed=True same_context=True same_pull=False
no-memory vs combined   winner=10 same_seed=True same_context=False same_pull=False

That is more informative than either rejecting all memory experiments or pretending their declarations are equal.

docs.title: What a winner means here
docs.text:
The primary score is 10 versus 0, so the memory-aware run wins inside this task. The comparison does not say:

  • which particular retrieved record caused the numerical gain beyond the proposer's declared claim;
  • that memory improves other tasks;
  • that larger context is cost-effective for a model;
  • that the winning artifact should be deployed.

Those require additional tasks, ablations, cost objectives, and external promotion policy.

docs.title: What to notice
docs.text:
• Derivation belongs to proposal causality, not evaluation success.
  • Every edge must come from an authorized ordered observation ledger.
  • Replay rebuilds edges without rerunning retrieval.
  • Comparison may intentionally vary memory strategy while holding the task contract fixed.
  • Compatibility flags make those independent-variable differences visible.
  • Promotion remains outside both search and comparison.

docs.title: Interpretation questions
docs.text:
1. Why retain derivation for a candidate that fails evaluation?
  2. Can a proposer cite a record returned after the proposal completed?
  3. Why does comparison permit different memory declarations here?
  4. Does derived_from prove the referenced information truly caused a model's internal reasoning?
Answers 1. The reference can still have caused the attempted candidate; outcome and causality are separate facts. 2. No. It was not in the strictly-prior committed observation ledger. 3. Memory strategy is the experiment's intended independent variable; the comparison reports rather than conceals that difference. 4. No. It is the proposer's explicit, validated usage claim. Stronger causal evidence requires controlled ablations or interventions.

docs.title: Change and predict
docs.text:
Modify the proposer to cite the same evaluation reference twice.

Predict: ProposalResult rejects duplicate derivation before a candidate can be treated as successful. No artifact from that proposal becomes rankable, and the invalid edge never enters the replayed graph.

Next: recover a durable run after interruption.

docs.title: Recover a durable run after a crash
docs.text:
A useful long-running experiment must survive process death without repeating committed work or inventing a different history. This chapter explains how durable-local storage, replay, registered components, and meta.resume compose to provide that guarantee.

Use the executed notebook to rerun the fault matrix; this page contains the full explanation.

docs.title: What it teaches
docs.text:
Crash recovery is not “start a similar run again.” It is:

reopen one exact run id
  → validate its committed event prefix
  → reconstruct the last complete logical state
  → rebuild verified components
  → continue only the missing authorized work
  → reach the same final event stream as uninterrupted execution

The guarantee depends on deterministic, retry-safe components and atomic commits. A live, non-reconstructable callback cannot honestly provide it.

docs.title: The running problem
docs.text:
The example climbs from 0 to target 6 by proposing parent + 1:

def propose(parent, context):
    return parent + 1

def evaluate(candidate):
    return -abs(candidate - 6)

Reaching 6 requires six successor trials and seven evaluations including the seed. The task permits eight evaluations and Greedy permits eight successor trials, leaving slack so the run stops because it satisfies the objective rather than because budget expires.

docs.title: Why ordinary local callables are insufficient
docs.text:
An in-memory function object cannot be reconstructed after the Python process dies. Durable mode therefore requires registered module-level components:

registry = meta.Registry()
proposer_ref = registry.register_proposer(
    "example:propose", "1", propose,
    deterministic=True,
    retry_safe=True,
)
evaluator_ref = registry.register_evaluator(
    "example:evaluate", "1", evaluate,
    deterministic=True,
    retry_safe=True,
    configuration={"target": 6},
)

The durable event stream records typed component references and manifests. On resume, the supplied registry must resolve compatible implementations whose source and configuration match those manifests.

The target belongs in evaluator configuration because changing it changes behavior even if the Python function name remains the same.

docs.title: Starting a durable run
docs.text:
run = meta.run(
    task=build_task(evaluator_ref),
    seed=0,
    proposer=proposer_ref,
    search=meta.Greedy(max_trials=8),
    storage=meta.Storage.durable(path),
    mode="durable-local",
    registry=registry,
)

Run identity derives from the declarations, not from the storage directory. Starting the same task, seed, component references, policy, and budgets on two paths produces the same run ID.

docs.title: Atomic batch commits
docs.text:
The coordinator groups each state transition into an all-or-none storage commit. A simplified run looks like:

batch 1  run + seed records
batch 2  search decision
batch 3  proposal/trial outcome
batch 4  evaluation
batch 5  next decision
...

If power fails between batches, every earlier batch is durable and the next is absent. If it fails while a batch is being written, the storage transaction commits all of it or none of it. Recovery never has to interpret half an evaluation.

The notebook's CrashAfter wrapper is only a deterministic test instrument. It permits the first n real commits and raises before the next. Production users do not install it or touch the internal commit strategy; real operating system or hardware failure supplies the interruption.

docs.title: The three recovery frontiers
docs.text:
Replay classifies the committed prefix:

Frontier Last durable fact What resume does next DECISION_READY Previous work complete Ask search for the next decision TRIAL_DECIDED Trial authorization committed Run the authorized proposer work EVALUATION_PENDING Candidate outcome committed Evaluate that committed artifact

These states prevent duplicate work. For example, a committed candidate with no evaluation is evaluated; the proposer is not called again to create a possibly different candidate.

Pull experience operations add a related boundary: an attempted but unresolved read is rolled forward using the same committed operation ID.

The sweep classifies every interior boundary:

phases = {}
total_a = boundaries + 1
for k in range(1, total_a):
    p = adir / f'phase{k}'
    s = meta.Storage.durable(p)  # install + run on one handle (see sweep note)
    install_crash(s, n=k)
    try:
        main.start_run(s, main.build_components())
    except CRASH:
        pass
    events = meta.Storage.durable(p).events.read(rid_a)
    phase = classify_frontier(events, replay_run_projection(rid_a, events)).name
    phases.setdefault(phase, []).append(k)
for name, ks in phases.items():
    print(f'  {name:<18} at boundaries {ks}')
Output
  DECISION_READY     at boundaries [1, 4, 7, 10, 13, 16, 19, 22]
  TRIAL_DECIDED      at boundaries [2, 5, 8, 11, 14, 17, 20]
  EVALUATION_PENDING at boundaries [3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21]

docs.title: The demonstrated lifecycle
docs.text:
The uninterrupted reference reaches best 6 in 49 events over 23 committed batches. Then the notebook interrupts the same logical run shape:

crash_after = max(1, committed_batches // 2)
assert 1 <= crash_after < committed_batches
path_b = tmp / 'path-B'
crash_storage = meta.Storage.durable(path_b)
crasher = install_crash(crash_storage, n=crash_after)
crashed = False
try:
    main.start_run(crash_storage, components)
except SimulatedCrash as e:
    crashed = True
    print('crashed:', e)
assert crashed and crasher.commits == crash_after
crashed_len = len(meta.Storage.durable(path_b).events.read(run_id))
print(f'events on disk  : {crashed_len}  (a genuine PARTIAL stream vs {complete_len} complete)')
Output
crashed: simulated process crash after 11 committed steps
events on disk  : 25  (a genuine PARTIAL stream vs 49 complete)

After meta.resume(...) fills the missing work, compare the interrupted and uninterrupted outcomes:

assert resumed.id == run_id
assert resumed_best == reference_best
ok = resumed_best == reference_best
print(f'interrupted == uninterrupted: {ok}  ({resumed_best} == {reference_best})')
print(f'partial stream {crashed_len} events -> recovered {resumed_len} events -> best {resumed_best}')
Output
interrupted == uninterrupted: True  (6 == 6)
partial stream 25 events -> recovered 49 events -> best 6

The advanced sweep repeats this after all 22 interior boundaries. Separate sweeps cover pushed context and pull experience:

_, _, eb, eok, ebest, rollfwd = sweep(advanced.experience_run, advanced.build_components, Path(tempfile.mkdtemp()))
print(f'experience run: {eb} boundaries, all equivalent = {eok}, best = {ebest}')
print(f'  mid-operation crash boundaries rolled forward on resume: {rollfwd}')
Output
experience run: 43 boundaries, all equivalent = True, best = 6
  mid-operation crash boundaries rolled forward on resume: 7

docs.title: Reopen is not resume
docs.text:
These operations answer different questions:

cold = meta.Run(rid_a, meta.Storage.durable(adir / 'ref'))
print('best() from a cold store :', cold.best().value)
print('winning lineage steps    :', [t.logical_step for t in cold.lineage()])
Output
best() from a cold store : 6
winning lineage steps    : [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]

Run(...) rebuilds a read-only result from committed facts. It performs no new work and can inspect a completed or partial history where queries are defined.

continued = meta.resume(
    run_id,
    storage=reopened_storage,
    registry=registry,
)

resume may invoke search, proposer, and evaluator to finish missing work. It therefore requires reconstruction authority and verified components.

Resuming an already completed run is a no-op. Concurrent resume attempts use optimistic append control: one commits, while a stale writer receives EventStreamConflict rather than duplicating a transition.

docs.title: What cannot resume
docs.text:
A run may retain durable history without being resumable. Local patch callbacks, command evaluator objects, provider sessions, or closures can be inspectable after reopening while lacking a portable reconstruction contract.

Meta-Evolve raises CapabilityError instead of silently substituting a different component. Durable storage is evidence retention; resumability is an additional capability.

docs.title: What to notice
docs.text:
• The event log is append-only; crash simulation never truncates it.
  • Atomicity prevents partial logical batches.
  • Replay determines exactly which work is missing.
  • Component manifests protect behavior across process restart.
  • Run identity is logical and independent of the storage path.
  • Resume does not mean arbitrary live-model output becomes reproducible.

docs.title: Interpretation questions
docs.text:
1. Why does a committed candidate with no evaluation not run its proposer again?
  2. Why must the evaluator's target be in its manifest configuration?
  3. What is the difference between reopening and resuming?
  4. Can a non-deterministic remote provider promise a byte-identical resumed result merely because events are durable?
Answers 1. The proposal result already exists; rerunning could create a second outcome for one authorized trial. Resume continues at `EVALUATION_PENDING`. 2. The target changes scoring behavior while the function's name and source may stay constant. 3. Reopen reads committed history; resume is authorized to reconstruct components and continue missing work. 4. No. Durable observations can be retained, but equivalent future provider output requires stronger provider-specific guarantees.

docs.title: Change and predict
docs.text:
Move the simulated crash from batch 11 to batch 12.

Predict which frontier the new prefix reaches, whether the event count grows, and which operation resume performs first. The final best and complete event stream must remain identical to the reference.

Next: evolve immutable source with an external grader.

docs.title: Evolve immutable source with an external grader
docs.text:
So far, artifacts were small Python values. This chapter follows the same declarative loop when the artifact is a directory of source files and the evaluator is a real subprocess outside candidate authority.

Open the canonical executed notebook only if you want to execute the cells; this page explains the full lifecycle.

docs.title: What it teaches
docs.text:
The complete repair is:

load immutable UTF-8 source
  → propose one exact file replacement in a private workspace
  → capture a new immutable SourceTree
  → materialize it in a fresh evaluation workspace
  → run an external grader under a declared process protocol
  → commit score, evidence, usage, and parent lineage

The original checkout is never modified. A candidate proposal cannot include grader edits because the grader is not part of the candidate artifact. Runtime host isolation is a separate concern explained below.

docs.title: The broken program
docs.text:
The candidate tree contains one file, clamp.py. Its documented job is to keep value between low and high. The seed implementation is wrong; the desired replacement is:

def clamp(value, low, high):
    return max(low, min(value, high))

The evaluator-owned tests include values below, inside, and above the interval. The seed scores 0; the repaired successor scores 1.

docs.title: Step 1: load an immutable SourceTree
docs.text:
source = meta.load_source_tree(staged)
print("loaded immutable source:", tuple(source) == ("clamp.py",))
Output
loaded immutable source: True

The loader recursively captures exact relative paths and UTF-8 text. It rejects:

  • symlinks;
  • binary or non-UTF-8 content;
  • non-regular files;
  • unsafe or ambiguous paths.

There are deliberately no ignore rules. A generated __pycache__ changes the directory being declared and is rejected rather than silently omitted. Stage only intended files into a clean directory when tools may have left debris.

SourceTree is immutable. A successor is new content with parent lineage, not an in-place edit of source.

docs.title: Step 2: describe one exact patch
docs.text:
def repair(tree, context):
    return meta.TextPatch(
        path="clamp.py",
        expected=tree["clamp.py"],
        replacement=FIXED,
    )

expected is optimistic concurrency for file content. The patch applies only if the private workspace still contains the exact parent text the proposer saw. This prevents a stale patch from overwriting an unexpected revision.

PatchProposer owns the workspace lifecycle:

materialize parent → invoke patch callback → validate path/expected/replacement
→ apply exact edit → capture SourceTree → dispose workspace

Invalid path, conflict, unchanged replacement, malformed patch, and cleanup failure remain typed proposal outcomes. They are not low task scores.

docs.title: Step 3: keep the grader external
docs.text:
The evaluator declaration is:

evaluator = meta.CommandEvaluator(
    command=meta.ProcessSpec(
        argv=(python, "run_grader.py", "grader.py"),
        environment={"PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE": "1"},
    ),
    environment=meta.EvaluationEnvironment(
        name="python-clamp-tests",
        version="1",
    ),
)

For each candidate, CommandEvaluator creates a fresh workspace, materializes only the candidate source, runs the fixed command, captures bounded output, and disposes the workspace.

grader.py and run_grader.py live outside the SourceTree. The candidate cannot propose changes to them because they are not in its artifact or proposal workspace.

docs.title: The exit protocol
docs.text:
The fixed runner translates process behavior into domain outcomes:

Exit Meaning Outcome Rankable? 0 Candidate passes score=1 Yes 1 Candidate fails tests or cannot load score=0 Yes Other Grader/protocol broke EvaluatorFailure No Timeout Process exceeded wall limit TimeoutFailure No

Candidate syntax error is rankable failure because the task is to supply working source. Missing grader is not candidate performance; scoring it 0 would reward infrastructure reliability as though it measured code quality.

fault = broken_evaluator(source)
process = next(item for item in fault.evidence if item.kind == "process-result")
print("grader fault:", type(fault.failure).__name__)
print("grader fault rankable:", bool(fault.metrics))
print("grader fault process exit:", process.data["exit_code"])
print("grader fault evidence kinds:", [item.kind for item in fault.evidence])
Output
grader fault: EvaluatorFailure
grader fault rankable: False
grader fault process exit: 2
grader fault evidence kinds: ['evaluation-environment', 'process-result']

docs.title: Step 4: budget seed and successor
docs.text:
budget = meta.Budget(evaluations=2, trials=1)
task = meta.Task(
    evaluator=evaluator,
    artifact=meta.SourceTree,
    budget=budget,
)

Two evaluations cover the broken seed and one proposed successor. One trial authorizes the patch. Passing the same effective budget at task and run level makes the ceiling explicit at both declaration boundaries.

docs.title: Step 5: run the ordinary loop
docs.text:
run = meta.run(
    task=task,
    seed=source,
    proposer=meta.PatchProposer(repair),
    search=meta.Greedy(max_trials=1),
    budget=budget,
    storage=storage,
    mode="local",
)

No coordinator branch knows this is Python repair. The artifact codec handles SourceTree; the proposer handles patches; the evaluator handles process execution; Greedy sees only rankable outcomes.

docs.title: Step 6: read immutable evidence
docs.text:
The saved run prints the evaluator-owned evidence and causal result:

print("source digests:", digests)
print("scores:", scores)
print("process exits:", exits)
print("failures:", failures)
print("evidence kinds:", kinds)
print("repaired best:", best.value["clamp.py"] == FIXED)
print("parent unchanged:", source["clamp.py"] != FIXED)
print("lineage length:", len(lineage))
Output
source digests: ['659bfe4a9f389018a5059f9045d6db37592c017591629d6baf5a7ab52792ca53', '08abe248cf356c0ee0322aa9329598221640460d6cf0202228097d7f4c4c21c0']
scores: [0.0, 1.0]
process exits: [1, 0]
failures: [None, None]
evidence kinds: [['evaluation-environment', 'process-result'], ['evaluation-environment', 'process-result']]
repaired best: True
parent unchanged: True
lineage length: 2

Each lineage entry includes a content digest. The repaired tree has a different digest and names the seed artifact as its parent. Reopening durable storage can read the same best artifact and lineage without touching the checkout.

Process wall time is occurrence evidence, not deterministic identity. Content, declarations, scores, and semantic outcome are the stable parts of this local example.

docs.title: Durable history is not cold resume
docs.text:
The run uses durable storage but mode="local". Its live patch callback, command evaluator, and workspace providers have no portable reconstruction manifest. Therefore:

with meta.Storage.durable(history) as reopened:
    durable = meta.Run(run.id, reopened)
    print("reopened best:", durable.best() == best)
    print("reopened lineage:", durable.lineage() == lineage)
    try:
        meta.resume(run.id, storage=reopened, registry=meta.Registry())
    except meta.CapabilityError as error:
        if "not resumable" not in str(error):
            raise
        print("cold resume: CapabilityError (local run is not resumable)")
    else:
        raise RuntimeError("local workspace run unexpectedly resumed")
Output
reopened best: True
reopened lineage: True
cold resume: CapabilityError (local run is not resumable)

Failing closed is important. Substituting a different grader or patcher after a restart would create one run ID with two behaviors.

docs.title: The subprocess boundary is not hostile isolation
docs.text:
DevelopmentSubprocessSandbox controls working directory, environment, timeout, process-group termination, and retained stdout/stderr. It does not isolate network, CPU, memory, syscalls, or arbitrary host filesystem access.

Use a hardened container or other isolation provider for untrusted code. Do not describe this development boundary as a security sandbox.

docs.title: What to notice
docs.text:
• Candidate authority is exactly the files inside the immutable tree.
  • Exact patches prevent stale overwrite and preserve the parent.
  • Proposal and evaluation use separate fresh workspaces.
  • The external grader remains outside candidate lineage.
  • Candidate-caused failure is rankable; evaluator failure is not.
  • Durable inspection does not imply resumable execution.

docs.title: Interpretation questions
docs.text:
1. Why include expected text in a patch?
  2. Why is a candidate syntax error score 0 while a missing grader has no metric?
  3. Does SourceTree prevent candidate code from accessing the host at runtime?
  4. Why can the run reopen but not resume?
Answers 1. It ensures the patch applies to the exact parent revision the proposer saw. 2. Syntax validity is task performance; missing evaluator infrastructure means the task was never measured. 3. No. It bounds the versioned artifact and workspace capture, not hostile-code runtime authority. 4. Stored artifacts/events are portable, but the local live callbacks and providers are not reconstructable from a registry manifest.

docs.title: Change and predict
docs.text:
Change the replacement to invalid Python.

Predict: the patch itself is structurally valid and commits a new source tree; the external runner exits 1; evaluation returns rankable score=0; Greedy keeps the original seed as best; the failed candidate and its process evidence remain in run.trials() but not in the winning lineage.

You now have the complete basic path: declare a task, choose search, compare it fairly, reuse experience causally, recover durable work, and evolve real source under an external evaluator.

docs.title: Feedback Descent: improve a prompt from textual feedback
docs.text: Optional executable companion: open the canonical notebook. This chapter contains the full explanation; the notebook is not required.

docs.title: The concrete problem
docs.text:
Who holds the all-time record at the Grammys for the most wins in the album of the year category?

The solver receives this question and a noisy document bundle. It does not receive the evaluator's answer, gold URL, gold-document label, or the fact that this is the Feedback Descent development row.

Two prompt candidates start from the same evidence:

candidate A
Answer the question from the supplied documents. Return only the answer.

candidate B
Find the document that directly resolves the question, ignore conflicting
distractors, and return only the answer.

The artifact being improved is the prompt itself, represented as meta.Text. The question, documents, exact-answer grader, and budget remain fixed.

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
Ordinary optimization says only “A scored 0 and B scored 1.” Feedback Descent adds an inspectable explanation of why one candidate is preferred, then asks an editor to derive a successor from that explanation.

prompt A ──► answer A ──┐
                         ├─► pairwise preference + textual feedback
prompt B ──► answer B ──┘                 │
                                           ▼
                              edit preferred prompt
                                           │
                                           ▼
                                  evaluate edited prompt

This lab isolates that mechanism. It does not implement the paper's full search strategy or claim to reproduce its results.

docs.title: From Meta-Evolve principles to this algorithm
docs.text:
Feedback Descent sounds specialized, but the teaching loop is assembled from ordinary evaluated-improvement roles:

Role Concrete component Why it is separate Mutable artifact Two seed meta.Text prompts, then one edited prompt The thing being optimized is explicit and immutable Task input Candidate-visible case.md Every solver receives the same question and noisy documents Proposal evidence Structured preference plus textual feedback The edit can name exactly what observation caused it Proposer Editor session constrained by EDIT_SCHEMA It may rewrite a prompt but cannot score it Evaluator Pairwise comparison session plus local exact grading Hidden answer and ranking stay outside prompt authority Search shape Compare two seeds, edit the preferred one once This is a fixed teaching schedule, not an unbounded optimizer Budget Five individually bounded sessions One bad step cannot trigger retries until improvement appears

There is no numeric gradient. “Descent” means turning an evaluator's natural language diagnosis into the direction of the next artifact change:

observed answer difference
  → evaluator says which behavior was better and why
  → editor converts that reason into a general prompt instruction
  → unchanged task measures the successor

The algorithm is simple because Meta-Evolve already supplies immutable text, bounded provider sessions, structured evidence, typed failures, usage, and identity. The lab only has to specify who sees which files and how those five sessions connect.

docs.title: How the implementation moves data
docs.text:
run() loads one full EvaluatorCase, but immediately renders only case.public for solver workspaces. _solve() combines one prompt with that public file and asks for the closed ANSWER_SCHEMA.

PROMPTS[name] + public case
  ── _solve ──► SessionRecord(answer or failure)
  ── grade_record(expected answer, evaluator side) ──► Measurement

Only _comparison_request() receives case.answer. It writes a private comparison.md containing the reference and both observed answers, then asks for COMPARISON_SCHEMA. That response is evaluator evidence, not a prompt artifact.

The editor gets a new SourceTree with exactly:

prompt.md    preferred seed prompt
feedback.md  comparator's textual feedback

It cannot recover the hidden answer from those files. After schema validation, the code lifts value["prompt"] into a new meta.Text, rejects an empty or unchanged edit, records edit_derived_from="feedback.comparison", and calls the same _solve() and grade_record() path used for the seeds.

This reuse is what makes the final comparison interpretable: the artifact is different, while public case, model, schema, grader, and bounds remain fixed.

docs.title: The five sessions
docs.text:
# Session Observes Produces 1 candidate_a solver Prompt A, public question and documents Structured answer A 2 candidate_b solver Prompt B, identical public question and documents Structured answer B 3 Pairwise evaluator Both answers and evaluator-only reference answer Preferred candidate and textual feedback 4 Prompt editor Preferred prompt and textual feedback only Rewritten prompt 5 Edited-prompt solver Rewritten prompt, original public question and documents Structured answer for exact grading

The editor never sees the reference answer or gold URL. Its input is exactly the preferred prompt plus the feedback, so the successor can record:

edited prompt derived_from feedback.comparison

If the comparison or editor fails, later dependent sessions do not run. Five is the ceiling for one complete path, not a promise to spend five calls after a typed failure makes the remaining comparison meaningless.

docs.title: Structured evidence
docs.text:
The evaluator must return this closed-world shape:

{
  "preferred_candidate": "candidate_a",
  "textual_feedback": "A general explanation of what the prompt should change."
}

preferred_candidate may be only candidate_a or candidate_b. Feedback must be non-empty, and extra fields are rejected. The independent validator runs for both live Claude output and injected test output.

The editor separately returns:

{"prompt": "The complete rewritten solver prompt."}

An empty or unchanged prompt is a typed ProposerFailure; it is not evaluated as if it were a new candidate.

docs.title: Minimal runnable mechanism
docs.text:
The real implementation is deliberately small:

from sealqa_labs import ClaudeSessionRunner
from sealqa_labs.feedback_descent import run

result = run(ClaudeSessionRunner())

print("preferred:", result.artifacts.get("preferred"))
print("feedback:", result.artifacts.get("feedback"))
print("edited:", result.artifacts.get("edited"))
print("derived from:", result.artifacts.get("edit_derived_from"))
print("edited measurement:", result.measurements.get("edited"))
print("usage:", result.usage)
Illustrative shape — live run, nothing captured
preferred: <candidate_a-or-candidate_b>
feedback: <structured evaluator rationale>
edited: <complete rewritten prompt>
derived from: feedback.comparison
edited measurement: <exact metric or typed failure>
usage: <aggregated provider usage>

Run it from the repository root after authenticating Claude Code:

META_EVOLVE_LIVE_CLAUDE=1 uv run --extra claude \
  python examples/18_sealqa_research_labs/run_all.py feedback_descent

The five sessions all use the pinned Haiku model, equal 50-turn ceilings, a 1,800-second adapter timeout, and a 1,860-second inner wall budget.

docs.title: How to read the result
docs.text:
Inspect these fields in order:

  1. sessions: did every requested session succeed, and what did it cost?
  2. measurements.candidate_a and candidate_b: were the initial answers exact?
  3. artifacts.preferred: which prompt did the evaluator select?
  4. artifacts.feedback: is the explanation general, actionable, and grounded in the observed difference?
  5. artifacts.edited: did the editor actually change the prompt?
  6. artifacts.edit_derived_from: does lineage name the comparison evidence?
  7. measurements.edited: did the one edited evaluation improve, tie, or regress?

Possible outcomes are intentionally broader than “success”:

Outcome Honest interpretation Edited score improves The edit helped this one development case. Tie Feedback and editing bought no measured gain here. Regression The edit damaged this case; preserve the negative result. Comparison invalid There is no preference to rank or edit from. Editor unchanged No successor exists. Provider/timeout failure The attempt is unrankable, not a zero score.

One development row cannot establish general prompt quality. A robust claim would require a separately declared held-out suite and repeated compatible comparisons.

docs.title: Leakage and validity checklist
docs.text:
• Only the pairwise evaluator may read the hidden reference answer.
  • Neither solver request contains source URLs, split roles, or gold labels.
  • The editor workspace contains only prompt.md and feedback.md.
  • The edited solver sees the same public case as both initial solvers.
  • All solver arms use the same model and resource declarations.
  • A favorable edit is reported once; it is not selected from repeated reruns.

docs.title: Change and predict
docs.text:
Remove “ignore conflicting distractors” from candidate B. Before running, predict:

  1. which prompt the evaluator will prefer;
  2. what general feedback it will produce;
  3. whether the edited prompt will improve, tie, regress, or fail;
  4. which evidence and lineage fields should stay unchanged.

The interesting result is not merely the final score. It is whether the recorded feedback caused an inspectable prompt change under a valid comparison.

docs.title: AutoData: improve a generation recipe with solver behavior
docs.text: Optional executable companion: open the canonical notebook. Everything needed to understand the lab is explained below.

docs.title: The concrete problem
docs.text:
What is the current age of the oldest person to sail solo across the Pacific Ocean?

This frozen row supplies the grounding documents from which a generator creates one new question-answer item. The artifact being improved is not the answer and not the generated row; it is the meta.Text generation recipe.

The seed recipe says:

Generate one unambiguous fact-seeking question answerable from the evidence.
Return its exact short answer and the document IDs used.

The lab asks whether solver behavior can identify a useful generated item and provide evidence for rewriting that recipe.

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
AutoData-style generation uses downstream behavior as a quality signal:

recipe ──► generated QA item
                    │
          ┌─────────┴─────────┐
          ▼                   ▼
 restricted solver      informed solver
 question only          question + evidence
          └─────────┬─────────┘
                    ▼
       deterministic acceptance checks
                    │
                    ▼
              rewrite recipe

The paper discusses weak and strong models. This lab deliberately uses the same pinned model with different context. The code roles are therefore named restricted_solver and informed_solver. Calling them weak and strong would hide the fact that context—not model capability—is the changed variable. That setup is a teaching simplification and a confounder.

docs.title: From Meta-Evolve principles to this algorithm
docs.text:
The important move is to optimize the recipe, not to keep whichever single question looks nice. Each component has one authority:

Role Concrete component What it contributes Mutable artifact meta.Text recipe A versioned instruction that can have a successor Generator Schema-constrained session Applies a recipe to public evidence and proposes one QA item Restricted probe Same model with question.md only Tests whether evidence is unnecessary or the answer leaks Informed probe Same model with selected evidence.md Tests whether cited evidence supports recovery Evaluator quality_checks() in local Python Converts observations into explicit acceptance reasons Proposer Recipe-rewriter session Turns the report into a generalized successor recipe Search shape Seed evaluation → one rewrite → successor evaluation Makes the causal comparison small and inspectable

The generated QA item is an evaluation episode, not the durable thing being optimized. A seed recipe and successor recipe may each generate different questions; comparison asks whether the recipe produces an item that passes the same quality protocol.

recipe artifact
  → generator applies it
  → two controlled solver contexts probe the item
  → deterministic evaluator produces accepted + reasons
  → rewriter uses that evidence to propose the next recipe artifact

This is why the method is easy to build with Meta-Evolve: artifact lineage, bounded sessions, evidence, schema failure, and usage already exist. AutoData's domain logic is the small quality_checks() function and the choice of what the two solver arms may see.

docs.title: How _evaluate_recipe() assembles one evaluation
docs.text:
The function first writes the public SealQA bundle to evidence.md and asks the generator for ITEM_SCHEMA. If generation fails validation, it returns one session plus a rejection report and spends no solver calls.

For a valid item it builds two fresh workspaces:

restricted_solver/
  question.md

informed_solver/
  question.md
  evidence.md   only documents named by evidence_doc_ids

The code resolves local document IDs against the available public bundle. An unknown ID therefore cannot smuggle in external evidence; it becomes the deterministic unknown_evidence_document reason.

Both _solver() calls use the same answer instructions, ANSWER_SCHEMA, Claude model, turns, timeout, and wall budget. Only the informed workspace has evidence. quality_checks() then reads the generator item and both SessionRecords. It never calls a model:

schema valid?
IDs known?
answer text absent from question?
both solver sessions healthy?
restricted answer differs from reference?
informed answer exactly matches reference?

The complete dictionary—generated item, solver outputs, accepted, and every reason—is written into LabResult.artifacts["evidence"]. The rewrite workspace contains the seed recipe and this report. The successor is lifted back into meta.Text and sent through the identical _evaluate_recipe() function.

docs.title: The seven sessions
docs.text:
One recipe evaluation uses three Claude sessions:

  1. generate a structured QA item from the frozen document bundle;
  2. ask the restricted solver with no documents;
  3. ask the informed solver with the generated item's selected documents.

The complete path is:

# Session Purpose 1 Seed generator Apply the seed recipe. 2 Seed restricted solver Test whether the question leaks or is already known. 3 Seed informed solver Test whether selected evidence supports the reference answer. 4 Recipe rewriter Generalize from the seed acceptance report. 5 Successor generator Apply the rewritten recipe. 6 Successor restricted solver Repeat the restricted check. 7 Successor informed solver Repeat the grounded check.

The local checks between sessions are deterministic and make no provider calls:

3 seed sessions + 1 rewrite + 3 successor sessions = 7 maximum

docs.title: The generated-item contract
docs.text:
The generator must return:

{
  "question": "One generated fact-seeking question",
  "reference_answer": "One exact short answer",
  "evidence_doc_ids": ["doc-03", "doc-09"]
}

The schema requires all three fields, non-empty strings, and no extra fields. Document IDs must exist in the candidate-visible bundle. They are stable local IDs—not upstream URLs or labels that reveal which source is gold.

The reference_answer here belongs to the synthetic item produced by the generator. It is not the evaluator-only answer of the frozen SealQA row.

docs.title: Deterministic quality checks
docs.text:
An item is accepted only when every check passes:

Check Rejection reason Meaning Schema structured-output failure Required fields are missing or malformed. Evidence IDs unknown_evidence_document The recipe cited a document it never received. Leakage reference_answer_leaked_in_question The question gives away its own answer. Restricted exact answer restricted_solver_already_knows_answer The item may be trivial, memorized, or leaking. Informed exact answer informed_solver_cannot_recover_answer Selected evidence does not establish the answer. Session health solver_failure At least one solver produced no rankable answer.

In compact form, the desired behavior is:

restricted answer != reference answer
informed answer    == reference answer

This is a proxy for grounded usefulness, not proof. The restricted model may guess incorrectly despite already knowing the fact, and the informed model may match for the wrong reason.

docs.title: Recipe rewriting and lineage
docs.text:
The rewriter sees:

  • the seed recipe;
  • the complete generated item;
  • both solver answers or failures;
  • the acceptance decision and rejection reasons.

It is told to generalize rather than copy the generated question or answer. Its structured output is simply:

{"recipe": "The complete successor generation recipe."}

The result retains both recipes, both generated examples, both solver pairs, both acceptance reports, evaluator identity, typed failures, and aggregate usage. That makes the causal story inspectable:

seed recipe + seed rejection evidence ──► successor recipe

docs.title: Minimal runnable mechanism
docs.text:
from sealqa_labs import ClaudeSessionRunner
from sealqa_labs.autodata import run

result = run(ClaudeSessionRunner())

print("seed recipe:", result.artifacts["seed_recipe"])
print("successor recipe:", result.artifacts.get("successor_recipe"))
print("evidence:", result.artifacts["evidence"])
print("measurements:", result.measurements)
print("usage:", result.usage)
Illustrative shape — live run, nothing captured
seed recipe: <original generation instructions>
successor recipe: <evidence-guided rewritten instructions>
evidence: <generated items, solver answers, decisions, and rejection reasons>
measurements: <seed and successor acceptance metrics or typed failures>
usage: <aggregated provider usage>

Run it with:

META_EVOLVE_LIVE_CLAUDE=1 uv run --extra claude \
  python examples/18_sealqa_research_labs/run_all.py autodata

docs.title: How to read the result
docs.text:
Compare the two acceptance reports rather than looking only at the final flag:

Seed Successor Interpretation rejected accepted The rewrite fixed the observed gate on this one attempt. rejected rejected Inspect whether the reason changed; the rewrite may still have altered behavior. accepted accepted There may have been no useful error signal for rewriting. accepted rejected The rewrite regressed the recipe. failure any The failed arm is unrankable and should not be treated as rejection.

One generated item per recipe is a mechanism demonstration. It does not estimate a stable acceptance rate, diversity, or downstream training value.

docs.title: Leakage and comparison checklist
docs.text:
• The restricted workspace contains only question.md.
  • The informed workspace adds evidence.md; model and bounds stay identical.
  • Neither solver receives the frozen row's hidden answer or URLs.
  • The generator may see public document text but no gold label.
  • The rewriter sees generated evidence, not the held-out behavior of future generated items.
  • Same-model/different-context results are not described as weak-vs-strong model evidence.

docs.title: Change and predict
docs.text:
Modify the recipe to require two independent evidence document IDs. Predict:

  1. whether unknown-document rejection becomes more common;
  2. whether the informed solver becomes more reliable;
  3. whether leakage changes at all;
  4. what a rejected successor would teach you about the recipe rather than the model.

docs.title: Meta-Harness precursor: improve a bounded local harness
docs.text:
Optional executable companion: open the canonical notebook. The notebook is not required to follow this chapter.

Pre-M8 teaching precursor

This local lab is not the M8 API. M8 remains the sole owner of HarnessArtifact, MutationSurface, portable episode suites, replay, and promotion. Update or retire this lab when M8 ships. See the M8 design capstone.

docs.title: The concrete problems
docs.text:
The diagnostic row asks:

How many NBA players have scored 60 or more points in a regular season game since 2023?

The mutator may inspect the baseline's attempt on that row. It does not see the unseen validation row, whose question asks how many current and former Real Madrid players appear in the latest Forbes top-ten highest-paid-athletes list.

The experiment asks whether changing a planner and context policy after one diagnostic failure helps on that separate validation case.

docs.title: What “harness” means here
docs.text:
The local harness is an ordinary shipped meta.SourceTree containing exactly two files:

planner.md
context_policy.json

The baseline is conceptually:

planner.md
  Answer from supplied evidence. Prefer recent documents.
  Return only the short answer.

context_policy.json
  {"max_documents": 5, "order": "given"}

planner.md controls how the solver reasons and formats its reply. context_policy.json controls how many documents enter the solver workspace. The order is fixed to given in this precursor.

This is intentionally smaller than a production harness. There are no new runtime types, portable manifests, automatic replay, or promotion records.

docs.title: From Meta-Evolve principles to this algorithm
docs.text:
This lab widens the artifact from one prompt to two coordinated files while keeping every control outside that tree:

Role Concrete component Boundary it demonstrates Mutable artifact Ordinary immutable meta.SourceTree Planner and context policy can change together Diagnostic evaluator Baseline solver plus local exact grade Produces evidence about current harness behavior Proposer Mutator session over read-only prior source/evidence Suggests file replacements but cannot apply arbitrary paths Mutation guard apply_mutation() Enforces allowlist and JSON semantics before evaluation Validation evaluator Same unseen row for baseline and candidate Measures the intended harness difference fairly Comparison compare() over two Measurements Reports improvement, tie, regression, or unrankable failure Promotion Constant False outside the candidate A better score does not deploy anything

The research algorithm is therefore only this composition:

observe baseline on development evidence
  → propose a bounded source change
  → reject changes outside authority
  → evaluate parent and successor on untouched validation
  → report comparison without promotion

Meta-Evolve already provides the versioned tree, session failures, evidence, usage, and evaluator identity. The precursor adds no coordinator behavior. Its domain code is a two-path allowlist, one JSON validator, document slicing, and an equal-arm comparison.

docs.title: How the two files affect solver execution
docs.text:
_solve() is the only function that interprets the harness. It parses context_policy.json, takes the first max_documents in fixed given order, renders them into validation.md, and uses planner.md as the solver instructions:

SourceTree.context_policy.json ──► number of visible documents
SourceTree.planner.md          ──► reasoning and answer instructions
public SolverCase             ──► validation.md
