This means a mutation has two understandable levers: change how the model is instructed, change how much evidence it receives, or change both. It cannot add a tool, swap a model, reorder documents, alter the grader, or spend more sessions because none of those controls are interpreted from the artifact.

_mutation_request() materializes prior files under prior/, diagnostic measurement/answer/trace under evidence/, and the lifecycle warning under controls/. The paths are read-only evidence in the mutator's workspace. The returned files object is not trusted as a patch until apply_mutation() checks paths, UTF-8 strings, non-identity, and policy JSON.

Only after that guard returns a new immutable tree are the two validation sessions authorized. Invalid mutation therefore cannot consume held-out evaluation or leave a partial successor.

docs.title: The four sessions
docs.text:
baseline harness ──► diagnostic attempt
       │                    │
       │                    ▼
       │            source + score + trace
       │                    │
       │                    ▼
       │              mutation session
       │                    │
       ├──────────────┐     ▼
       ▼              ▼  candidate harness
baseline validation  candidate validation
       └──────────────┬───────────────┘
                      ▼
          equal-declaration comparison
# Session Candidate-visible inputs Output 1 Baseline diagnostic Baseline harness and diagnostic public case Structured answer, trace, usage or failure 2 Harness mutator Complete prior source and diagnostic record Proposed file edits 3 Baseline validation Baseline harness and unseen public validation case Structured answer 4 Candidate validation Candidate harness and the same validation case Structured answer

The mutator's read-only workspace materializes:

  • the complete prior planner.md and context_policy.json;
  • the diagnostic exact score;
  • the baseline's candidate answer or typed failure;
  • recorded tool-trace kinds;
  • the lifecycle and authority warning.

It does not contain the validation case, evaluator answer, permission state, budget controls, audit history, or promotion decision.

docs.title: Mutation authority
docs.text:
The structured mutation shape is:

{
  "files": {
    "planner.md": "Complete replacement planner text",
    "context_policy.json": "{\"max_documents\": 10, \"order\": \"given\"}"
  }
}

The local validator applies an exact allowlist:

allowed
  planner.md
  context_policy.json

protected examples
  evaluation_data.json
  permissions.json
  budgets.json
  audit_history.jsonl
  evidence.jsonl
  promotion.json

Any path outside the two-file allowlist is a typed PolicyViolation. Protected controls are named in its evidence, and no successor SourceTree is created. Invalid UTF-8 values or malformed context-policy JSON are typed InvalidOutput. Empty or unchanged edits are typed ProposerFailure.

The policy JSON must contain a positive integer max_documents and "order": "given". This validates the candidate before any held-out provider session is spent.

docs.title: Equal validation
docs.text:
Baseline and candidate are evaluated on the same unseen row with:

  • the same pinned Claude model;
  • the same answer schema and normalized exact grader;
  • the same turn, timeout, and wall declarations;
  • the same public document order;
  • the same fixture-row checksum in evaluator identity.

The harness artifact is the intended difference. A comparison result is one of:

Result Meaning improvement Candidate exact score is higher. tie Both valid arms have the same exact score. regression Candidate exact score is lower. unrankable_typed_failure At least one arm produced no valid metric.

The result also states automatic_promotion = False. Search or comparison may identify a better local artifact; neither the candidate nor this evaluator may deploy it.

docs.title: Minimal runnable mechanism
docs.text:
from sealqa_labs import ClaudeSessionRunner
from sealqa_labs.meta_harness import run

result = run(ClaudeSessionRunner())

print("baseline:", result.artifacts["baseline"])
print("candidate:", result.artifacts.get("candidate"))
print("comparison:", result.artifacts.get("comparison"))
print("automatic promotion:", result.artifacts.get("automatic_promotion", False))
print("measurements:", result.measurements)
print("usage:", result.usage)
Illustrative shape — live run, nothing captured
baseline: <planner and context-policy SourceTree>
candidate: <allowlisted successor SourceTree or None>
comparison: <improvement, tie, regression, or unrankable typed failure>
automatic promotion: False
measurements: <equal-declaration validation measurements>
usage: <aggregated provider usage>

Run it with:

META_EVOLVE_LIVE_CLAUDE=1 uv run --extra claude \
  python examples/18_sealqa_research_labs/run_all.py meta_harness

If mutation is invalid, only two sessions are needed: the diagnostic and mutator. The baseline/candidate validation pair is skipped because there is no admissible successor to compare.

docs.title: How to interpret a result
docs.text:
An improvement means only that one diagnostic-informed mutation performed better on one unseen row. It does not establish that:

  • the planner change rather than the context-size change caused the gain;
  • the candidate generalizes to a broader repository task distribution;
  • the extra context is cost-effective;
  • the harness should be promoted;
  • the experiment can be durably replayed.

A tie can still reveal that the mutation changed cost, document visibility, or failure behavior without changing exact accuracy. A regression is valuable evidence that the diagnostic adaptation overfit or removed useful context.

docs.title: Authority and validity checklist
docs.text:
• Did the candidate change only the two permitted paths?
  • Was a forbidden-control proposal rejected without a successor?
  • Did the mutator see complete diagnostic evidence but no validation row?
  • Did both validation arms use identical declarations and document order?
  • Are failures reported by kind rather than converted to zero?
  • Is promotion still explicitly false?
  • Is this chapter still labeled a pre-M8 precursor?

docs.title: Change and predict
docs.text:
Lower max_documents from 5 to 2 without changing the planner. Before running, predict:

  1. whether the useful document remains visible;
  2. whether cost or usage should change;
  3. whether the candidate will improve, tie, regress, or fail;
  4. why even an improvement would not authorize promotion.

docs.title: EvoSkill: induce a reusable skill from recorded failures
docs.text: Optional executable companion: open the canonical notebook. This chapter is complete without it.

docs.title: The concrete problem
docs.text:
One held-out question asks:

How many airlines are members of IATA, the organization that supports airline activity and helps formulate industry policy and standards?

The skill builder never sees that row. It receives experience from two separate induction rows, then the unchanged baseline and skill-augmented agents are compared on this and one other held-out row.

The artifact being improved is a shipped meta.SkillSet: an immutable mapping from a path such as skills/sealqa.md to one inspectable Markdown document.

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
An EvoSkill-style loop turns concrete agent failures into reusable procedures:

induction case 1 ──► recorded failure ──┐
                                        ├─► failure analysis ──► Markdown skill
induction case 2 ──► recorded failure ──┘                           │
                                                                    ▼
held-out case 1 ──► baseline vs skill-augmented comparison          │
held-out case 2 ──► baseline vs skill-augmented comparison ◄────────┘

This lab separates three questions that are often blurred together:

  1. Did the baseline agent fail on induction cases?
  2. Did an analyzer actually read and generalize from those failures?
  3. Did the resulting skill help unchanged agents on held-out cases?

docs.title: From Meta-Evolve principles to this algorithm
docs.text:
EvoSkill becomes a short composition once failure collection, proposal, and held-out evaluation are kept as different components:

Role Concrete component Why it exists Episode runner _solve() using the common bounded session adapter Produces comparable answers or typed failures Evaluator Local grade_record() Keeps expected answers outside agent authority Experience Two EvidenceDraft induction records Makes prior failure observable without leaking gold answers Analyzer Pull-enabled session Chooses which prior records to inspect and generalizes patterns Proposer/builder Separate schema-constrained session Converts analysis into an inspectable skill artifact Mutable artifact Shipped immutable meta.SkillSet Versions the reusable procedure as ordinary Markdown Validation Two baseline/skill held-out pairs Tests transfer without reusing induction cases

The “algorithm” is not hidden inside one giant prompt:

run baseline episodes
  → grade externally
  → expose bounded failure evidence
  → analyze through audited experience pull
  → build a typed skill artifact
  → inject only that artifact into fresh held-out agents
  → compare each pair externally

This is simple to build because Meta-Evolve already supplies SkillSet, experience grants, derivation, session accounting, typed failure, and immutable artifacts. The lab-specific code decides what a safe failure record contains and how the Markdown is inserted into the held-out instruction block.

docs.title: How records become a skill without leaking evaluation
docs.text:
For each induction row, _solve() receives only its public case. Local grading then creates a Measurement. _failure_evidence() deliberately projects that full evaluator state into a smaller candidate-visible record:

included: case_id, prediction, exact-if-valid, failure_kind
omitted:  expected answer, URLs, gold document, held-out content

Those two records become seed_evidence in the analyzer's inner run. Because the analyzer also receives PullAccess, it must actively search/open them; the run records whether it did. ANALYSIS_SCHEMA forces separate failure_patterns and procedures, so the next step receives structured generalization rather than raw hidden evaluator state.

The builder is a new session with only analysis.json. It cannot query the induction experience or inspect held-out rows. Its validated Markdown is lifted into:

meta.SkillSet({"skills/sealqa.md": skill_markdown})

For held-out evaluation, _solve() is reused unchanged. The skill arm differs only by appending the rendered skill to BASE_INSTRUCTIONS. This makes the skill artifact—not a model, case, schema, or budget change—the intended cause of any measured difference.

docs.title: The eight sessions
docs.text:
# Session Purpose 1 Induction episode 1 Run the unchanged baseline on frozen row 5. 2 Induction episode 2 Run the unchanged baseline on frozen row 6. 3 Failure analyzer Pull both recorded failure records and propose patterns/procedures. 4 Skill builder Convert the analysis into one Markdown skill with checks. 5 Held-out 1 baseline Run unchanged instructions on frozen row 7. 6 Held-out 1 skill Run identical instructions plus the skill on row 7. 7 Held-out 2 baseline Run unchanged instructions on frozen row 8. 8 Held-out 2 skill Run identical instructions plus the skill on row 8.

There is no skill evaluation on induction rows and no skill construction from held-out rows. That isolation prevents the builder from simply encoding the answers on which the skill is judged.

docs.title: What an induction failure contains
docs.text:
Each completed induction episode is graded locally. The experience record contains:

{
  "case_id": "longseal-004",
  "prediction": "the agent's answer, if any",
  "exact": 0.0,
  "failure_kind": null
}

If the provider or adapter fails, exact is absent and failure_kind names the typed outcome. The record deliberately omits:

  • the evaluator's expected answer;
  • source or gold URLs;
  • the gold-document label;
  • held-out row contents.

This makes the failure complete as an observation of what the agent did without turning evaluator secrets into proposer-visible experience.

docs.title: Shipped experience-pull seam
docs.text:
The analyzer is not handed a manually concatenated failure report. The two failure records are committed as seed evaluation evidence in an ordinary inner run, and the analyzer receives bounded meta.PullAccess:

meta.PullAccess(
    max_operations=20,
    max_results=20,
    max_records=100,
    max_chars=32_000,
)

Claude's native experience tools can search and open those strictly prior records. The proposal must declare which experience it derived from. Pull usage is retained separately from provider token/wall usage.

That distinction yields two different null results:

skill did not help, analyzer used experience
skill did not help, analyzer never read the offered experience

The second says nothing about whether failure-driven induction helps; it says the configured agent did not exercise the mechanism.

docs.title: Analyzer and skill contracts
docs.text:
The analyzer returns:

{
  "failure_patterns": ["General pattern observed across failures"],
  "procedures": ["Reusable action an agent should take"]
}

The separate builder sees this analysis—not the held-out cases—and returns:

{
  "skill_markdown": "# Skill title\n\nProcedure...\n\n## Verification\n- Check..."
}

The emitted meta.SkillSet contains one path:

skills/sealqa.md

Keeping it as Markdown makes the learned procedure directly inspectable. The builder instruction requires explicit verification checks so the skill is more than generic advice such as “be careful.”

docs.title: Held-out comparison
docs.text:
For each held-out row, two fresh sessions receive the same public question, documents, model, answer schema, turn/timeout/wall bounds, and exact grader. Only the instruction block differs:

baseline arm
  base solver instructions

skill arm
  base solver instructions
  + rendered skills/sealqa.md

Each pair is classified independently:

Result Meaning improvement Skill exact score is higher. tie Both valid arms have the same score. regression Skill exact score is lower. unrankable_typed_failure At least one arm has no metric.

The report retains both results. It does not average a provider failure into a low score or hide a regression behind the other row's improvement.

docs.title: Minimal runnable mechanism
docs.text:
from sealqa_labs import ClaudeSessionRunner
from sealqa_labs.evoskill import run

result = run(ClaudeSessionRunner())

print("analysis:", result.artifacts.get("analysis"))
print("skill set:", result.artifacts.get("skill_set"))
print("experience usage:", result.artifacts.get("experience_usage"))
print("held-out comparisons:", result.artifacts.get("held_out_comparisons"))

Illustrative shape — live run, nothing captured
analysis: <failure patterns and procedures>
skill set: <one inspectable Markdown skill>
experience usage: <operations, records, characters, and unused evidence>
held-out comparisons: <two improvement, tie, regression, or failure labels>
measurements: <induction and held-out measurements>

Run it with:

META_EVOLVE_LIVE_CLAUDE=1 uv run --extra claude \
  python examples/18_sealqa_research_labs/run_all.py evoskill

If analysis or building fails, held-out sessions are skipped: there is no valid skill artifact to compare. Eight is the maximum complete path.

docs.title: How to interpret the result
docs.text:
Read these facts separately:

  1. Were the induction episodes valid wrong answers or typed failures?
  2. How many experience operations, records, and characters did the analyzer use?
  3. Are the reported failure patterns supported by both episodes?
  4. Does the Markdown skill contain concrete procedures and verification checks?
  5. What happened on each held-out pair—improvement, tie, regression, or failure?
  6. Did skill augmentation change provider usage as well as correctness?

Two held-out examples demonstrate the comparison mechanism; they do not support a general claim that the skill transfers across SealQA or other task families.

docs.title: Isolation and validity checklist
docs.text:
• Rows 5–6 appear only in induction and failure evidence.
  • Rows 7–8 appear only in the four held-out sessions.
  • Failure evidence omits reference answers, URLs, and split labels.
  • Analyzer and builder are separate provider sessions.
  • Pull counters show whether offered experience was actually used.
  • Baseline and skill arms otherwise share compatible declarations.
  • Ties, regressions, failures, and unused experience remain visible.

docs.title: Change and predict
docs.text:
Remove the requirement for verification checks from the skill-builder instruction. Before running, predict:

  1. whether the skill becomes shorter but less actionable;
  2. whether analyzer pull usage should change;
  3. which held-out arm is most likely to tie or regress;
  4. what evidence would distinguish a bad skill from unused experience.

docs.title: Milestone 2 tour: one loop, replaceable search¶
docs.text: Milestone 2 keeps task execution fixed while making search replaceable and results fairly comparable. M2.1 introduced replayable archive decisions, linked decision explanations, and a shared policy conformance contract. M2.2 added independent BestOfN. M2.3 added a retained Population with deterministic tournament selection. M2.4 added immutable run summaries, strict comparison, and the canonical policy benchmark.

docs.title: 1. Keep the task fixed and swap only search¶
docs.text: The seed is evaluated once. max_trials counts successor proposals, while the task budget counts all evaluations including that seed.

docs.title: 2. Compare only compatible runs¶
docs.text: Run.compare() rejects mismatched evaluator/proposer declarations, objectives, budgets, or starting artifacts. Different policies, policy configurations, and root seeds are allowed. Exact score equality is a tie; usage never breaks one.

docs.title: 3. Optional kernel inspection: decisions explain themselves¶
docs.text: The public callable path ends above. The underscore projection below is an internal diagnostic used here to show the M2 record model: every policy decision has a linked explanation; Population additionally records one ArchiveUpdate for every completed evaluation.

docs.title: 4. Rebuild the same projection from retained facts¶
docs.text: M2 replay means folding the retained in-memory event tuple and reproducing historical policy decisions. It does not yet mean process restart, persistent storage, or resume; those remain later milestones.

docs.title: Where to go next¶
docs.text: Run main.py for the concise 40-seed report, then open policy_comparison.ipynb for complete distributions and representative star/chain/tree lineages. Those results are a small deterministic illustration in the locked project environment, not broad scientific evidence or a cross-version CPython guarantee. Local callable equality is declaration-based (module:qualname) and does not prove behavioral equivalence.

docs.title: Fair comparison of three search policies¶
docs.text: This canonical Milestone 2 sweep compares BestOfN, Greedy, and Population on the same target 12, moves (-2, 1, 5), initial artifact 0, primary score -abs(value - 12), nine-evaluation/eight-trial budget, and root seeds 0 through 39. Population has size 3 and tournament size 2.

docs.title: What the lineages mean¶
docs.text: BestOfN always expands zero, so [0, 5] is one spoke from a star. Its result is also a proof: independent one-step successors are limited to {-2, 1, 5}, making 5 and score -7 the best possible. Greedy's representative is the accepted chain [0, 5, 10, 11, 12]. Population creates a tree through tournament expansion and retention; [0, 5, 10, 11, 12] is the winning branch of that larger tree.

docs.title: Evidence boundary¶
docs.text: This is a small deterministic illustration in the locked project environment, not broad scientific evidence and not a cross-version CPython guarantee. The user proposer continues to use random.Random.choice through context.rng, matching the existing accepted example contract. Local callable comparison uses module:qualname declaration identity; it does not prove behavioral equivalence.

docs.title: Derivation, replay, and fair memory comparison¶
docs.text: This lab focuses on the M3.4 distinction between experience observed and experience declared as causal. It then checks that derivation survives replay and that runs with different memory strategies remain comparable.

docs.title: 1. See where reuse changes the outcome¶
docs.text: All variants spend the same task budget. Only the three memory-aware runs can turn the two failed evaluations into the successful value 10.

docs.title: 2. Inspect exact committed derivation¶
docs.text: A failed evaluation may still carry useful derivation. The second ordinary proposal cites one failure; the third cites two failures and, for pull variants, the compared trial occurrences.

docs.title: 3. Replay the same edge graph¶
docs.text: Replay validates the event stream and rebuilds derivation from durable proposals. It does not call the live context selector, reader, filtering code, or renderer.

docs.title: 4. See the serialization compatibility rule¶
docs.text: Empty derivation is omitted, so old proposal and event bytes remain unchanged. Non-empty derivation is encoded normally. An explicitly encoded empty default is rejected as non-canonical.

docs.title: 5. Compare different memory strategies fairly¶
docs.text: Memory declarations may differ. Compatibility still requires equal evaluator, proposer, objective, task/run budgets, artifact declaration, and initial digest. The comparison reports memory-declaration equality rather than rejecting the pair.

docs.title: Takeaway¶
docs.text: M3.4 does not claim that every observed record caused a result. It preserves the proposer's explicit usage intent while the coordinator independently enforces visibility, ordering, budgets, failure semantics, and evaluation authority.

docs.title: Milestone 3 tour: experience that remains causal¶
docs.text:
Milestone 3 makes earlier work useful to later proposers without turning memory into ambient authority. This tour follows the four slices in order: M3.1 temporal graph, M3.2 pushed context, M3.3 audited pull access, and M3.4 declared derivation and comparison.

The deterministic experiment deliberately produces two failed evaluations. Memory-aware variants can then reuse those failures to reach 10; the no-memory variant cannot.

docs.title: 1. Run the same experiment four ways¶
docs.text: Task, seed, proposer, evaluator, chain search, random seed, and task/run budgets stay fixed. Only the memory declaration changes.

docs.title: 2. M3.1 — the temporal experience graph¶
docs.text: The graph is a read model over committed trials and records. Nodes are causal occurrences, not deduplicated payloads. An as_of boundary can reveal the past without leaking future trials.

docs.title: 3. M3.2 — policy-pushed context¶
docs.text: A context policy chooses a bounded, exact bundle before the proposer runs. The bundle stores structured records, a canonical rendering, a reason, truncation, and usage. It is replayed rather than selected again.

docs.title: 4. M3.3 — agent-directed pull access¶
docs.text: The reader lets a proposer search, open, traverse, and compare within a strictly-prior grant. Every attempt is charged and resolves to success, opaque denial, or content-free exhaustion. Usage is cumulative inside each grant.

docs.title: 5. M3.4 — declare what actually caused the proposal¶
docs.text: Observation and use are distinct. derived_from must be a unique ordered subsequence of the committed push-then-pull ledger. Valid edges survive failed evaluations and typed proposer failures; unauthorized declarations become policy failures.

docs.title: What to keep in your head¶
docs.text:
• Graph: what committed experience existed at a logical time.
  • Push: what a policy placed in front of the proposer.
  • Pull: what the proposer chose to inspect through a bounded capability.
  • Derivation: which observed references the proposer says it actually used.
  • Evaluation: still independent of proposer authority.

The example is a small deterministic illustration, not broad scientific evidence. Its purpose is to make the authority and replay contracts tangible.

docs.title: Push and pull lab: two routes to the same experience¶
docs.text:
Push and pull share committed records but express different decisions. Push records a policy's selection before execution. Pull records the proposer's own bounded investigation during execution.

This lab inspects both channels and then reconstructs the canonical observation ledger used by M3.4.

docs.title: 1. Inspect pushed bundles¶
docs.text: The demo's FailedAncestors policy pushes only failed ancestor evaluations. Notice how the number of selected failures grows as the chain advances.

docs.title: 2. Inspect pull grants and operations¶
docs.text: Each successor gets a new grant with as_of = logical_step - 1. The final proposer searches two failed evaluations, opens both, and compares their trials.

docs.title: 3. Reconstruct the push-then-pull ledger¶
docs.text: The ledger is ordered by committed observation: bundle references first, then successful pull results in operation order. References and structured record references are deduplicated by first occurrence.

docs.title: 4. Compare channel-specific usage¶
docs.text: Memory access is measured but does not consume task or run budgets. Context usage counts selected records and rendered characters. Pull usage additionally counts attempts and returned references.

docs.title: Try next¶
docs.text: Change FailedAncestors to push only one failure, lower PullAccess.max_operations, or remove the comparison call. Predict the changed ledger and usage before rerunning. The interesting question is not merely whether memory helps, but which access decision helped at what cost.

def propose(parent: object, context: object) -> object:
    """Climb toward the target by one each step. Deterministic and retry-safe:
    the same parent always yields the same child, so replaying it during
    recovery reproduces the identical candidate.

    ``context`` is deliberately ignored: this is a fixed +1 climb with no
    randomness. (Sibling example 01 instead draws from ``context.rng`` -- that
    is where the per-step context earns its keep.)"""

    return parent + 1

def evaluate(candidate: object) -> float:
    """Higher is better; the search maximizes this score. Closer to the target
    scores higher, and the target itself is the ceiling."""

    return -abs(float(candidate) - TARGET)

    """Register the example callables and retain their typed references."""

    two different durable paths produces runs with the SAME id."""

        storage=storage,
        mode="durable-local",

class CrashAfter:
    """Commit-strategy wrapper: perform the first ``n`` commits for real, then
    raise ``SimulatedCrash`` on the next one. Never touches what was committed."""

    def __init__(self, inner: object, *, n: int) -> None:
        self._inner = inner
        self._n = n
        self.commits = 0

    def commit(
        self,
        run_id: RunId,
        expected_version: int,
        *,
        events: Iterable[EventEnvelope],
        occurrences: Iterable[Artifact],
    ) -> int:
        if self.commits >= self._n:
            raise SimulatedCrash(f"simulated process crash after {self._n} committed steps")
        version = self._inner.commit(
            run_id, expected_version, events=events, occurrences=occurrences
        )
        self.commits += 1
        return version

What this proves. The crash left a genuine partial durable stream; resume replayed the committed prefix, found the recovery frontier, re-drove the deterministic search from exactly there, and reached the identical best() — with a byte-identical final event stream. That is the M4 durable-runs guarantee.

The same guarantee holds for runs that use M3 policy-pushed context and pull experience (see tests/test_resume_context.py / tests/test_resume_experience_faults.py).

docs.title: Crash recovery for durable runs (meta.resume)¶
docs.text:
The central promise of a durable Meta-Evolve run: a process that dies partway through loses no committed work, and once resume-d reaches the exact result an uninterrupted run would have reached.

Interrupted is logically equivalent to uninterrupted.

This notebook walks the lifecycle end to end:

  1. Run a durable-local run to completion, uninterrupted, on path A — its best() is the reference.
  2. Start the same run on path B, but simulate a process crash after a few committed batches.
  3. Reopen path B and resume the run.
  4. Assert the resumed best() equals the uninterrupted reference.

Key concepts: atomic batch commits (a crash leaves only whole batches, never a half-written one), the recovery frontier (resume replays the committed prefix and continues deterministically from the last decided step), and deterministic run identity (the run id is derived from the inputs, so the run on path B shares path A's id and resume can address it).

docs.title: Components — imported from the example module¶
docs.text: durable-local mode requires registered, source-digestible, module-level functions so resume can verify the components it replays are byte-for-byte the ones recorded. Functions defined inside a notebook cell have no resolvable source file, so durable-local would reject them (CapabilityError). We therefore import the real components from examples/04_crash_recovery/main.py (an importable module) and show their source below — the notebook orchestrates the lifecycle with the example's own building blocks.

docs.title: Simulating a crash — you never write this¶
docs.text:
A real crash (power loss, kill -9, OOM) needs no code; the OS/hardware supplies it. CrashAfter exists only so a deterministic notebook can stand in for one — in production you never author it or touch storage._commit_strategy.

A faithful crash never truncates the append-only store: it just stops committing after some whole batch n, so the n committed batches on disk are exactly what an uninterrupted run would have written, with no partial batch.

docs.title: (1) Uninterrupted reference run on path A¶
docs.text: A counting wrapper with an unreachable threshold rides along to tally path A's own committed batches.

docs.title: (2) Start the same run on path B — then crash mid-way¶
docs.text: The run id matches path A's by construction, so we can resume it by id.

docs.title: (3) Reopen path B and resume(run_id, ...)¶
docs.text: No crash wrapper this time — a fresh durable handle on the same path, exactly as a restarted process would.

docs.title: Advanced examples¶
docs.text: The basic lifecycle resumed from a single mid-run crash. These show the guarantee is total — resume works from every committed boundary — and extends to M3 policy-pushed context and pull experience. All components come from main.py / advanced.py (importable + source-digestible, as durable-local requires).

docs.title: A. Fault matrix — resume from every committed boundary¶
docs.text: Crash after each batch K in turn; each resume reaches the identical best() and a byte-identical final stream.

docs.title: B. The recovery frontier¶
docs.text: resume classifies where the crash left the run (via classify_frontier) before continuing deterministically. The phases seen across boundaries:

docs.title: C. Cold rebuild from empty tables¶
docs.text: A fresh process reopens the durable store; the read model is rebuilt purely from the committed event log — no in-memory state carried over.

docs.title: D. Resumable with M3 policy-pushed context (AncestorsOnly)¶
docs.text: The run records a context-policy manifest, its declaration, and each per-trial selection. resume rebuilds the context policy from the registry and reuses the committed selections — equivalent at every boundary.

docs.title: E. Resumable with M3 pull experience (PullAccess)¶
docs.text: Here the proposer reads experience each step, audited as an attempt then a resolution (two atomic batches). A crash between them leaves a trailing unresolved attempt; resume rolls it forward — recomputing the resolution and reusing the committed operation id — to a byte-identical stream.

docs.title: F. Resume is safe to re-run¶
docs.text: Resuming an already-complete run is a no-op returning the same result. (Two processes racing to resume one crashed run is also safe: exactly one commits and the other gets EventStreamConflict — never a double-commit or partial write. See tests/test_resume_faults.py.)

docs.title: Milestone 5 tour: immutable source, external evidence¶
docs.text: This tour follows the canonical clamp repair in six small steps. The declaration path stays at source, patch, evaluator, budget, and search vocabulary. Returned lineage entries provide optional inspection after the run.

docs.title: 1. Load immutable source¶
docs.text: The source tree contains exact UTF-8 text. The tour stages only the declared tracked candidate/clamp.py bytes into its temporary evidence directory before loading. This isolates the tour from checkout-generated __pycache__ without adding ignore rules: production load_source_tree still rejects every undeclared file.

docs.title: 2. Declare the exact-file repair¶
docs.text: The patch names one file, commits the parent text it expects, and supplies its replacement. A conflict, invalid path, or unchanged replacement is a typed proposal outcome.

docs.title: 3. Declare the independent evaluator¶
docs.text: The grader remains outside the candidate tree, and the fixed run_grader.py owns the exit protocol: exit 0 passes, exit 1 is a rankable task failure, and any other exit is a typed evaluator failure.

docs.title: 4. Declare one budget¶
docs.text: Two evaluations cover the broken seed and one successor. The same budget is passed to the task and run.

docs.title: 5. Run one local Greedy step¶
docs.text: Proposal and evaluation each receive a fresh workspace. Durable storage retains the committed history, while the live local callbacks remain non-portable.

docs.title: 6. Inspect the result and durable boundary¶
docs.text: The public lineage query is progressive disclosure: it returns immutable lineage entries for inspection without putting kernel construction types into the declaration story. Content digests and semantic outcomes are deterministic; observed process wall time is intentionally omitted.

docs.title: Failure boundary: a broken grader is not a low score¶
docs.text: Candidate-caused breakage remains the rankable score 0 seen above. This separate probe removes the grader itself: runner exit 2 becomes EvaluatorFailure, with no metric to rank.

docs.title: Feedback Descent lab
docs.text:
Terminology. A candidate is a meta.Text solver prompt. A pairwise evaluator chooses between two answers and emits textual feedback; an editor derives one successor prompt from that evidence. This is a small teaching implementation inspired by Feedback Descent, not a reproduction of its results or an official SealQA evaluation.

docs.title: Autoresearch, in miniature¶
docs.text: Can an outer Meta-Evolve run improve the recipe used by an inner researcher while private tasks, budgets, and promotion remain outside candidate authority? This notebook executes the deterministic teaching example. The standalone chapter contains the complete explanation.

docs.title: Run the outer loop¶
docs.text: The seed and two successors each receive the same four inner benchmark tasks and the same five-evaluation inner budget. Public task scores are evidence; private quality is the selection metric.

docs.title: Read the evidence boundary¶
docs.text: The proposer derives each edit from a public-report evidence record. Private task details never enter that evidence. Held-out scores are calculated only after result.best() has fixed the selected recipe, and promotion=none is explicit.

docs.title: Change and predict¶
docs.text: Reduce INNER_TRIALS from four to two and update INNER_BUDGET. Predict the selected recipe first. If it changes, did the researcher become worse, or did the evaluation choose a different researcher for a different resource regime?
